note: Rows of every page's 'Fitting the design to a situation' table, keyed by the evidence-dimensions.json tags in their first cell. Generated by scripts/build_situation_index.py; do not edit.

facts.ask: given a simplified version of the task, can they do each part on its own?
facts.fact: How much of the domain learners already have
facts.why: An open-ended realistic task asks novices to coordinate parts they have not practised; unguided discovery learned less than explicit instruction.

facts.ask: what happens to the learner if the score is wrong by one level?
facts.fact: What the result decides
facts.why: A formative task can tolerate inconsistent scoring and invite risk; a grade, progression or licensure decision needs calibrated assessors, a defensible threshold and more than one task.

facts.ask: what does a practitioner do with this, and can it be shown without doing it?
facts.fact: Whether the outcome is a performance or a body of knowledge
facts.why: Authentic tasks fit capabilities that are performances (`complex-skill`, `procedure` in context); for well-defined facts or procedures a conventional test may be more efficient and reliable.

facts.ask: have they completed a self-paced or online course before, and what happened to their study when no one was checking?
facts.fact: How well the learners study without a teacher
facts.why: The online part shifts pacing, attendance and persistence onto learners, and what it needs in support depends on that.

facts.ask: in the final task, what does the learner do that a teacher must watch or respond to live?
facts.fact: Which parts of the goal need someone present
facts.why: Practice that needs a teacher's observation, a partner, equipment or a safe space decides what must stay in person; the rest can move.

facts.ask: compared with the current course, will learners get more practice, more feedback or more time, or only a different delivery?
facts.fact: What the blend replaces and what else changes with it
facts.why: The only recorded gain for blends comes with extra time and resources, so the design should say what it adds.

facts.ask: given one strong and one weak example, can they say which is stronger and why, without help?
facts.fact: Whether learners know the domain well enough to see quality
facts.why: Learners with weaker command of material judge their own performance least accurately, and accuracy rises with familiarity and domain specificity.

facts.ask: who has judged these objects already, and would informed judges agree?
facts.fact: Whether there is a defensible reference judgment
facts.why: Without one, the group can only agree with itself, and the step that corrects shared misjudgments disappears.

facts.ask: will any learner's mark depend on a peer's or a group's rating?
facts.fact: What the judgments are for: learning, or a grade
facts.why: Peer assessment's effects are on learning when it is used formatively; rubric use has come with more stress and a performance-avoidance orientation.

facts.ask: given one instance, can they name its parts and say which features might matter?
facts.fact: Whether learners can already read the instances and the domain they come from
facts.why: Induction needs learners who can see the candidate attributes; unsupported discovery learned less than explicit instruction.

facts.ask: are the examples pictures, symbols or sentences, and which concept is it most often confused with?
facts.fact: What kind of material the instances are
facts.why: Interleaving labelled exemplars of confusable categories helped for paintings, photographs and mathematical tasks, and reversed for word-based categories.

facts.ask: will learners be asked to recognise instances, or to carry out a procedure?
facts.fact: Whether the target is a concept or a rule to apply
facts.why: Concepts are where induction is argued to fit; for a rule or procedure, a rule-then-examples order is the older recommendation.

facts.ask: what do learners predict about one familiar case, and why?
facts.fact: What learners already think about the idea, and whether it is wrong
facts.why: A coherent wrong idea is not removed by a clear explanation alone, and a learner who already explains the idea needs little of steps 2–3.

facts.ask: can they explain one case of this idea now, unaided?
facts.fact: The learner's task-specific expertise
facts.why: For a `novice`, explaining the idea and guiding its use beats leaving them to discover it; for an `advanced` learner, the same worked cases and prompts can become redundant.

facts.ask: during guided cases, who reads a learner's explanation before the next case, and how soon?
facts.fact: Whether anyone can read learners' explanations during the lesson
facts.why: The explanation prompts and contingent help depend on someone or something responding to what learners write; most contingent-support evidence is one-to-one.

facts.ask: can they sketch how the main ideas relate and place a detail, unaided, before instruction?
facts.fact: Whether learners already hold an organisation for this content
facts.why: A learner without one needs the epitome and explicit syntheses; a learner who has one needs a quick check and the level they lack.

facts.ask: what will they be asked to do with this content, explain and solve, or recall specific details?
facts.fact: Which tasks they will face
facts.why: The organisation helped the tasks that matched the ideas at its top and showed no detected benefit on tasks resting on single details.

facts.ask: can one idea be understood without the others?
facts.fact: How much the ideas interact, against the learner's prior knowledge
facts.why: If the epitome's ideas must be held together and the learner knows none of them, an overview first may not be followable.

facts.ask: have the learners ever made this kind of decision for real, and how would a practitioner rate their first attempt?
facts.fact: Whether learners are new to the practice or already in it
facts.why: Novices need modelled decisions, frequent in-fiction feedback and a gradual hand-over; practitioners need atypical cases that break their framing.

facts.ask: who are the practitioners we can interview or watch, and what decisions do they say are hard?
facts.fact: Whether anyone has studied how the practice reasons
facts.why: Without an epistemography the game rehearses a textbook's idea of the job.

facts.ask: after the unit, what case will learners be given, and who will judge their answer against what?
facts.fact: What the outcome is and how it will be judged outside the game
facts.why: Decisions justified in the practice's terms, content knowledge, transfer and identity are different targets and need different measures; a log of play is hard to score reliably.

facts.ask: after the experience, can a learner say in one sentence what it showed?
facts.fact: Whether learners can already make sense of the experience or text
facts.why: The routine adds questions; it does not supply content. Activating what learners already know did not by itself improve comprehension.

facts.ask: what idea should the answers reach, and who or what will compare them with it?
facts.fact: Whether the "what have you learned" prompt can be made content-specific, and who checks it
facts.why: Specific prompts beat generic ones, and guided reflection was analytic more often than free reflection; an unchecked answer can harden an error.

facts.ask: will anyone read the answers, how soon, and are learners in one room, remote, or on phones?
facts.fact: How much facilitator time there is, and in what mode answers come
facts.why: The routine is cheap to run but expensive to read.

patterns/experience-with-languaging-acti.title: Experience with Languaging Activities (ELAs) guided by a sequence of experience-based questions

facts.ask: have they done or seen a task like this before, and can they say what they would watch for?
facts.fact: What learners already know about the task the experience is meant to teach
facts.why: A `novice` cannot tell which parts of an experience matter, so an unguided first loop is mostly noise; an experienced practitioner can interpret more of it unaided.

facts.ask: what will the learner do differently afterwards, and how would we see it?
facts.fact: The kind of goal
facts.why: A `procedure` gains from repeated attempts to a standard with feedback; a `concept` from manipulation linked to its formal representation; a judgement or `attitude-motivation` goal has only self-reported evidence here.

facts.ask: who is with the learner straight afterwards, for how long, and can the task be tried again in a changed form?
facts.fact: Who can debrief and whether there is a second attempt
facts.why: The steps that rest on claims (specific prompts, practice with feedback) both need someone or something to structure them; an experience with no debrief and no retry is not this pattern.

facts.ask: can these learners read the sources, and do they know enough of the domain to tell a good explanation from a wrong one?
facts.fact: Whether learners can learn a subtopic from the sources well enough to teach it
facts.why: The pattern assumes each expert can research their part; unguided discovery of essential content learns less than explicit instruction, and a tutor with gaps may pass on errors.

facts.ask: how many weeks, and how many sessions a week?
facts.fact: Whether there is time for more than one cycle
facts.why: The handover from teacher to learners, and the reading routine, need several sessions to take hold.

facts.ask: what will each learner be tested on, and will anyone outside the class use the product?
facts.fact: What the assessment will weigh
facts.why: Individual understanding of every part, the group's product, or strategy use each lead to different checks and recognition.

facts.ask: before the project, can learners explain the core idea in a few sentences?
facts.fact: Whether learners already know the content the product must carry
facts.why: A product built while the content is still being discovered by novices leaves them learning the content and the tools at once, and unassisted discovery learned less than explicit instruction.

facts.ask: what will the assessment weigh, and is the product scored for content apart from its polish?
facts.fact: Whether the target is the content or the media skill
facts.why: If media literacy is the objective, production time is the learning; if the content is, production time is overhead to be kept short.

facts.ask: how many teams per facilitator, how many minutes per team per session, and how many devices per team?
facts.fact: How much facilitator time and equipment there is per team
facts.why: The content checks on the blueprint and the individual checks are where the evidence-backed parts of the sequence live, and they need someone's time.

patterns/learning-by-producing-pattern.title: Learning by Producing (multimedia production as learning)

facts.ask: how many learners per teaching person, and how many hours a week does that person have for this course?
facts.fact: How much of a teacher's time there is per learner
facts.why: The weekly cycle above assumes a teacher who answers in 48–72 hours and posts in each group every week; at large enrolments without assistants that is not possible, and the design has to move feedback onto answers, peers and summaries.

facts.ask: can every learner attend a 30-minute call at one time in the week, and on what device?
facts.fact: Whether learners can meet live at all
facts.why: Synchronous contact is where correction and the first-week contact are cheapest; some cohorts (shift workers, several time zones, phone-only) cannot meet.

facts.ask: who are they, what are they studying for, and what else is competing for their time?
facts.fact: Who the learners are and why they enrolled
facts.why: Adults studying around work are most at risk in the first week and least able to follow a fixed weekly time; school-age learners need more structure and contact with an adult.

facts.ask: what will an observer see in a lesson when the practice is in place?
facts.fact: How specific and observable the target practice is
facts.why: Coaching studies that targeted fidelity of a specific academic task met more quality indicators and showed more sustained outcomes than those targeting general teacher behaviors, and knowing a framework did not make teachers able to design lessons with it.

facts.ask: how many hours of a coach's or facilitator's time per teacher per month, for how many months, and is there release time?
facts.fact: How much coach or facilitator time each teacher gets, and over what span
facts.why: Short, fragmented training is reported as hindering change, and the one recorded long program gave hundreds of hours; most real PD is a few hours.

facts.ask: what does one of their lessons look like now, and how confident are they in the subject the practice serves?
facts.fact: Each teacher's content familiarity and current enactment of the practice, not years of experience

facts.ask: will the learners' own teacher teach and cue this every week, and for how long?
facts.fact: Who will deliver it, and how often
facts.why: The syntheses found skill and academic effects for programmes run by learners' own teachers and not, or not significantly, for programmes run by outside personnel or as multicomponent programmes, and implementation problems lowered effects.

facts.ask: what result would count as success, and how will it be measured?
facts.fact: Which outcome the brief is buying
facts.why: Social and emotional skills moved most; conduct, distress and attitudes less; academic achievement least, and in rigorous recent trials by a negligible amount.

facts.ask: how old are the learners, and will they see this as theirs or as something done to them?
facts.fact: Age or stage, and whether the learners chose to be there
facts.why: The evidence is from school children and adolescents (and one synthesis of ages 2–6); nothing here tests adults.

facts.ask: given one strong and one weak draft, can learners say which is stronger and point to why, without help?
facts.fact: Whether reviewers can see quality in this kind of draft
facts.why: Rater training was the strongest moderator of peer assessment's effect, and rubric guidance helped most on subjective, complex criteria; but stronger secondary-school writers found real problems no more often than weaker ones, only commented more helpfully.

facts.ask: how many days lie between the draft deadline and the final deadline, and will the final version be scored?
facts.fact: Whether the author can still revise before the work is judged
facts.why: The tested comparisons are of feedback on work that was then improved or retested; comments on finished work have nowhere to go.

facts.ask: what does a serious error in this draft look like, and could a classmate spot it?
facts.fact: Whether quality turns on correctness or on judgment
facts.why: Where it turns on technical or factual correctness, peers can be confidently wrong; where it turns on structure, clarity and audience fit, peer comments are where the writing evidence lies.

facts.ask: can the learner attempt one representative task now, and say where it went wrong?
facts.fact: What the learner can already do and say about the task
facts.why: A learner who cannot yet attempt the task needs a model before a consultation is useful; one who can already diagnose their own errors needs critique, not explanation.

facts.ask: how many learners per expert, how many minutes each, how often, and live or written?
facts.fact: How much of the expert's time each learner gets, and in what form
facts.why: The evidence for contingent help is one-to-one; a guest visit, a drop-in office hour and a weekly mentor meeting allow very different designs.

facts.ask: who is the expert, have they taught or mentored before, and will someone brief them?
facts.fact: What the expert is expected to do
facts.why: A practitioner with no teaching experience tends to tell; the design may need to brief them to ask first and to think aloud.

facts.ask: can they solve or explain a routine case of this, unaided, today?
facts.fact: Prior knowledge of this relation
facts.why: Novices need an explanation or example before generating; learners who already hold the relation can be asked to compare or justify at once.

facts.ask: what should a learner be able to do with this on a case they have not seen?
facts.fact: The kind of goal
facts.why: Activation is aimed at concepts, principles and flexible use of procedures; for facts or vocabulary, retrieval with feedback is the more direct move.

facts.ask: when, and on what task, will anyone check whether this was learned?
facts.fact: The outcome and horizon that count
facts.why: The evidence is strongest for immediate tests; if the brief cares about a delayed exam or use at work, plan the probe and the delay explicitly.

facts.ask: can they complete a standard case of this kind unaided, and what do they do with a case where the usual rule does not fit?
facts.fact: How rigid or how thin the learner's current knowledge is
facts.why: A learner who has nothing to be rigid about needs a first, simple version (step 2); a learner applying a rule mechanically needs varied cases (step 3).

facts.ask: do experts in this field disagree about cases, or apply the same rule differently in different settings?
facts.fact: Whether the domain really varies across situations
facts.why: In a well-structured procedure with one right method, varied cases add load for little gain (the theory and the earlier page both say so; no claim here tests it).

facts.ask: what will the learner be judged on, a new case, or what they remember?
facts.fact: What the assessment rewards
facts.why: The one direct test found a trade-off: better transfer, worse factual recall. If the stakes sit on recall, the design must protect recall separately.

facts.ask: what will be decided from this result, by whom, and how soon?
facts.fact: What decision the result will inform, and who acts on it
facts.why: A teacher choosing what to teach next needs a skill-level criterion-referenced report; an admissions panel with limited places needs relative standing plus second evidence; a referral team needs a diagnostic profile.

facts.ask: who owns the test, and can you see its technical manual (norm group, standard error, how the cut was set)?
facts.fact: Whether you can change the test, or only how its scores are read
facts.why: A teacher writing their own checks can define skills and set the cut; a user of a state, national or commercial test can change only what is combined with the score and how near-cut learners are handled.

facts.ask: what are the learners' ages, language backgrounds and prior schooling, and what curriculum or job tasks define the skills?
facts.fact: Who the learners are relative to the norm group and the defined skills
facts.why: A percentile is only as meaningful as the norm group is like the learner; a criterion-referenced check is only as useful as its skills match what this learner is being taught.

facts.fact: What experience learners actually have with this content, and how the designer knows it
facts.why: A connection chosen from what learners told you is a different design from one chosen from an assumption about their group. If the brief does not say, ask: where do these learners meet this content outside the course, and has anyone asked them?

facts.fact: The kind of goal and how it will be assessed
facts.why: A critical or attitudinal goal can be built on personal experience for weeks; a procedure assessed on a standard test needs the connection to stay short and the practice to stay. If the brief does not say, ask: what must the learner be able to do, in which context, and does the assessment accept performance in familiar contexts?

facts.fact: How safe it is to share personal experience in this group
facts.why: Mixed groups, grades, a new teacher, power differences or recent hostility change what learners will offer. If the brief does not say, ask: who will hear what a learner shares, and what happens to it?

facts.ask: what have learners or families said about how questions, help and turn-taking work for them, and what does your own audit show about who answers and who is corrected?
facts.fact: Which norms differ, and for whom, as learners and families describe them
facts.why: A teacher's guess from a learner's group is the error to avoid; differences also run along class, religion, region and schooling history, not only ethnicity.

facts.ask: in one recorded lesson, how long is the pause after a question, how many questions go to one named learner in public, and how is lateness or calling out handled?
facts.fact: What the classroom's own norms are, measured
facts.why: Wait time, the share of public test questions, the competitive structure of grading and the management repertoire are what can be changed.

facts.ask: does the learner engage in some settings (a club, one subject, one adult) and not others, and do they say school is not for people like them?
facts.fact: Whether the issue is an unfamiliar convention or alienation from schooling
facts.why: The first is met by explicit teaching and wider options; the second is not.

facts.ask: have they done this task before, and can they say, before the debrief, which decision mattered most and whether they got it right?
facts.fact: The learners' expertise on this task and whether they can judge their own performance
facts.why: Novices miss the cues that matter and misjudge their own performance; the facilitator must lead, focus on process and supply the criterion. Advanced learners can run the debrief.

facts.ask: who is with the learners straight after, how long do they have, and how many learners per leader?
facts.fact: Who will lead the debrief, for how long, and for how many learners
facts.why: The claims behind the default rest on someone who can ask specific questions, respond to answers and give task-level feedback; a facilitator with five minutes for thirty learners, a volunteer, or no one at all changes the design.

facts.ask: when will learners next do something like this, and what observable change would show the debrief worked?
facts.fact: Whether a next attempt follows, and what counts as success
facts.why: The debrief is expected to pay off through a changed next performance.

facts.ask: what does a good attempt look like, who can say whether this attempt meets it, and how soon?
facts.fact: Whether the performance can be judged against a standard, and how fast
facts.why: Deliberate practice is easiest to design where each attempt can be scored at once (a clinical procedure on a simulator, a musical passage, a maths step) and hardest where quality is diffuse and feedback slow (an essay's argument, teaching, management).

facts.ask: can they do the whole task once now, unaided, and which part goes wrong most often?
facts.fact: Where the learner is on the whole task
facts.why: A learner who cannot yet do the task unaided needs a model and guided practice, and isolating components early can overload them; one who performs but has plateaued is the case this page is for.

facts.ask: who will look at each attempt, and what does the learner want from getting better at this?
facts.fact: Who supplies the feedback and the effort
facts.why: The evidence pools designs with a coach or simulator judging every attempt; with one teacher and thirty learners, or none, the judging moves to rubrics, peers or software, and the learner's willingness to keep at effortful practice becomes the limit.

facts.ask: what does this educator decide about learners that you would like decided differently, and how would you see it?
facts.fact: Which decision the awareness must change
facts.why: Discipline and referrals, who speaks and is praised, materials and examples, grading and expectations, and relations with families call for different evidence and different changes.

facts.ask: can a colleague observe one lesson, is there participation or referral data, and can learners give anonymous feedback?
facts.fact: What outside evidence about the educator's own practice exists or can be collected
facts.why: Without it the cycle runs on self-report, which is the weakest part of the design.

facts.ask: how many sessions over how long, and did these educators choose to come?
facts.fact: Time and voluntariness
facts.why: One mandated workshop, a staff meeting a month, and a chosen year-long group are different starting points; defensiveness is likelier when attendance is mandated and the topic arrives as an accusation.

facts.fact: What the digital tool will do that cannot be done otherwise
facts.why: More practice with feedback, adaptive selection, replay, or reach to learners who cannot attend all justify it. "Engagement" or "modernising" do not. If the brief omits it, ask: which activity gets more attempts, more feedback or more access because it is on a screen, and how many more?

facts.fact: Whether a person is in the loop, and how quickly
facts.why: Fully self-paced work with no human contact loses learners early and puts the whole burden of pacing on them. If the brief omits it, ask: who will see a learner's work or absence in the first week, and how soon will they respond?

facts.fact: The learners' access and their starting response on the task
facts.why: Devices, bandwidth and accessibility needs decide what can be required. Prior knowledge decides how much guidance the software should give. If the brief omits it, ask: can every learner reach the platform on the device they have, and can they do one item of the target kind unaided now?

facts.ask: what is the one relation (where, what causes what, in what order, which is part of which) a learner must grasp, and can it be drawn?
facts.fact: Whether the content has a visual structure
facts.why: A diagram helps where it shows a relation the words describe; for list-like or purely verbal content it adds load and no meaning.

facts.ask: can these learners, before instruction, sketch or explain the structure unaided?
facts.fact: The learner's prior knowledge of this content
facts.why: A supplied visual is a support for a learner who cannot build the model alone; for one who can, it may add nothing.

facts.ask: how many minutes per idea are there, and who will compare a learner's drawing with a correct one?
facts.fact: Time, and who checks learner-made visuals
facts.why: Drawing and mapping are slow, and a wrong diagram studied as right does harm.

facts.ask: how many learners are involved, how often, and has anyone been hurt?
facts.fact: Whether the problem is the group or one learner, and how serious it is
facts.why: Group-wide low-level disruption is what a classroom plan addresses; one learner's recurring behavior needs an individual assessment; dangerous behavior needs a safety plan first.

facts.ask: how old are they, how often do they meet this teacher, and in what setting?
facts.fact: Who the learners are and where they meet
facts.why: Age, whether they meet one teacher or many in a day, and whether they are in a room, online or both change what a routine, a greeting and a redirection look like.

facts.ask: is there a school or programme policy or routine already in place, and how much time is there to set the plan up?
facts.fact: What the plan has to fit into
facts.why: A school behavior policy, an existing points system or rubric, a fixed number of sessions, or a few minutes of adult time each set limits a plan must work within.

facts.ask: what does the learner do when the task starts, and what do they say when asked why they stopped?
facts.fact: Why participation is low, for this learner, on this task
facts.why: No visible reason, doubt about success, a weak relationship, an attention difficulty, or a task that is too hard each call for a different move; raising interest does nothing for a learner who believes they cannot succeed.

facts.ask: if engagement rose and test scores did not change, would the design have succeeded?
facts.fact: Which outcome counts
facts.why: On-task time, interest, completion, voluntary return and learning of the target are separate outcomes and can move in opposite directions.

facts.ask: during work time, what can anyone see of each learner's activity, and how soon can they respond?
facts.fact: Who can see participation, and how often
facts.why: A teacher at the door, a teacher with thirty learners, and an unattended platform can each observe different signals.

facts.ask: what will the learner have in front of them when they have to decide what to believe, and what decision follows?
facts.fact: Which kind of evidence the learner must judge
facts.why: Gains have been recorded only for the standard taught, so a design for web sources and a design for research studies are different designs.

facts.ask: how many sessions, and is there a later point where the learner judges new material?
facts.fact: Time available
facts.why: The recorded gains come from two to eight lessons or a semester; a single session produced modest, method-independent gains.

facts.ask: can the learner already tell a reliable reference source in this area from an unreliable one?
facts.fact: What the learner already knows about the topic and the domain
facts.why: Children applied an accuracy criterion from their own biological knowledge; checking a source laterally requires knowing which outside sources are reliable.

facts.ask: what will the learner have in front of them when they decide what to trust, and what will they do with it (cite it, share it, act on it)?
facts.fact: What kind of source, and what follows from the judgment
facts.why: An organisation's website or a news story can be checked laterally; a research article is judged by its methods; a primary document with no outside coverage is read closely.

facts.ask: how many lessons, over what span, and is there a later task where the learner must judge new sources?
facts.fact: How many sessions there are
facts.why: The tested doses are two to eight lessons; one-session teaching of either method produced modest gains that did not differ by method.

facts.ask: given an unfamiliar site, what does the learner do first, and can they name a reliable reference source for this topic?
facts.fact: What the learner already does and knows
facts.why: Learners who already leave the page have less to gain; learners who leave the page but consult unreliable sites need to know which reference sources are trustworthy in the topic.

facts.ask: what will the learner read, hear, say or write in the next few weeks, and which words in it would stop them?
facts.fact: Which words the learner must understand or use, in which texts and tasks, and by when
facts.why: A designer who knows the coming texts can pre-select and recycle; one who does not will teach lists that never recur.

facts.ask: in which language does the learner read best, how many of the words in a typical coming text do they already know, and can they read the target words aloud?
facts.fact: The learner's current vocabulary, language background and decoding
facts.why: A first-language child, a second-language beginner, a fluent adult entering a new field and a learner who cannot yet read the word need different selection, glossing and modes.

facts.ask: what should the learner be able to do with these words, and how will you check it?
facts.fact: Whether the outcome is recognising words, comprehending texts that use them, or using them productively
facts.why: Recognition can be reached with a few explicit encounters; productive use needs speaking and writing tasks; general comprehension is barely moved by a small set.

facts.ask: after an attempt, who will look at it, and when will the learner make the next attempt?
facts.fact: Who can read each performance and how soon the next attempt follows
facts.why: One-to-one tutoring, a teacher with thirty learners, peers, software and the learner alone close the loop at very different rates; most evidence for responsive loops is one-to-one.

facts.ask: what will the learner do differently next time, on what task, and how will anyone see whether they did?
facts.fact: What the next attempt is
facts.why: A matched item minutes later, a revised draft days later, and a performance next term make different loops.

facts.ask: shown their own attempt and a correct one, can the learner say what differs?
facts.fact: Whether the learner can judge their own work yet
facts.why: A novice needs the information supplied; a learner who can compare their work with the target can run the loop with occasional checks.

facts.ask: what should each group be able to do at the end of the session, and what did the last check on this task show?
facts.fact: What the grouping is for, and what evidence it rests on
facts.why: Targeted support needs similar-need groups formed from a recent check; discussion and projects need mixed groups with interdependence; neither should be formed from a general ranking.

facts.ask: how many adults, for how many minutes, and who sees each learner's work before the next session?
facts.fact: How much facilitator attention there is
facts.why: The evidence for responsive support is one-to-one; with one teacher and many groups, or a volunteer for a few minutes, the support has to come from roles, materials, peers and a short individual check.

facts.ask: who decides membership, how often does it change, and what do learners and families see?
facts.fact: How the groups could become labels
facts.why: Fixed or visible "levels", self-chosen groups in a class split by language, and support groups that never empty all turn grouping into tracking.

facts.ask: what share of these learners did last term's assigned preparation, and what device, connection and time do they have between sessions?
facts.fact: Whether learners will and can do the pre-class work
facts.why: Access, time outside class, and whether earlier assigned reading was done decide whether the session can assume preparation.

facts.ask: when learners met similar material without a teacher before, could they answer a simple question on it afterwards?
facts.fact: Whether the first explanation can be understood alone
facts.why: A learner with prior knowledge of the topic can learn from a video; a `novice` facing complex material may stall with nobody to ask.

facts.ask: during the session, who will look at what each learner or group produces, and how soon?
facts.fact: Who gives feedback in the live session, and to how many
facts.why: The gain is expected from coached application; one teacher with 200 learners, a volunteer tutor with ten minutes, and a small seminar call for different session designs.

facts.ask: how many times a day or week, in which lessons or places, and has anyone been hurt?
facts.fact: How often, where and how dangerously the behavior occurs
facts.why: Frequent behavior in some settings and not others suits recording and a trigger hypothesis; rare or dangerous behavior needs a safety plan and specialist help first; behavior everywhere suggests a skill gap or a wider need.

facts.ask: who sees the learner during the problem times, and how much time a week can they give to recording and review?
facts.fact: Who can observe and record, and for how long
facts.why: The plan above assumes an adult can make a one-minute note after each incident for two weeks and meet for ten minutes every two weeks.

facts.ask: what would count as success, by when, and is there an existing written plan?
facts.fact: What the plan is for, and who must agree to it
facts.why: Fewer disruptions in one lesson, staying in school (avoiding exclusion), or the learner managing their own behavior in a new setting need different targets and different checks; a formal plan (IEP or behavior plan) sets who must agree to changes.

facts.ask: have they solved a task like this before, unaided, outside a game?
facts.fact: Whether the learner already has a strategy for the target task
facts.why: A learner with none tends to flail through trial and error; one with a usable strategy can use play as practice.

facts.ask: who is present while they play, and will that person talk about the content or only the rules?
facts.fact: Whether an adult or peer will play alongside
facts.why: The tested child gains came with an adult running the game, and the board-game claim's own Discussion names the facilitator as a possible critical ingredient.

facts.ask: what will the learner be able to do afterwards, outside the game, and how will you check?
facts.fact: What outcome must change, and where it will be measured
facts.why: A game can raise enjoyment while a plainer tool raises test scores.

facts.ask: do learners do this task now without being made to, and do they say they enjoy it?
facts.fact: Whether learners already find the task interesting
facts.why: Rewards for doing a task risk lowering later engagement most when interest is already there; a dull, necessary drill carries less of that risk.

facts.ask: what should learners be able to do afterwards, and is the real problem that they stop practising?
facts.fact: Which outcome must change
facts.why: A capability on a later test, continued practice over weeks, and enjoyment are different outcomes, and the evidence is firmest for the first.

facts.ask: will anyone other than the learner see points, ranks or badges, and will they affect a grade?
facts.fact: Who sees the scores
facts.why: Private progress, team scores and a public individual ranking are three different designs with different risks for those ranked low.

facts.ask: have they carried out a task like this before, unaided, to the standard required?
facts.fact: The learner's experience with this task
facts.why: A `novice` needs a process goal and small sub-goals; an experienced learner can work to an outcome goal and may set their own.

facts.ask: what will the learner be able to do afterwards, measured how and when?
facts.fact: What the goal is for: a behaviour, a completion, or learning
facts.why: Most goal evidence here is on task performance, health behaviour and course completion; a goal to "finish the module" can be met without learning.

facts.fact: Whether the learner accepts the goal and believes it reachable
facts.why: An assigned goal the learner rejects or doubts is expected to fail however well it is written. If unstated, ask the learner what they are aiming for and how confident they are of reaching it this week.

facts.ask: before instruction, can the learner sketch or explain how the main ideas fit together?
facts.fact: What the learner already holds of this material's structure
facts.why: A learner who can already say how the ideas relate needs little or no provided organizer and may be slowed by one; a learner who cannot needs the organizer given before being asked to build it.

facts.ask: what must the learner do, unaided, at the end, and when?
facts.fact: What the organizer is for: comprehension now, remembering later, or a product (writing, a plan, a solution)
facts.why: Each changes who builds it and when: studying a provided organizer for comprehension, building from memory for retention, a planning organizer for writing.

facts.ask: what relation is central here (order, kind-of, comparison, cause, cycle), and will the assessment ask about that relation?
facts.fact: Whether the content has one clear structure, and whether the later task uses it
facts.why: A template whose shape does not match the content or the task can mislead.

facts.ask: can they do one item of this kind now, unaided, and explain a step?
facts.fact: The learner's starting response on this task
facts.why: A learner who cannot begin needs the model again and closer items; one who succeeds unaided on the first item needs little or no guided practice, and extra guidance can become redundant.

facts.ask: during practice, who will look at a learner's attempt before the next one, and how long after?
facts.fact: Who can see each attempt, and how soon
facts.why: The evidence for contingent help comes mostly from one-to-one tutoring; with one teacher and thirty learners, or no teacher, the feedback has to come from the items, peers or software.

facts.ask: what must the learner do, unaided, with what aids, and when?
facts.fact: The capability and horizon that count
facts.why: Accurate steps on items like the model, explaining why, solving changed problems, and doing it a week later need different practice and different checks.

facts.ask: before instruction, can they sketch how the main ideas relate, or carry out a simple complete version of the task, and place one detail?
facts.fact: Whether learners already hold an organisation for this content or task
facts.why: Without one they need the whole and the closing placements; with one they need a quick check and the part they lack, and an overview costs time.

facts.ask: will they explain, solve and transfer, or recall specific facts, and in what form will they be assessed?
facts.fact: What they will be asked to do
facts.why: A whole organised around general ideas helped tasks that drew on those ideas and showed no detected benefit on tasks resting on single details.

facts.ask: can one of the top-level ideas be understood without the others?
facts.fact: How much the ideas interact, against the learner's prior knowledge
facts.why: If the whole only makes sense once several new ideas are held together, a novice may not be able to follow it first.

facts.ask: in the moments that go wrong, who is there, and how much time and capacity do they have?
facts.fact: Which adult is present when the young person needs to regulate, and whether that adult is available and able
facts.why: A teacher can cue a skill in class, a carer at home, a supervisor at work; an adult under heavy stress may need support for their own regulation before they can co-regulate.

facts.ask: how old are the learners, and have they agreed to the adults being involved?
facts.fact: The young person's age and wishes
facts.why: At 14 the adults around them shape most settings; at 22 the young person chooses whom to involve, and an adult cueing them uninvited can read as control.

facts.ask: what would the young person and the adults see differently, where, and by when?
facts.fact: What counts as success, and in which setting
facts.why: Fewer incidents at school, coping at work, a self-reported skill and achievement are separate outcomes; the adult component should sit in the setting where the target outcome happens.

principles/include-caregivers-as-self-re.title: Include parents, teachers, or mentors in any self-regulation intervention and support their own skills and coaching capacity

facts.ask: when do learners do the work, on what device, and who could they ask at that moment?
facts.fact: When and where learners get stuck, and how they can reach anyone then
facts.why: A learner stuck on a weekday evening in an asynchronous course needs a different route from a pupil stuck in a lesson with the teacher in the room.

facts.ask: how many learners, how many staff hours a week for questions, and when are the deadlines?
facts.fact: How many learners per instructor hour, and how demand peaks
facts.why: Promises that work for 15 learners fail for 300, and demand piles up before deadlines.

facts.ask: who has dropped out or gone quiet in past runs, and why?
facts.fact: Who is least likely to ask
facts.why: Learners who most need help are often the ones who do not use optional routes (low confidence, first in family at university, working full-time, different language or culture of schooling).

facts.ask: who reads an entry, how soon, and what changes because of it?
facts.fact: Will anyone use the entries, and when?
facts.why: A journal that feeds the next class, a feedback reply or the next attempt has evidence behind it; one that is filed and never read had none in the one trial that tested it.

facts.ask: what should a learner be able to do or understand at the end that they could not before, and how will that be checked?
facts.fact: What is the journal for?
facts.why: Understanding course content, planning and self-regulation, professional reflection on practice, language practice with a teacher, and emotional processing are different aims with different evidence and different prompts.

facts.ask: who sees each entry, and does anything about it count towards a mark?
facts.fact: Who reads it, and is it graded?
facts.why: Private, ungraded entries were more analytic than public ones in one course; graded or shared entries invite performance.

facts.ask: name three things learners must do with this topic afterwards, unaided, and when.
facts.fact: What the learner will have to do with the knowledge
facts.why: The organization should be built for those tasks; one built for another task can help nothing or help the wrong task.

facts.fact: How the learner holds the topic now
facts.why: A learner with isolated facts needs a given organization; one with an organization of their own may need it challenged or extended, not replaced; one who cannot yet use any organization may not benefit. If unstated, ask the learner to sort ten items from the topic into groups and say why, before teaching.

facts.ask: do the tasks need learners to connect items, or only to recall each one?
facts.fact: Whether the content has relational structure at all
facts.why: Causes, hierarchies, principles and developments have it; a list of independent items does not, and imposing one adds work without benefit.

facts.ask: have they used the innovation yet, and when they think about it, what are they concerned about?
facts.fact: Where each person stands now, in concerns and in use
facts.why: A group of nonusers with high informational and personal concerns needs different support from experienced users whose concerns are about student effects.

facts.ask: who will be in touch with each person once they start using it, how often, and for how long?
facts.fact: How much facilitator contact there is after launch
facts.why: The guidance depends on continued, adaptable contact; a one-day event with nothing after it cannot be matched to anyone over time.

facts.ask: can they choose, and will what they say about their concerns, or their use, be seen by anyone who evaluates them?
facts.fact: Whether taking up the innovation is voluntary, and what is at stake for the person
facts.why: Mandated change linked to evaluation is likely, though untested here, to raise personal concerns and make honest reports of concerns less likely.

principles/match-interventions-to-stages.title: Match the form and content of staff development interventions to clients' assessed Stages of Concern

facts.ask: when must the learner do this unaided, in what form, and with what aids?
facts.fact: The horizon and what counts at it
facts.why: A quiz tomorrow, an exam in six weeks and use at work next year need different spacing, different checks and different evidence.

facts.ask: after today, when will the learner next meet this material, and who decides?
facts.fact: How many later encounters the design controls
facts.why: A course with weekly sessions can schedule returns; a one-off workshop or a self-paced app with irregular use cannot, and the returns must be handed to the learner or the software.

facts.fact: What the learner can already do with this material
facts.why: A learner who cannot yet recall or use it needs first learning and short-gap returns; one who already can needs only occasional spaced checks, and extra review is time taken from something else. If unstated, ask for one unaided item now, and another a few days later.

facts.ask: can they produce one example of this performance now, unaided, and say why they made its main choices?
facts.fact: What the learner can already do on this task
facts.why: A learner who cannot begin needs a full, slowed, narrated model first; one who succeeds unaided needs at most a brief model of the new decision, and a full model may be redundant.

facts.ask: where do novices' attempts go wrong, and can that choice be seen in the finished work?
facts.fact: Which decisions the finished product hides
facts.why: If the product shows every step (a solved equation), an annotated product may do; if the decisions are invisible (why a writer cut a paragraph, why a nurse checked a line first, how a mentor defused a classroom incident), they have to be narrated or they are not modelled.

facts.ask: is the problem that learners cannot do it, or that they do not try?
facts.fact: What the model is for: the performance, or the learner's belief they can do it
facts.why: Accurate performance calls for an expert's clear, narrated model; confidence and persistence may call for a model the learner sees as similar to themselves, who struggles and recovers.

facts.ask: what does the learner do when the task starts, and what do they say when asked why they stopped or why they did it at all?
facts.fact: Which component is low for these learners
facts.why: The same withdrawal can come from doubt about success, no reason to care, resentment of control, or not belonging, and each calls for a different move.

facts.ask: can the learner leave, and what happens if they do?
facts.fact: Whether taking part is voluntary
facts.why: In a required course, motivation shows in effort and quality; in a voluntary one (an open online course, an optional programme, adult learning in spare time) it shows first as dropout, and anything that discourages early can cost the learner entirely.

facts.ask: how often does anyone look at each learner's work or attendance, and for how long?
facts.fact: Who can see a learner's effort and respond, and how often
facts.why: A tutor with one learner can diagnose and adjust each session; a teacher with thirty, a volunteer with ten minutes, or an unattended platform cannot.

facts.ask: if a learner showed this capability by speaking, drawing or doing instead of writing, would you accept it as the same capability?
facts.fact: Which response modes belong to the goal
facts.why: If the goal includes writing, speaking or performing in a particular way, that mode stays fixed and only other demands vary; if it does not, the format is free to change.

facts.ask: what decision will this result change, for whom, and can it be reversed?
facts.fact: What the result will decide, and how much rides on it
facts.why: A check that steers tomorrow's lesson needs one quick method and a second only where it misleads; a grade, placement or certification near a cut needs at least two methods and calibrated markers.

facts.ask: who will look at the second piece of evidence, for how many learners, and how many minutes each?
facts.fact: Who can collect and read a second kind of evidence, and how much time they have
facts.why: An oral check costs teacher time per learner; peer and self-assessment cost learner time and training; a portfolio costs marking time.

facts.ask: give a 5-minute segment and look at the notes. Do they hold the main points, in whose words, and is anything wrong?
facts.fact: The learner's current notes on material like this
facts.why: A learner who transcribes, or captures little, needs an outline, modelling and pauses; a learner whose notes already catch the main points needs only a purpose and a review routine.

facts.ask: can learners stop or replay the input, and how fast and dense is it?
facts.fact: Pace, mode and control of the stream
facts.why: Live speech the learner cannot pause, a video they can pause, and a text they can reread need different supports.

facts.ask: what will the learner do with these notes, how long after, and will they have them in hand?
facts.fact: What the notes will be used for, and when
facts.why: A recall test next week, a discussion tomorrow, a procedure on the job, and an essay combining several sources call for different notes and a different review.

facts.ask: after watching ten minutes of this work, can the learner name what the performer attended to and why, in terms a practitioner would accept?
facts.fact: How much of the practice the learner can already see
facts.why: A newcomer needs a narrow written focus, short or recorded segments and a full debrief; someone already partly competent can choose their own focus, watch whole live performances and compare with their own practice.

facts.ask: who will talk with the observer about what they saw, for how long, and how soon after?
facts.fact: Who can explain the performance, and when
facts.why: If the performer or a mentor can talk with the observer before and after, the debrief carries the interpretation; if not (a busy shift, a stranger's lesson, a recording), the record and a written key have to.

facts.ask: when will the learner next do this work themselves, and with what support?
facts.fact: What the learner will do next
facts.why: Observation that leads into the learner's own attempt can be judged by that attempt; observation for orientation, career exploration or confidence is judged differently and should not be loaded with a performance check.

facts.fact: What the learner can already do with print
facts.why: A child who knows no letter sounds, an eight-year-old who decodes single syllables but stalls on longer words, and an adult who reads familiar words but cannot attempt new ones need different starting points and different amounts of phonics. If the brief omits it, ask: can the learner say the sounds of the letters, blend three spoken sounds into a word, and read a short invented word?

facts.ask: how old are the learners, how long have they been taught to read, and has a reading difficulty been identified?
facts.fact: The learner's age and the reason they are behind
facts.why: Effects are largest in kindergarten and first grade and smaller, mainly on decoding, for older readers with difficulties; a diagnosed reading disability changes the dose and the expected gain.

facts.ask: what must the learner be able to read or write, and how will it be checked?
facts.fact: Which outcome counts
facts.why: Decoding unfamiliar words, reading taught words, spelling, reading fluently and understanding text respond differently; phonics predicts the first most strongly.

facts.ask: at the point it goes wrong, can the learner say what to do next?
facts.fact: What goes wrong at the hard moment
facts.why: A learner who does not know the next step needs an instructional cue (or the step taught); one who knows it but stops or freezes needs a motivational or reframing cue; one already fluent needs little or none.

facts.ask: is this a new skill with steps to remember, a familiar task done under pressure, or a long effortful task?
facts.fact: The kind of task and how practised it is
facts.why: The direct evidence is on motor and sport tasks, and stronger on novel and fine-motor ones; academic tasks are a transfer.

facts.ask: how many sessions, and minutes in each, can go to modeling and rehearsing, and will anyone prompt the cue at the hard moment?
facts.fact: How much time and support there is to teach and rehearse the cues
facts.why: Trained self-talk did better than untrained.

facts.ask: after reading, what must the learner be able to say or do, and about which parts of the text?
facts.fact: What the later check will ask about
facts.why: If it tests the whole text, factual pre-questions on part of it may cost the rest; if it tests a few central ideas, pre-questions on those are the best-evidenced case.

facts.ask: does this text answer each question, and when will learners compare their guesses with it?
facts.fact: Whether the text resolves the questions, and whether someone checks the attempts against it
facts.why: The benefit on record depends on the answer arriving after the attempt.

facts.ask: who are the readers, how confident are they, is anything scored, and can they leave (an optional course, a self-paced module)?
facts.fact: How the learner will take being wrong
facts.why: Most pre-question attempts fail; a learner who reads that as proof of inability may stop.

facts.ask: can they do one item of this kind now, unaided, and name the first step?
facts.fact: The learner's starting response on this procedure
facts.why: A learner who cannot begin needs the model, parts and supported attempts; one who completes a representative item unaided needs little more than mixed and spaced practice, and extra guidance can become redundant.

facts.ask: does the procedure always run the same way, and where must the performer choose?
facts.fact: What kind of procedure it is
facts.why: A fixed sequence that must run the same way every time (a dosage calculation, a lab protocol, a safety check) needs accuracy then speed; a procedure full of decisions (choosing a method, debugging, diagnosing) needs the decisions practised and the conditions of use taught. A procedure whose steps interact heavily may need parts first.

facts.ask: what must the learner do, unaided, with what aids, how fast, and when?
facts.fact: When and how it must work
facts.why: Accurate on today's worksheet, fast enough in a real job, still accurate in a month, or adapted to a case not seen before each need different practice and a different check.

facts.fact: How the writer currently plans and revises
facts.why: A writer who already plans and makes global revisions needs a lighter cycle and their own choice of focus; one who writes once and corrects spelling needs explicit strategy teaching, not only more drafts. If unstated, ask for one draft and its revision, written under ordinary conditions, and look at what changed between them.

facts.ask: who will read each draft before the final version, how long after it is written, and how many drafts per writer per week can they read?
facts.fact: Who can read drafts, and how often
facts.why: Teacher response is the scarce resource; peer and self-review stretch it only with criteria and practice.

facts.ask: what must the writer produce unaided, for whom, under what conditions, and when?
facts.fact: The text, reader and horizon that count
facts.why: A timed exam essay, a report for a real client and a portfolio piece need different cycles.

facts.ask: have they seen a strong and a weak example of this task and said which is which?
facts.fact: Can the learner judge this kind of work?
facts.why: A learner who cannot tell good work from weak work will reflect fluently and wrongly; the design must then supply a criterion, an exemplar or feedback first.

facts.ask: when will they next do something like this, and will anyone see whether they changed it?
facts.fact: Is there a next attempt?
facts.why: Reflection is expected to pay off through a changed next move; with no comparable task to follow, the expected benefit is unsupported.

facts.ask: what would the learner do differently, observably, if the reflection worked?
facts.fact: What is the outcome that counts?
facts.why: Better reflections, better course exams and better practice are separate outcomes, and the evidence here is strongest for the first two.

facts.ask: when this learner says they understand, how often are they right? Try two items and compare.
facts.fact: What the learner knows about this task
facts.why: A `novice` cannot judge their own work well and is often overconfident; an `advanced` learner may monitor well enough without a checklist.

facts.ask: what exactly should the learner notice, and what would they compare it with?
facts.fact: What is monitored, and against what
facts.why: Comprehension, the steps of a procedure, a draft against a rubric and on-task behaviour are different checks with different evidence.

facts.ask: will a teacher, a peer, an answer key or software ever compare the learner's record with the work, and when?
facts.fact: Who can check the learner's judgement, and how often
facts.why: Without an outside comparison, a learner's record cannot be corrected.

facts.ask: can the learner do one item from the first stage and one from a middle stage now, unaided?
facts.fact: What the learner can already do on this target
facts.why: A learner who already performs the early steps needs a shorter path and fewer protective orders; one who cannot start needs the prerequisites first.

facts.ask: at the end, what must the learner do, on what kind of item, and when (end of session, a week later, on the job)?
facts.fact: The kind of goal and the test that will count
facts.why: Fluent procedure, conceptual understanding and transfer, and discrimination between confusable categories each favour a different order.

facts.ask: can any part be understood or done without the others?
facts.fact: How tightly the parts depend on each other
facts.why: A chain where step 3 is meaningless without step 2 forces an order; a set of loosely related topics leaves the order open and makes the transitions matter more.

facts.ask: how will the grade or recognition be computed, and how will you know what each member can do alone?
facts.fact: What, exactly, each member's success depends on, and how it is checked
facts.why: A shared grade on one product, a team score built from individual quizzes, and a role that others need are three different structures with different failure modes.

facts.ask: can each member, alone, do or explain a first part of this task now?
facts.fact: Whether members can contribute
facts.why: Dependence on a member who does not yet know enough produces copying or resentment, not explanation.

facts.ask: will the group meet live, for how many sessions, and over how long?
facts.fact: Setting and duration
facts.why: The achievement evidence comes from face-to-face school and undergraduate classes over several weeks; the one online experiment found no achievement effect of interdependence type.

facts.ask: will learners ever see or hear each other live, and on what devices?
facts.fact: The medium, and how much of it is live
facts.why: In a room, people already see each other; in an asynchronous text course, nothing about them is visible unless the design invites it.

facts.ask: how many learners, in what groups, for how many weeks?
facts.fact: How long the group stays together, and how big it is
facts.why: Trust between peers needs repeated contact with the same people; a one-off workshop or a 2,000-learner course cannot rely on it.

facts.ask: what do learners already share with each other, and is anything off limits?
facts.fact: What learners are willing to show, and to whom
facts.why: Norms about self-disclosure, emotional expression and talking to a teacher differ by culture, age, profession and past experience of school, and some learners have reasons to keep their lives private.

facts.ask: what does the score decide, for whom, and which of the test, the sitting and the decision rule can you change?
facts.fact: What the score decides, and whether you control the test
facts.why: A user of an external test (an admissions office, a gifted programme) can change how the score is combined and where the cut sits, not the items; an item writer or test owner can change the items and the sitting; a teacher preparing learners can change only the preparation.

facts.ask: which groups are in the population (sex, race or ethnicity, home language, social class, disability), and roughly how many test-takers in each per cycle?
facts.fact: Which groups the decision must be fair to, and how many learners are in each
facts.why: Prediction checks and DIF statistics need sizeable groups; small groups leave you with content review and second evidence.

facts.ask: what later outcome is the score supposed to predict, and is it recorded for each group?
facts.fact: Whether a later outcome is available to check the score against
facts.why: Differential prediction can only be checked when the criterion (grades, completion, job performance) is recorded for the people the score selected.

facts.ask: what has this learner been seen to do well on a task, by whom, and what labels or records will the teacher meet first?
facts.fact: What the learner has actually been seen to do, and who has been describing them
facts.why: A learner with a record of deficit labels, referrals or failure needs strengths collected from new evidence, not read from the file; one already well regarded needs little framing and mainly harder tasks.

facts.ask: on this course's targets, where is the learner now, and what accommodation or explicit teaching is already planned?
facts.fact: What the learner cannot yet do, and what support that needs
facts.why: The approach adds strengths to an accurate account of barriers; it does not decide whether support is needed.

facts.ask: who will look at each learner's work, how often, and through what channel will feedback reach them?
facts.fact: Who sees the learner's work, and how often
facts.why: Naming specific performances needs someone who sees them: a teacher with five learners can hold a conference each fortnight; one with two hundred, or none, cannot.

facts.ask: what happens to a learner who passes, and to one who fails, and can it be undone?
facts.fact: What decision rides on the result, and for whom
facts.why: A unit grade a teacher can revisit, a course grade on a transcript, and a licence or progression decision call for different breadth, scorer checks and reassessment routes.

facts.ask: what would a learner who has reached the outcome be able to do that one who has not cannot, and with what aids?
facts.fact: What the outcome asks the learner to do
facts.why: Recalling facts, applying a procedure to a new case, analysing, and carrying out a whole performance need different tasks, and a test of one does not report another.

facts.ask: what low-stakes practice of this kind and this format did learners have, and how recently?
facts.fact: What the learners have met before the end-point
facts.why: Learners who have practised retrieval and higher-level questions during the course, and seen the format, are judged on the capability; learners meeting the format or the level for the first time are partly judged on that.

facts.fact: What the student does now on this unit's own work
facts.why: A student who does the end-of-unit task before teaching needs compacting and replacement work; one who learns faster but does not yet do it needs faster pacing within the unit, not removal from it. If a brief omits it, ask: what does the student do, unaided, on this unit's end-of-unit task before it is taught?

facts.fact: Whether the subject is cumulative and whether harder work is available
facts.why: Acceleration needs a next unit, a next course or adaptive material to move into; enrichment needs a task the teacher or a mentor can follow. If omitted, ask: what comes after this unit, and who can read and judge the student's harder work?

facts.fact: How the student came to be identified, and who else shows the same response
facts.why: Provision tied to a label and a test cut-off can miss students who show the response. If omitted, ask: how are students chosen for this provision, and could a student who is not labelled take it on the same evidence?

facts.fact: What the student can do now on this task, and with how much help
facts.why: A student who stops at the first step needs smaller steps and a model; one who does most steps with a prompt needs fewer prompts and the real setting. If a brief omits it, ask: what does the student do now when they try this task alone, and where do they stop?

facts.fact: The level of support needed and who provides it
facts.why: Intermittent support for one routine is a classroom teacher's plan; extensive or pervasive support means a specialist, family and aide share the plan. If omitted, ask: who works with the student during the week, for how long, and who can watch their practice?

facts.fact: What the target is for
facts.why: A school examination item, a daily-life routine, participation in class life and a voice in the student's own plan each need different practice and different checks. If omitted, ask: what should the student be able to do unaided, where, and by when, and what does the student want to be able to do?

facts.ask: is this task about understanding the content, or about reading it unaided?
facts.fact: Whether reading the words is part of what is being learned or assessed
facts.why: If it is, speech is withheld for that practice and its check; if it is not, speech is an access route like any other.

facts.ask: when this learner reads this text, where does it break down, and do they understand it when it is read to them?
facts.fact: The learner's barrier
facts.why: Decoding, low vision, fatigue, a second language, attention or limited vocabulary each call for a different set-up, and only some are helped by speech.

facts.ask: will the learner be looking at anything besides the words, and can they pause and replay?
facts.fact: What else is on the screen and who controls pace
facts.why: Plain text, text with a diagram, and system-paced video each change what should be spoken and what shown.

facts.fact: How far the target situation is from the taught one
facts.why: A new surface in the same domain (`near-transfer`) is supported here. A different domain or form (`far-transfer`) is barely moved in the evidence the wiki holds. If the brief does not say, ask: what new situations must the learner handle, and how different are they from the ones in the course?

facts.fact: Whether the original learning is secure
facts.why: A learner who cannot do the taught case unaided has nothing to transfer, and extra varied cases add load. If the brief does not say, ask: can the learner do one taught item now, unaided, and explain why it works?

facts.fact: Whether the target setting supports the use
facts.why: In workplaces, transfer depends on cases, equipment and colleagues in the setting as well as on the course. If the brief does not say, ask: will the learner meet the situations, and have the resources, to use this within weeks of the course?

facts.ask: what must the learner be able to do at the end, with what aids, and which parts of each activity are only the way in?
facts.fact: Which demands belong to the goal
facts.why: An alternative to a demand that *is* the goal (spelling in a spelling course, reading the drug label as printed) removes the learning, not a barrier.

facts.ask: who has struggled with this unit before, what accommodations are on record, and which languages and devices do learners use?
facts.fact: Who is in the cohort and what stops them
facts.why: Learners with a sensory or motor impairment, learners in a second language, learners with little prior knowledge and learners who have stopped engaging meet different barriers, and the options that help one can burden another.

facts.ask: can learners already do one task of this kind unaided, and have they chosen supports for themselves before?
facts.fact: What the learners can manage choosing
facts.why: Novices pay for every option in attention; experienced learners can choose well and are slowed by supports they no longer need.

facts.ask: what decision will this result change, for whom, and can it be reversed?
facts.fact: What the score will be used for, and how much rides on it
facts.why: A check that steers tomorrow's lesson tolerates a few items and one marker; a grade, placement or certification needs more items, calibrated scoring and caution at the cut.

facts.ask: who are the learners (languages, literacy, background, access needs), and what must they do to show the capability that is not the capability?
facts.fact: Which demands besides the target capability the task makes, and whether they differ across the learners
facts.why: Language, reading load, cultural reference, speed, anxiety and the response mode are the usual ones.

facts.ask: is the response scored by key or by judgement, by how many people, and with what criteria and examples?
facts.fact: Who scores, and how
facts.why: Selected-response items remove rater variation but narrow what can be assessed; performances and constructed responses widen it but depend on the rater.

principles/validity-reliability-and-bias.title: Validity, Reliability, and Bias in Classroom Assessment

facts.ask: who gives the feedback, who receives it, how long have they worked together, and has the learner had reason to read criticism as a low expectation?
facts.fact: Whether the learner has reason to doubt the giver's intent
facts.why: The framing is aimed at a learner for whom critique is ambiguous: across a racial or ethnic difference, in a domain where their group is stereotyped, early in a course before trust exists, or after a history of low expectations. Where the learner already trusts the giver, it adds little.

facts.ask: what will the comment say, against which criteria, and what can the learner do next with it?
facts.fact: Whether the critique is real and usable
facts.why: The framing is a frame around specific critique the learner can act on. If the feedback is a grade, a mark or general praise, fix that first.

facts.ask: is there a revision or re-attempt, and what else does this learner hear from this giver and this institution?
facts.fact: Whether the learner gets a next attempt and the giver's other conduct agrees
facts.why: An assurance with no revision, or amid grading, discipline or comments that say otherwise, has nothing to stand on.

principles/wise-feedback-across-differen.title: Wise Feedback Across Racial and Ethnic Difference

rows.basis: [Instructional guidance that helps novices can become redundant or counterproductive as expertise grows.](claims/expertise-reversal-effect.md) [~M] (review of cognitive-load studies, not consultations; gives no crossover point)
rows.change: Drop the explanation and modelling steps; the learner presents work and their own critique, and the expert adds only what the learner missed; use peer critique between consultations
rows.if: Learners are `advanced` on this task, or already self-diagnose most errors

rows.basis: [Contingent scaffolding improves learning more than fixed or absent support.](claims/contingent-scaffolding-improves-learning.md) [+M] (fourth and fifth graders, long division, 8 per condition, one-to-one)
rows.change: Keep the consultation one-to-one or with two or three children, short (10 minutes), on one problem, with the expert moving up the question–hint–model ladder and back down after each success
rows.if: Learners are `child` (primary age)

rows.basis: [Mentor modelling and a school-wide behaviour program's strategies transferred to the mentee's classroom management practices](claims/mentor-modelling-strategies-transfer-mentee-behaviour-management.md) [+W] (one preservice teacher, qualitative case study)
rows.change: Hold consultations on real cases from the learner's work; the mentor models the decision on one case, then observes the learner on the next and debriefs; plan when the mentor stops being present
rows.if: Learners are `adult` professionals or trainees in a `workplace-clinical` setting

rows.basis: [Contingent scaffolding improves learning more than fixed or absent support.](claims/contingent-scaffolding-improves-learning.md) [+M] (interactive tutoring gave better transfer with similar immediate scores) and [Human tutoring has a medium effect over no tutoring, and in one small study students learned as well when tutors only prompted them as when tutors also explained and gave feedback](claims/tutoring-effectiveness-comes-from-scaffolding-and-feedback.md) [~M] (eighth graders, circulatory system)
rows.change: Have the expert ask and prompt more and explain less; include one changed problem in each consultation for the learner to reason through aloud
rows.if: Goal is a `concept`, `principle` or transfer, not only a `procedure`

rows.basis: untested proposal; content expertise alone did not predict learning in one meta-regression of problem-based-learning tutors ([In a re-analysis of PBL tutor-background data, neither a meta-regression nor subgroup comparisons found that tutor expertise predicts student learning](claims/tutor-background-meta-regression-not-predictive.md) [~M], PBL tutors, not guest experts)
rows.change: Brief them for ten minutes: ask the learner to explain first, give a hint before an answer, think aloud about what they notice; pair them with the course teacher, who manages questions and follow-up
rows.if: The expert is a content specialist or practitioner with no teaching experience (guest, clinician, engineer)

rows.basis: [In two secondary-school writing studies, peer reviewers' own performance predicted how helpful their feedback was but not how accurately it identified problems](claims/peer-feedback-accuracy-depends-on-expertise.md) [~M] (secondary and AP English writing: peers' expertise predicted helpfulness, not accuracy; with a well-specified rubric, accuracy did not differ by school performance)
rows.change: Give the peer a rubric and annotated strong and weak examples, ask for comments tied to criteria, and keep the instructor's review for conceptual errors
rows.if: The "expert" is a more knowledgeable peer

rows.basis: untested proposal; human and intelligent tutoring had similar effects over no tutoring in one review read from its abstract ([tutoring claim](claims/tutoring-effectiveness-comes-from-scaffolding-and-feedback.md) [~M])
rows.change: Use an asynchronous question queue: each question carries the learner's attempt; the expert answers the commonest ones with a recorded think-aloud and the rest in writing within a set time (say two working days); add an adaptive tutor or worked-feedback items for routine steps
rows.if: Setting is `online-self-paced`, no expert live

rows.basis: Untested proposal
rows.change: Keep remote learners in the live exchange rather than giving them a recorded or written reply afterwards: take their prepared questions first, pair each with an in-room partner who describes what the expert is showing and relays follow-ups, and ask the expert to say aloud what they see, check and rule out
rows.if: Some learners join remotely (video or phone) while others are in the room with the expert

rows.basis: untested proposal; drop-in tutoring visits were usually unrelated to course grades in one observational study ([Tutoring center visits usually showed no significant difference in individual course performance, and sometimes tutored students performed worse](claims/tutoring-visits-no-course-grade-advantage.md) [~M], college tutoring centre, self-selected visitors)
rows.change: Collect question cards in advance, triage them, spend open time on the commonest stalls with a think-aloud, and book short individual slots for learners who have not come; do not count attendance as evidence of benefit
rows.if: `classroom` with one expert and a large group (office hours, drop-in)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Collect learners' questions beforehand and send them to the expert; spend the session on the expert's reasoning about two or three of them; set a follow-up task within a week that applies one point, reviewed by the course teacher; do not claim lasting change
rows.if: Time is one session only (a guest visit, a site visit)

rows.basis: [Passing individual microphones discouraged some students from asking questions during telelectures](claims/microphone-use-discourages-student-questions.md) [~W] (one 1972 course, students' reports); otherwise untested
rows.change: Accept written or anonymous questions, consult in pairs or small groups, give question stems; avoid formats that put one person on the spot in front of everyone
rows.if: Learners have low confidence, low status in the group, or are working in a second language
