rows.if: `child` (primary school)

rows.basis: [high-confidence errors](claims/high-confidence-errors-improve-retention.md) [+M]; tested on recall, untested on professional judgement
rows.change: Collect a confidence rating on each answer; review confident errors first and in most depth; low-confidence errors may need re-teaching, not analysis.
rows.if: `adult` or professional, `intermediate`

rows.basis: [corrective feedback after failed retrieval](claims/feedback-enhances-retrieval-practice.md) [+M]; [multiple-choice feedback](claims/feedback-after-multiple-choice-tests-halves-lure-intrusions.md) [+M]
rows.change: Skip erroneous-example analysis. Use retrieval attempts followed by the correct answer after every error; always give feedback on multiple-choice items.
rows.if: goal is `verbal-association` (facts, vocabulary, terms)

rows.basis: [erroneous examples](claims/erroneous-examples-build-conceptual-knowledge.md) [+M] (children, decimals, one session); [productive failure](claims/productive-failure-improves-conceptual-learning.md) [~M] (gain on conceptual, not procedural, outcomes)
rows.change: Build one incorrect/correct pair around the misconception, require a written "why" explanation, and test with changed problems, not only the practised procedure.
rows.if: goal is a `concept` or `principle` with a known misconception

rows.basis: [noticing particular errors in writing](claims/noticing-errors-decreases-errors-preserves-quality.md) [+W] (one study, reported in a review, EFL college writing)
rows.change: Ask learners to look for one or two named error types in their own draft or performance, then revise; do not mark every error at once.
rows.if: goal is a `complex-skill` (writing, a whole clinical or technical task)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Make error analysis routine and ungraded; use peer-anonymous errors; measure willingness to attempt, not only accuracy.
rows.if: goal is an `attitude-motivation` (comfort with error, persistence)

rows.basis: [confusion with prior incorrect trials](claims/confusion-amplifies-negative-effect-of-incorrect-trials.md) [~W] (exploratory); the switch rule is an untested proposal
rows.change: The system must supply the correct solution and the explanation; log error streaks and self-reported confusion, and switch to a worked example after repeated errors on one item type.
rows.if: `online-self-paced`, no teacher present

rows.basis: [erroneous examples](claims/erroneous-examples-build-conceptual-knowledge.md) [+M] (brief session, immediate outcome)
rows.change: Use one comparison set per target misconception with explanation prompts and a short immediate check; do not expect the delayed effect to be shown.
rows.if: `single-session`: one lesson or less

rows.basis: untested; from the earlier page
rows.change: Use constructed erroneous examples or simulation rather than live errors; analyse errors privately or in writing; keep error analysis out of graded assessment.
rows.if: high stakes, public setting, or `workplace-clinical` where real errors are unsafe

rows.basis: [Civic Online Reasoning Instruction Improves Evaluation](claims/civic-online-reasoning-instruction-improves-evaluation.md) [+M] (high-school field study with matched controls, and eleventh graders without a control)
rows.change: Embed six or so 50-minute lessons in the subject's own topics, with teacher preparation beforehand; practise on live sites about the unit's questions
rows.if: `adolescent` learners in a school subject (government, history, science)

rows.basis: [Civic Online Reasoning Instruction Improves Evaluation](claims/civic-online-reasoning-instruction-improves-evaluation.md) [+M] (randomised pilot, four sections; five-week posttest)
rows.change: Two or more 75-minute lessons inside a writing or critical-thinking course, with a check on unseen sites several weeks later
rows.if: `adult` learners at university

rows.basis: Untested; the claim's adults are university students. From the earlier page's target learners
rows.change: Start from sources they already use (health, benefits, news, job information); teach the off-page move on those first; keep reading load of practice sites manageable and model searching step by step
rows.if: `adult` learners re-entering study, or adult basic education

rows.basis: Untested; no claim here tests source-evaluation teaching with children
rows.change: Use a curated set of sources and a single question ("who made this, and what do others say about them?") asked with the teacher; do not expect the full routine
rows.if: `child` learners (primary age)

rows.basis: [One-session checklist (CRAAP) instruction did no better than the alternatives it was compared with](claims/checklist-evaluation-ineffective-online.md) [~M] (first-year business and nursing students; one session of either method, modest gains, no difference)
rows.change: Teach one move (leave the page and search the source's name) and one practice round rather than a long checklist; tell the course teacher what to follow up
rows.if: Only one session (a library visit, an orientation)

rows.basis: [One-session checklist (CRAAP) instruction did no better than the alternatives it was compared with](claims/checklist-evaluation-ineffective-online.md) [~M] (learners kept using domain and design cues after training); the re-purposing is untested
rows.change: Keep the checklist questions as prompts for what to look up elsewhere, not as on-page criteria; add practice on polished but unreliable sites where the checklist misleads
rows.if: The existing course teaches a checklist (CRAAP or similar)

rows.basis: [Collaborative critique-and-redesign instruction shifts students from a value-free view of objectivity toward a procedural one](claims/collaborative-evidence-critique-shifts-students-toward-procedural-objectivity.md) [~M] (one psychology course; source-credibility judgments did not change)
rows.change: Teach the standards for judging a study (valid methods, replication) as a separate target, with small-group critique and redesign of flawed studies; assess source credibility separately
rows.if: Goal is judging research studies, not websites

rows.basis: Untested; all studies were taught in classes
rows.change: Short recorded demonstrations of the off-page move; practice items where the learner commits a verdict, a reason and a confidence rating before a model answer and the fact-checker's search are shown; a delayed check on new sites
rows.if: `online-self-paced`, no teacher present

rows.basis: [One-session checklist (CRAAP) instruction did no better than the alternatives it was compared with](claims/checklist-evaluation-ineffective-online.md) [~M] (nursing students, one 110-minute session); the multi-session design is untested in this setting
rows.change: Practise on the health sites and summaries they will meet, including misinformation sites; add judging study methods if they read research
rows.if: `workplace-clinical` learners (e.g. nurses and health information)

rows.basis: Untested; the claim's discussion names this constraint, and no study tests it
rows.change: Supply a packet of outside documents about each source (reviews, a reference entry, a fact-check) and teach learners to look for them; or shift the target to the reasoning inside the source
rows.if: No open web access, locked devices, or an offline exam

rows.basis: [Instructional guidance that helps novices can become redundant or counterproductive as expertise grows.](claims/expertise-reversal-effect.md) [~M] (cognitive-load studies, carried to this skill)
rows.change: Skip the modelling; give harder cases (reliable sources that look poor, unreliable ones with good coverage elsewhere) and peer critique of reasons
rows.if: Learners already check sources off the page on the first judgment

rows.basis: Untested; constructed-response tasks were used in the eleventh-grade study
rows.change: Grade on unseen sources with constructed responses, scoring the reason and the verdict separately; a verdict alone can be right for the wrong reason
rows.if: High stakes, or the skill is graded

rows.basis: [Unassisted discovery produces less learning than explicit instruction, while discovery enhanced with guidance outperforms other instruction](claims/guided-discovery-outperforms-pure-discovery.md) [~S]; tested on discovery tasks, school and mixed domains, not on placements
rows.change: Teach or demonstrate the key idea first, with a worked example; narrow the experience to one or two variables; supply the reflection prompts and the vocabulary for naming the concept; check an unaided step before removing support
rows.if: Learners are `novice`s on the target task

rows.basis: untested proposal; the guided-inquiry claim's narrative review argues that the advantage of guidance recedes with prior knowledge, which no recorded study tests here
rows.change: Shorten the preparation, make the experience less structured, and have learners write their own debrief questions; keep the second attempt with feedback
rows.if: Learners are `advanced` or experienced practitioners

rows.basis: [Hands-on learning improves achievement](claims/hands-on-learning-improves-achievement.md) [+M] (mathematics, kindergarten to college); [Unassisted discovery produces less learning than explicit instruction, while discovery enhanced with guidance outperforms other instruction](claims/guided-discovery-outperforms-pure-discovery.md) [~S] (third and fourth graders)
rows.change: Use short, concrete hands-on tasks and connect each to its symbol or written form in the same session; tell them what to try, not only to explore
rows.if: Learners are `child`ren, or school-age

rows.basis: [Simulation Based Education With Deliberate Practice](claims/simulation-based-education-with-deliberate-practice-improves-clinical-outcomes.md) [+M]; medical education, procedural skills only; boosters untested
rows.change: Replace one-off exposure with simulated practice repeated to a stated mastery standard, immediate feedback after each attempt, rising difficulty, and a debrief; add booster sessions if the skill is not used soon
rows.if: Adult professionals, `workplace-clinical`, a `procedure` or psychomotor skill

rows.basis: [Physical Experience Enhances Science Learning](claims/physical-experience-enhances-science-learning.md) [~M] (undergraduate physics); [Hands-on learning improves achievement](claims/hands-on-learning-improves-achievement.md) [+M]
rows.change: Have learners manipulate the system (physical or virtual), predict before acting, and map the result onto the formula or diagram afterwards; if a physical lab is unavailable, a virtual one is a fair substitute
rows.if: The goal is a science or mathematics `concept`

rows.basis: [Service-learning is associated with improvements in self-efficacy and social responsibility](claims/service-learning-improves-civic-and-personal-outcomes.md) [+W]; second-hand and self-reported
rows.change: Use service or community experience with structured reflection, and measure a behaviour or a decision in a new case, not only self-report; treat any benefit as unconfirmed
rows.if: The goal is an attitude or disposition (civic responsibility, empathy, respect for diversity)

rows.basis: [Reflective Practice Improves Outcomes When Structured](claims/reflective-practice-improves-outcomes-when-structured.md) [+M] for specific written prompts (engineering undergraduates, in a classroom course); untested online
rows.change: Replace the live debrief with specific written prompts after each task and a model answer to compare against; let learners retry a changed task with automatic feedback
rows.if: `online-self-paced`, no facilitator present

rows.basis: untested proposal, from the experiential-learning-cycle pattern
rows.change: Run one complete loop (brief experience, prompted debrief, named rule, one retry) rather than a long experience with no debrief; cut loops, not stages
rows.if: One session (`single-session`)

rows.basis: untested proposal, from the pattern; the reflection synthesis reports peer interaction as a moderator but the claim page does not say in which direction
rows.change: Run debriefs in pairs or small groups against a shared written protocol; spend facilitator time on the conceptualization step, where a wrong rule is hardest for peers to catch
rows.if: Large group, one facilitator

rows.basis: untested; from the earlier page's constraint that reflection must go beyond narration
rows.change: Assess performance on a new unaided task; do not grade journals for completion; score explanation and performance separately
rows.if: Assessment is high-stakes, or credit attaches to reflection

rows.basis: untested proposal, from the pattern's personalization
rows.change: Offer written or recorded reflection, in the language they choose, before any group debrief; give sentence starters for the prompts
rows.if: Learners reflect in a second language, or are uncomfortable reflecting in public

rows.basis: [Vocabulary Instruction Improves Comprehension](claims/vocabulary-instruction-improves-comprehension.md) [+S] (pre-K–12; students with reading difficulties gained most on custom measures); doses untested
rows.change: Keep the set small (3–4 words per session), teach orally with pictures and actions, read texts aloud with the words in them; expect taught-word gains, not general reading gains
rows.if: Learners are `child` (pre-K to primary), or are weaker readers

rows.basis: [Glossing yields medium-to-large positive effects on L2 vocabulary learning…](claims/glossing-medium-large-effects-l2-vocabulary.md) [+W] (second-hand report of meta-analyses); [Correct word inference in reading requires knowing roughly 95–98% of surrounding words…](claims/vocabulary-coverage-thresholds-for-inference.md) [~W] (second-hand); [Proficiency moderates gloss effects…](claims/proficiency-moderates-gloss-vocabulary-effects.md) [~M] (one EFL study: benefits at middle proficiency levels only)
rows.change: Gloss unfamiliar words in the text (first-language or picture glosses), teach the most frequent words first, and do not rely on inference from context until most surrounding words are known
rows.if: Learners are second-language learners, `novice` in the language

rows.basis: untested; carried from school-age evidence on taught words and word parts ([Morphological Instruction Improves Vocabulary](claims/morphological-instruction-improves-vocabulary.md) [~M], school-age children only)
rows.change: Take the words from their real documents and tasks; teach word parts that recur in the field; check use in the job task (a handover, a report, a conversation with a client), not in a quiz
rows.if: Learners are fluent `adult`s or professionals entering a new field (technical or workplace terms)

rows.basis: [Task-essentialness and productive use of new words…](claims/task-essentialness-goal-directed-vocabulary-retention.md) [+W] (second-hand, five learners); otherwise untested
rows.change: Add at least two speaking or writing tasks per word in which the word is needed to complete the task; give a sentence frame at first, then withdraw it
rows.if: The goal is productive use (speaking, writing) rather than reading

rows.basis: [Vocabulary Instruction Improves Comprehension](claims/vocabulary-instruction-improves-comprehension.md) [~S] (d = 0.10 on standardised measures against 0.50 on researcher-built ones)
rows.change: Say plainly that a small taught set will not move a general comprehension score; spend more time on wide supported reading with glosses, and teach words that recur across many texts
rows.if: The goal is reading comprehension in general, not of particular texts

rows.basis: [Supplemental computer-based spaced repetition…](claims/spaced-repetition-supplement-triples-vocabulary-retention.md) [+M] (EFL cadets, alongside classroom teaching, not instead of it)
rows.change: Build each word as a short card (meaning, example, picture, audio) with recall prompts scheduled by the app over two to three weeks; put the words into short readings or audio inside the course; ask for one typed or spoken use per word
rows.if: Setting is `online-self-paced`, phone-only, or no teacher present

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Put the word set, examples and the shared text where both groups see them (shared screen or document); take uses in the chat or a shared document as well as aloud, and pair a remote learner with an in-room one for the speaking task
rows.if: Some learners are remote and some in the room

rows.basis: untested proposal; the review part rests on [Supplemental computer-based spaced repetition…](claims/spaced-repetition-supplement-triples-vocabulary-retention.md) [+M]
rows.change: Teach the set to everyone at once in 10 minutes; let spaced review run on cards or an app; in the check-in, look at one thing only: a written or spoken use of two or three of the week's words
rows.if: One teacher with a large group, or scarce facilitator time (a volunteer, one short check-in a week)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Teach 3 words, not more: 6–8 minutes introducing them, 8–10 minutes reading or doing a task that uses them, 3–4 minutes of use in the learner's own sentence; give a take-away card for later review; do not claim retention
rows.if: A single session only, or a fixed short time budget (for example 20 minutes)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Let learners show they know a word by pointing, sorting pictures or acting before saying or writing it; use pairs before whole-group use; never correct misuse in front of the group
rows.if: Learners have low confidence, low literacy or anxiety about speaking

rows.basis: [Pairing Contextual Encounters…](claims/pairing-contextual-encounters-with-explicit-instruction-produces-stronger-vocabulary-outcomes-than-either-alone.md) [+M]; [Vocabulary Knowledge Grows Incrementally…](claims/vocabulary-knowledge-grows-incrementally-with-repeated-encounters-in-varied-contexts.md) [+M]
rows.change: Keep the routine; change only what the evidence says matters: put each word into a text or task soon after it is entered, bring it back several times across weeks, and ask for one use, not only a definition
rows.if: The brief names its own routine (a word wall, a Frayer-style chart, a vocabulary log, a glossary its course uses)

rows.basis: untested
rows.change: Teach from that list in its own categories; select within it by what the next texts and tasks need, rather than replacing it
rows.if: The brief gives its own word list, categories or rubric (a course list, a standards list, a job's terminology)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: The learner decides what goes in it and who sees it; check use through a separate task, not by reading the journal
rows.if: Learners keep a personal word journal or notebook, or the material is private

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Teach the words the performance needs beforehand and rehearse them in parts of the real task, then let the performance run whole; do not turn it into a vocabulary test
rows.if: The output is a product or performance for a real audience (a presentation, a client conversation, a published text), and the brief wants it kept whole

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Raise the criterion for "known": correct unprompted use in three tasks, plus recognition in the exact form the exam or job uses; keep spaced review until the event
rows.if: Stakes are high (an exam with a set word list, a safety or medication term at work)

rows.basis: [Contingent scaffolding](claims/contingent-scaffolding-improves-learning.md) [+M] (children, one-to-one, long division)
rows.change: Run the loop for them: task-level information on every attempt, a matched retry at once, the step re-modelled after two failed cycles
rows.if: Learners are `novice` on the task

rows.basis: [Expertise reversal](claims/expertise-reversal-effect.md) [~M] (review of guidance studies, carried to feedback; no crossover point given)
rows.change: Shorten external loops: ask for self-evaluation first, give information only on what the self-evaluation missed, and loop on harder or transfer items
rows.if: Learners are `advanced`, or already accurate unaided

rows.basis: Praise: [Praise for intelligence, rather than for effort, after success undermines children's motivation and performance after a later failure](claims/feedback-praise-reduces-learning.md) [-M] (fifth graders). Cycle length: untested
rows.change: Shorter cycles with the adult reading each attempt; praise the strategy or the work, never ability; small groups so attempts can be seen
rows.if: Learners are `child` (primary age)

rows.basis: [Peer Feedback Improves Writing](claims/peer-feedback-improves-writing.md) [+M] (higher education, 24 studies; against no feedback); revision interval untested
rows.change: Loop over drafts: draft, structured peer or teacher feedback against criteria, revision within a few days, then a new piece checked for the same targets
rows.if: Goal is a written or made product (`complex-skill`)

rows.basis: [Corrective feedback on L2 errors](claims/corrective-feedback-effect-on-l2-development-is-significant-and-durable.md) [+S] (gains held on delayed tests; prompts larger than recasts in one synthesis)
rows.change: Correct errors in the exchange itself, with prompts that ask the learner to reformulate rather than only recasts; keep it up over many sessions
rows.if: Goal is spoken second-language accuracy

rows.basis: [Trained teachers' loop time](claims/training-increases-feedback-corrective-loop-time.md) [+M] (secondary mathematics, time allocation only, no learning outcome); [rubrics and peer feedback](claims/rubrics-improve-peer-feedback-quality.md) [~M] (rubrics changed peer comments, one study found less reflective feedback)
rows.change: Collect every learner's attempt at once (mini-whiteboards, a poll, a short written item), give whole-class information on the commonest error, have everyone do one matched item, then go to those who still fail; use peers with a rubric for drafts; budget class time for the loop
rows.if: `classroom`, one teacher and a large group

rows.basis: Untested proposal; peer reading carried from [peer feedback on writing](claims/peer-feedback-improves-writing.md) [+M], which tested drafts, not practical tasks
rows.change: Run the loop in buddy pairs: one partner watches an attempt against a posted checklist of two or three points, names one thing to change, and the other retries at once; a wall tally records which checklist points were met; the facilitator rechecks a sample (one new unaided attempt from two or three people per shift) and changes the checklist if the same point keeps failing. No paperwork beyond the tally
rows.if: Little facilitator time or equipment: volunteers, busy shifts, no devices

rows.basis: [Adaptive learning improves outcomes](claims/adaptive-learning-improves-outcomes.md) [+S] (intelligent tutoring beat large-group, textbook and other computer instruction, not human tutoring or small groups)
rows.change: Build automatically checked items with a retry on a new item after each piece of information; route a learner who fails twice to a worked example; keep a delayed recheck in a later session
rows.if: `online-self-paced`, no teacher present

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Use one submission channel everyone can reach (a shared form or chat poll), return information in that channel, and give remote learners the same matched retry; for phone-only learners keep items short and one target per message
rows.if: Mixed modes: some learners remote, some in the room, or phone-only

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Run at least two complete cycles inside the session and end with one unaided new item; report what that item shows and claim no retention
rows.if: One session only

rows.basis: untested; [Assessment for Learning](principles/assessment-for-learning.md) holds the stakes model ([retakes and revisions](strategies/retakes-and-revisions.md) is a recipe, untested)
rows.change: Keep loop items ungraded and separate from the graded task; judge readiness only on unaided new items; let a revision replace an earlier mark if revision is the point
rows.if: Stakes are high, or the work is graded

rows.basis: untested proposal; person-focused praise is the one thing with evidence against it ([Praise for intelligence, rather than for effort, after success undermines children's motivation and performance after a later failure](claims/feedback-praise-reduces-learning.md) [-M], children)
rows.change: Give information privately, about the task, in short spoken or shown form (a demonstration, a marked example) rather than long written comments; one target per cycle
rows.if: Learners have low confidence or low literacy

rows.basis: untested; in one teacher-education case, probing feedback with required resubmission helped one candidate and not another ([probing feedback](claims/probing-feedback-revise-resubmit-evidence.md) [+W])
rows.change: Loop on real work outputs (a case note, a call, a procedure); a supervisor or peer reads one output per cycle against a stated criterion, and the next output is the re-observation
rows.if: Adults in work settings (`adult-workplace`, `workplace-clinical`)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Run the loops in rehearsal with a critic using the criteria, before the audience; treat the audience's response as information for the next product, not a judgement on this one; do not show the audience the drafts or the critique if it should see only the finished work
rows.if: A product or performance for a real audience

rows.basis: [revise-summary compliance](claims/revise-summary-compliance-predicts-learning-gains.md) [~M] (associational, 28 college students, one tutoring system)
rows.change: Make the use visible: the learner marks what they changed, or answers "what will you do next?" before the next attempt; no new information until the last was used
rows.if: Learners receive feedback but do not use it

rows.basis: [hypercorrection](claims/high-confidence-errors-improve-retention.md) [~S] (mostly recall; carried to misconceptions untested)
rows.change: Ask for confidence before revealing answers; correct confident errors explicitly and bring the item back later
rows.if: Learners answer confidently and wrongly (misconceptions)

rows.basis: For one outcome, immediate and delayed feedback were equally effective ([feedback after multiple-choice tests](claims/feedback-after-multiple-choice-tests-halves-lure-intrusions.md) [+M], reported second-hand); timing is held on [Immediate Feedback](principles/immediate-feedback.md)
rows.change: Keep the loop closed by attaching a task: the learner uses the returned comments on a new item before the next unit, rather than reading and filing them; whether earlier would be better is not settled
rows.if: Information can only come later (marking takes days)

rows.basis: [Instructional guidance that helps novices can become redundant or counterproductive as expertise grows.](claims/expertise-reversal-effect.md) [~M] (cognitive-load studies, not grouping); [Learning By Teaching Improves Tutor Learning](claims/learning-by-teaching-improves-tutor-learning.md) [+M] (tutors' own gains)
rows.change: Skip the support group for them; form an extension group with a harder or wider task, or place them in mixed groups as explainers with an explaining role, not answer-givers
rows.if: Learners are `advanced` on this task, or most already pass the check

rows.basis: [Contingent scaffolding improves learning more than fixed or absent support.](claims/contingent-scaffolding-improves-learning.md) [+M] (fourth and fifth graders, one-to-one); format and timing untested
rows.change: Fewer formats, taught as routines with visual role cards; similar-need groups with the teacher for 10–15 minutes; other groups do practice they can check themselves
rows.if: Learners are `child` (primary age)

rows.basis: untested proposal; the earlier page names adults, including those with learning disabilities and multilingual learners
rows.change: Group by the task or job role in hand and by what learners say they need, not by test scores; let adults choose to join a support session; use mixed groups to pool workplace experience
rows.if: Learners are `adult`, including adults in a work setting or adult basic education

rows.basis: [Students segregated into language cliques whenever allowed to choose peer interactions, despite the 50-50 enrollment design](claims/language-clique-segregation-peer-choice.md) [~W] (one dual-language school, observation); the design move is untested
rows.change: Assign mixed-language groups for discussion and projects, with a role that needs each language; use short similar-language groups only for a stated language goal, then dissolve them
rows.if: Multilingual learners, or a dual-language class

rows.basis: untested proposal; from the earlier page (participation alongside peers, strengths shown)
rows.change: Keep them in mixed groups for shared tasks, with a role matched to a strength (reader, builder, timekeeper, presenter of a drawing); give targeted support in short similar-need sessions that others also join; check unaided work orally or by doing where literacy blocks writing
rows.if: Learners with disabilities, low confidence or low literacy

rows.basis: untested proposal; contingent support is shown one-to-one only ([Contingent scaffolding improves learning more than fixed or absent support.](claims/contingent-scaffolding-improves-learning.md) [~M])
rows.change: One similar-need group with the teacher per segment while the rest work in mixed groups with roles and self-checkable tasks; rotate which group meets the teacher across the week; whole-class reteach when more than half share a gap
rows.if: One teacher, many learners (30 or more), or a class of about 50

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Spend the minutes on the similar-need group the last check identified, not on circulating; give mixed groups a printed task card with roles, criteria and an answer check; collect one individual item from everyone for the next check
rows.if: Scarce facilitator time: a volunteer, a busy shift, a tutor who checks in for a few minutes

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Do not split groups by location by default: put remote learners in mixed groups with a shared document and one in-room member who reads the work aloud, or make one remote group with its own facilitator; for phone-only learners, use text-based roles and a short checkable item at the end
rows.if: Mixed mode: some learners remote, some in the room; or phone-only

rows.basis: untested here; individualised routing is modelled in [Adaptive Learning](principles/adaptive-learning.md)
rows.change: Replace live regrouping with branching: a short check routes each learner to a support module or an extension; asynchronous discussion groups are assigned by the course for mixing, and change each unit
rows.if: `online-self-paced`, no live teacher

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: No regrouping cycle is possible: run a two-minute opening check, one similar-need group with the teacher for 15 minutes while others work in mixed pairs, and an individual exit item; do not claim regrouping effects
rows.if: One session only

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Keep one grouping format per session: 3–5 minutes check or recap, 10–12 minutes in groups, 3–5 minutes individual check; regroup only between sessions
rows.if: A fixed short time budget (for example 20 minutes a session)

rows.basis: untested proposal; the formative-evidence step rests on [Assessment for learning improves achievement](claims/assessment-for-learning-improves-achievement.md) [+M]
rows.change: Keep that routine and its categories; change only what the evidence here says matters: groups formed from a recent check on the task, membership reviewed at a set interval, an individual check at the end
rows.if: The brief names its own grouping routine, categories, criteria or rubric (its own station rotation, reading levels, competency list or check-in)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Form groups from task evidence only; never display levels or reasons; let the learner choose whether to tell peers why they are in a session; keep the placement log to the teacher
rows.if: Placement data are private or sensitive (diagnoses, test scores, immigration or family circumstances)

rows.basis: untested proposal; individual accountability as in [In school studies, cooperative and peer-learning methods that reward groups on every member's individual learning raised achievement more than methods without such rewards](claims/cooperative-learning-group-rewards-and-individual-accountability.md) [+M]
rows.change: Keep the whole task in one mixed group from start to finish; pull members out briefly into similar-need sessions for a component skill, then return them; assess each member's part and the whole
rows.if: A whole-task performance or product for a real audience (a project, an exhibition, a client report)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Judge readiness only on individual unaided checks, never on group products; ensure support groups end with the same item types as the assessment
rows.if: High stakes or an unaided final assessment

rows.basis: [Learning By Teaching Improves Tutor Learning](claims/learning-by-teaching-improves-tutor-learning.md) [+M]; the concern itself is in [Cooperative learning has drawbacks including slow learners depending on fast achievers, so teachers should stress both cooperative and individual work](claims/cooperative-learning-versus-individual-endeavors.md) [~W] (opinion)
rows.change: Use explaining roles and individual checks so contribution is visible; show the tutor-gain evidence; keep some extension groups
rows.if: Teachers or parents resist mixed groups because high achievers "carry" others

rows.basis: untested; [Active learning improves exam performance](claims/active-learning-improves-exam-performance.md) [~S] is a course-level average that does not separate novices; the guidance limit for novices is on [Active Learning](principles/active-learning.md)
rows.change: Keep the first explanation live, or use a worked-example video with a pause-and-try item after each step; flip only the later, more practised topics; give the opening check before any independent application
rows.if: Learners are `novice` on the topic and the material has many interacting parts

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Make pre-class material a short brief or a reading, and use the session for cases, disagreement and their own examples; drop the note-taking guide and the recap
rows.if: Learners are `advanced` on the topic, or professionals updating practice

rows.basis: untested; [Contingent scaffolding…](claims/contingent-scaffolding-improves-learning.md) [~M] (fourth and fifth graders, one-to-one tutoring) supports the circulating teacher, not the flip
rows.change: Do not set pre-class video as homework; run the exposure in class at a station or as a short whole-class video, then move to guided practice with the teacher circulating ("faux-flipped")
rows.if: Learners are `child` (primary age)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Keep pre-class work to 10 minutes or less on a phone, tied to a task they will do in the session; use the session for practice on their own work tasks; do not penalise missed preparation, run a 5-minute catch-up at the start instead
rows.if: Learners are `adult` in a work setting (`workplace-clinical`), preparing between shifts

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Prefer video with captions and a one-page glossary to reading; add one easy item early in the opening check; let learners show understanding by doing before explaining; make the check private
rows.if: Learners have low confidence or low literacy, or study in a second language

rows.basis: untested; the access constraint is from the earlier page
rows.change: Keep each pre-class item under 5 minutes, downloadable and readable on a phone; give the same material as a printed page; schedule in-class time for those who could not access it
rows.if: Learners have unreliable access, or a phone only

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Give remote learners the same opening check in the same tool; put remote learners in their own breakout group with a named facilitator rather than mixing one remote learner into a room group; route the teacher's circulation through the breakouts on a fixed timetable
rows.if: Mixed modes: some learners join remotely while others are in the room

rows.basis: untested proposal; see the [Blended Learning pattern](patterns/blended-learning.md) for the online part's self-regulation
rows.change: Run the check as a poll, application in small breakout rooms with shared documents the teacher can see, and the teacher visiting rooms in turn; keep total screen time per session to what was there before
rows.if: The live session is online (`online-instructor-led`)

rows.basis: [Active learning improves exam performance](claims/active-learning-improves-exam-performance.md) [+S] (held across class sizes, largest in small classes); [Peer-teaching flipped classroom students show higher calculus conceptual understanding…](claims/ptfc-beats-cfc-conceptual-understanding.md) [+M] (two intact classes; the procedure is not described on the claim page)
rows.change: Use the opening check as a poll, pairs or small groups for application, and whole-class feedback on the commonest error, then go to groups still stuck; trained peer teachers or assistants can extend the circulation
rows.if: One teacher with a large group (100+)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Put the feedback into the materials: answers and worked solutions after each pre-class question and each in-class item; let the facilitator spend their minutes only on learners who failed the opening check
rows.if: Scarce facilitator time: a volunteer, a busy shift, a tutor who checks in briefly

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Do not flip; give 10 minutes of exposition in the session, then application with feedback and an exit item
rows.if: Only one session, with no time before it

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Fit to it: 15 minutes pre-class (one short video, two questions); in session 5 minutes check, 5 clarification, 40 application, 10 exit and next step; cut topics before cutting application time
rows.if: A fixed short time budget (for example a 60-minute workshop with 15 minutes of preparation)

rows.basis: untested; [Time-on-task is frequently unequal…](claims/time-on-task-unequal-in-active-learning-comparisons.md) [~M] for the time budget
rows.change: Keep it; change only what the evidence speaks to: make its first item a check on the pre-class material, make sure most of the live time is application, and keep total home time within budget
rows.if: The brief names its own routine (its own pre-class quiz, worksheet, readiness test or discussion protocol)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Use them for the opening check, the in-class tasks and the exit item; do not substitute this page's items
rows.if: The brief gives its own categories, criteria or rubric

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: The learner controls who sees it; the opening check asks only about the shared content; in class, learners choose what to bring
rows.if: Pre-class work includes private or sensitive material (reflections on practice, personal experience)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Keep the task whole in the live sessions: pre-class work supplies only the knowledge the task needs, and each session advances the whole task with feedback, rather than splitting it into paper items
rows.if: The course ends in a whole-task performance or a product for a real audience (a presentation, a client case, a performance)

rows.basis: untested; [Active learning improves exam performance](claims/active-learning-improves-exam-performance.md) [+S] (gateway STEM courses, lower failure under active learning)
rows.change: Keep the opening check low stakes; judge readiness only on unaided exit items; record who did the preparation and who did not, and offer the catch-up route before the exam
rows.if: Stakes are high (a licensing exam, a gateway course)

rows.basis: untested; see [Active Learning](principles/active-learning.md) on lecture and information acquisition
rows.change: A flip adds little; give the information directly (in writing, or a short talk) and use any live time for questions
rows.if: The goal is information acquisition alone (a factual update, a policy change)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Keep that structure: put the pre-class check where the brief puts it and give the application or simulation the session the brief names; change only the pre-class dose, what the opening minutes check, and how peers support each other when facilitator cover is thin
rows.if: The brief fixes its own session structure (two short sessions a week, a retrieval check before class, a simulation in one session)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Make the pre-class material printable or downloadable once on school wifi (one page or a 5–8 minute clip), or do the first exposure in the first 10 minutes of class (an in-class flip); keep both practical application and a structured discussion in the live time, each with its own task
rows.if: Learners have little or no home internet, or lessons are short

rows.basis: [Universal classroom management](claims/universal-classroom-management-reduces-problem-behavior.md) [~M] (12-study meta-analysis, K–12 classrooms; universal practices without functional information)
rows.change: Do not start individual assessments; put universal management in place first (taught routines, clear expectations, frequent positive contact), then reassess which learners still stand out
rows.if: The whole class is disruptive, not one learner

rows.basis: untested proposal; the only functional-analysis claim here is one 4-year-old in a feeding programme ([escape and attention](claims/inappropriate-behavior-maintained-by-escape-and-attention.md) [+W])
rows.change: Rely on adult observation and family interview, not the child's report; use a picture card or gesture as the replacement response; keep consequences immediate and the reinforcer frequent; check sleep, hunger and illness first
rows.if: Learner is a young `child` (preschool or early primary)

rows.basis: [Self-monitoring of on-task behavior](claims/self-monitoring-improves-on-task-behavior.md) [+M] (single-case studies, grades 4–12, students with or at risk for disabilities; behavior, not achievement)
rows.change: Interview the learner as a main source of trigger information; agree the replacement with them; add self-recording of on-task behavior from week 4 or so
rows.if: Learner is an `adolescent` (about grade 4 and up)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Drop the IEP and parent steps; ask the person directly what makes the session hard (shift fatigue, a task they cannot read, being put on the spot); agree the change with them privately; document only what the organisation's policy requires
rows.if: Learners are `adult`s in a work setting or adult education

rows.basis: untested proposal; from the strategy pages (rare behavior cannot be sampled)
rows.change: Do not wait to observe a pattern; put a safety plan in place and refer to a behavior specialist; record each incident in full
rows.if: The behavior is dangerous, or rare but severe

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Use a tally sheet with three columns (time, activity just before, what followed) during the two lessons where the behavior is worst, for one week; test one trigger change in the second week
rows.if: One teacher with a full class, no support staff

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Cut recording to a three-question card after each incident (when, what just before, what the learner got), and replace the two-weekly meeting with a five-minute weekly look at the cards by one named person
rows.if: Scarce adult time (volunteers, a busy shift, one tutor checking in briefly)

rows.basis: [Greetings at the door](claims/positive-greetings-at-the-door-improve-engagement.md) [+M] (middle-school classes, carried to a single session it did not test); the rest untested
rows.change: Do not attempt an assessment; use antecedent defaults: greet each learner by name at the door, give instructions one step at a time, show a way to ask for help or take a short break, and pass a note on what happened to the regular teacher
rows.if: Only one session (a cover teacher, a one-off workshop)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Add connection, camera, noise at home and screen size to the environmental trigger list; record from chat and platform logs as well as observation; give remote learners a private channel (direct message) as the help or break request
rows.if: Mixed modes (some learners remote, some in the room; or phone-only)

rows.basis: not an evidence claim: the plan is an agreement among teacher, professionals, learner and parents (earlier page)
rows.change: Keep the existing plan; record against it; bring proposed changes to the team and the family rather than changing it alone
rows.if: The learner has an IEP or a behavior plan

rows.basis: untested proposal; see [Check In Check Out](strategies/check-incheck-out.md) and [Daily Behavior Report Cards](strategies/daily-behavior-report-cards.md)
rows.change: Keep the routine; add one functional check (does the reward or attention the routine gives match what the behavior was getting?) and change only what the check shows, for example the timing of the check-in to just before the known trigger
rows.if: The brief names its own routine (a point sheet, a daily behavior report card, check-in/check-out, a class reward chart)

rows.basis: [Expected tangible rewards](claims/rewards-undermine-intrinsic-motivation.md) [~M] (two meta-analyses of experiments, mostly laboratory tasks; they disagree on size; stronger for children)
rows.change: Use specific praise and the natural payoff (help, a break, time on a chosen task) instead; if tangible rewards are needed, tie them to meeting a standard and fade them
rows.if: The plan is to reward the learner with prizes for an activity they already enjoy

rows.basis: [Empathic discipline](claims/brief-intervention-empathic-discipline-cuts-suspensions.md) [+M] (middle-school math teachers; suspensions; overall effect small and marginal in the preregistered replication, larger for previously suspended students)
rows.change: Present the record and the hypothesis; agree consistent, pre-planned consequences; offer teachers a short empathic-discipline exercise
rows.if: Staff or the school want harsher consequences or exclusion

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Make the replacement response non-verbal (a card, a gesture, a signal); interview through the family or an interpreter; treat unclear instructions as a likely instructional trigger
rows.if: Learners with low literacy, a language barrier or limited communication

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Hypothesise escape from being seen to fail; offer a rehearsal with one adult first, then a small group, then the audience; allow an alternative format while that builds
rows.if: The behavior occurs when the learner must perform for others (reading aloud, presenting, a public performance)

rows.basis: [Low fidelity](claims/low-fidelity-pbis-smaller-student-improvements.md) [~W] and [teacher fidelity](claims/tkss-fidelity-ancova-interaction-problem-behavior.md) [~M] (one study, 37 students with emotional disturbance in self-contained classrooms, no control group)
rows.change: Coach the adults on the plan in the classroom and check, at each review, whether each step was done as written before judging the plan
rows.if: Staff carrying out the plan have little training

rows.basis: [Worked examples between rounds, puzzle game](claims/worked-examples-improve-problem-solving-strategy-transfer-in-a-puzzle-game.md) [~M]; tested with university students, untested with children
rows.change: Add one or two worked examples or a modelled round before unaided play and again between rounds; keep game controls minimal
rows.if: Learners are `novice` on the target task

rows.basis: [Board-game study](claims/number-board-games-improve-numerical-knowledge.md) [+M]; [guided play](claims/guided-play-improves-academic-outcomes.md) [~W] (guided play, not games specifically)
rows.change: Use a simple game whose board or move *is* the representation (e.g. a numbered linear track); an adult plays alongside naming the numbers or quantities; four sessions of 15–20 min over two weeks
rows.if: Learners are preschool or early-primary `child`ren

rows.basis: untested proposal; the earlier page's whole-task argument is a design argument, not a tested effect
rows.change: Build the game around one job decision with real consequences in its rules; debrief against the real procedure; keep competition optional
rows.if: Learners are `adult` or professionals in a `workplace-clinical` setting

rows.basis: [Kahoot! and outdoor games with migrant children](claims/game-based-practice-outperforms-traditional-l2-vocabulary-instruction.md) [+W] (confounded); [adventure game with supplementary material](claims/adventure-games-supplementary-material-vocabulary.md) [+W] (second-hand)
rows.change: A quiz or practice game is a reasonable vehicle; add glosses or supplementary word material inside it, and test recall a week later, not only at the end of play
rows.if: The goal is `verbal-association` (vocabulary, facts)

rows.basis: untested; from the earlier page
rows.change: Make the core move the reasoning itself; add a debrief and one non-game transfer task; expect slower gains than for facts
rows.if: The goal is a `concept`, `principle` or `complex-skill`

rows.basis: [DragonBox vs Lynnette](claims/intelligent-tutor-lynnette-outperformed-dragonbox-on-test.md) [~W]
rows.change: Measure enjoyment and the capability separately; do not report one as the other; a game can win on the first and lose on the second
rows.if: The goal is `attitude-motivation` (interest, confidence)

rows.basis: untested proposal; the tested child gains had an adult present
rows.change: Put the modelling, hints and debrief questions inside the game (a worked example screen between levels, a "why did that work?" prompt after each level); log attempts per level to find where learners stall
rows.if: `online-self-paced`, no teacher present

rows.basis: untested proposal; the board-game dose is the only tested schedule here
rows.change: Use one short game round, a worked example, a second round and a debrief; do not expect durable gains; if `days-weeks` are available, prefer several short sessions
rows.if: Time is a `single-session`

rows.basis: untested; from the earlier page
rows.change: Do not grade the in-game score unless its measurement has been designed for that ([Assessment Mechanic](elements/assessment-mechanic.md)); assess on an aligned external task
rows.if: Stakes are high or the game feeds a grade

rows.basis: untested; from the earlier page
rows.change: Choose a mechanic with no timing or precision demands beyond the target; offer a paper or board version; read text aloud or reduce it
rows.if: Devices, motor demands, reading load or disability limit access

rows.basis: [Rewards claim](claims/rewards-undermine-intrinsic-motivation.md) [~S] and [overjustification claim](claims/rewards-undermine-intrinsic-motivation.md) [~S] (lab tasks, free-choice time; carried to courses)
rows.change: Do not attach expected points, prizes or badges to doing or finishing it; give informational feedback and a progress view only
rows.if: Learners already find the task interesting, or practise it voluntarily

rows.basis: untested here: the rewards claim's Discussion argues there is little interest to undermine, but no recorded entry tests uninteresting tasks; the [overjustification claim](claims/rewards-undermine-intrinsic-motivation.md) [~S] reports less undermining for well-defined tasks with a clear standard
rows.change: Points for accuracy and improvement are reasonable; set a clear quality standard for earning them; plan the week without points (step 8)
rows.if: The task is a dull, necessary drill (fact fluency, verb forms, keyboard practice)

rows.basis: [Rewards claim](claims/rewards-undermine-intrinsic-motivation.md) [-S] (tangible rewards more detrimental for children than college students, lab); [praise claim](claims/feedback-praise-reduces-learning.md) [~M] (fifth graders)
rows.change: Prefer verbal, informational feedback and effort-focused badges to tangible prizes; avoid prizes for completion; no public individual ranking
rows.if: Learners are `child`ren (under 12)

rows.basis: [Seductive details](claims/seductive-details-effect.md) [~M] (school and university readers, not gamified); [cognitive overload](claims/cognitive-overload-degrades-learning.md) [~M]
rows.change: Strip theme, animation and decoration from the screen while items are worked; celebrate only between levels
rows.if: Learners are `novice`s, or the material is complex

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Let them test out of early levels on the step 4 check; give harder challenge levels rather than more points on easy items
rows.if: Learners are `advanced`, or already accurate

rows.basis: untested proposal; the earlier page's view that adults prefer progress views to badges has no claim behind it
rows.change: Tie levels to job tasks passed at a criterion; no badges for completion or seat time; no public ranking among colleagues; keep the theme sober
rows.if: `adult`s in a `workplace-clinical` setting (compliance, onboarding)

rows.basis: [Mangomon app, 21 Thai undergraduates](claims/mangomon-rpg-gamification-improves-business-vocabulary.md) [+W] (pre-post, no control); [Quizizz](claims/quizizz-gamification-better-memorization.md) [+W] and [mixed-methods study](claims/gamification-raises-motivation-satisfaction.md) [+W] (both known only through one review)
rows.change: A quiz or points layer is a reasonable vehicle; test recall a week after the last session, not only in the app
rows.if: Goal is `verbal-association` (second-language vocabulary, terms)

rows.basis: untested; from the earlier page (timed leaderboard formats reward speed and suit fluency more than reasoning)
rows.change: Award points for correct explanations and for solving changed problems, not for speed; avoid timed, speed-ranked quiz rounds
rows.if: Goal is a `concept`, `principle` or `complex-skill`

rows.basis: [Group rewards on individual learning](claims/cooperative-learning-group-rewards-and-individual-accountability.md) [+M] (school studies, four weeks or more, not gamified)
rows.change: Use team scores from individual quizzes (step 5), updated once a week on a class board; the teacher reviews the board, not every point
rows.if: `classroom` with one teacher and a large group

rows.basis: untested proposal; the meta-analysis pooled informal and online settings with school ones
rows.change: The software must give the informational message after each item (step 3) and run the level checks (step 4); if streaks are used, allow a missed day without losing the streak, so one absence does not end practice
rows.if: `online-self-paced`, no teacher present

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Run all scoring and feedback through one tool every learner reaches the same way; make teams mixed across room and remote; avoid speed-ranked live rounds, which penalise slow connections and small screens
rows.if: Mixed modes: some learners remote, some in the room, or phone-only

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Automate points, feedback and level checks; the facilitator spends about five minutes a week on the team or progress board and contacts learners whose practice stopped
rows.if: Scarce facilitator time (volunteers, a busy shift, a tutor who checks in briefly)

rows.basis: untested; no claim here tests a single gamified session
rows.change: Do not build a points economy; at most one team quiz round with feedback after each question and a short debrief; do not claim a motivational effect
rows.if: Time is a `single-session`

rows.basis: untested proposal; the earlier page's warning that leaderboards demotivate low-ranked learners has no claim behind it
rows.change: No public ranking; self-referenced progress only; badges and messages short, with icons and audio; first level designed so everyone succeeds
rows.if: Learners have low confidence or low literacy

rows.basis: untested; noted in the [autonomy claim](claims/autonomy-supports-intrinsic-motivation.md) [~W]'s Discussion with no study recorded
rows.change: Offer two options with a recommended default rather than an open menu
rows.if: Learners are uncomfortable choosing (some high power-distance settings, anxious novices)

rows.basis: untested; from the earlier page (effects weaker in high-stakes settings, no claim behind it)
rows.change: Keep points formative and separate from the grade; grade on an aligned task outside the game
rows.if: Points or badges feed a grade, or stakes are high

rows.basis: [Rewards claim](claims/rewards-undermine-intrinsic-motivation.md) [~S]; [group rewards on individual learning](claims/cooperative-learning-group-rewards-and-individual-accountability.md) [+M]; the combination is untested
rows.change: Keep it; change only what the evidence says matters: give points for accuracy and improvement rather than attendance or completion, add an informational sentence to each award, and base any team score on each member's learning
rows.if: The brief names its own routine (house points, a class reward chart, an existing app's XP or streaks)

rows.basis: [Process goals for novices](claims/process-goals-outperform-outcome-goals-for-novices.md) [+M]; tested with high-school writers, untested in other domains
rows.change: Novices: process goals naming the strategy steps, split into proximal sub-goals, outcome goals only once the process runs unprompted. Experienced learners: outcome goals with a stated criterion, which they may set or negotiate (learner-set goals are an untested proposal)
rows.if: Learners are `novice` on the task (new procedure, first attempts); or `intermediate`/`advanced`

rows.basis: [Goal setting improves performance](claims/goal-setting-improves-performance.md) [~M] (smaller on complex work tasks, not learning tasks)
rows.change: Expect a smaller effect from goal difficulty; prefer learning or process goals for the components over a hard overall score target; monitor strategy use, not only the score
rows.if: Goal is a `complex-skill` (whole task, many interacting parts)

rows.basis: [Specific, difficult goals](claims/specific-difficult-goals-lead-to-higher-performance.md) [+W]; work-task evidence, untested for learning
rows.change: A specific numeric target with frequent progress checks is reasonable (e.g. "18 of 20 items correct on Friday's check")
rows.if: Goal is facts or a `procedure` with a clear score

rows.basis: untested proposal; the self-monitoring evidence is from students in grades 4–12 with or at risk for disabilities and measures on-task behaviour, see [self-monitoring](claims/self-monitoring-improves-on-task-behavior.md) [~M]
rows.change: Teacher sets the goal with the child, one proximal sub-goal at a time, made visible on a chart; monitor with a simple tally or check-in rather than a written plan
rows.if: Learners are `child` (primary age)

rows.basis: [Implementation intentions](claims/implementation-intentions-improve-goal-attainment.md) [+M]; mostly university students and online-course adults
rows.change: Elicit the learner's own goal first and tie the task goal to it; add an if-then plan for the named obstacle (work, family time)
rows.if: `adult` or `adult-workplace` learners

rows.basis: [Implementation intentions](claims/implementation-intentions-improve-goal-attainment.md) [~M] (course completion rose for learners in individualist cultures, not collectivist)
rows.change: Build goal setting and an if-then plan into the first session (a short writing activity); show progress against the goal on every return; do not expect the prompt to help every learner
rows.if: `online-self-paced`, no teacher present

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Use one shared goal template and peer or self check-ins against the criterion; teacher reviews goals only for learners whose progress stalls
rows.if: Large class, one teacher

rows.basis: untested proposal; proximal goals evidence is [second-hand](claims/proximal-goals-feedback-peer-models-build-learning-efficacy.md) [+W]
rows.change: Set one proximal goal for the session and one check at its end; skip multi-week goal sheets
rows.if: Time available is one session

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Do not grade goal attainment itself; grade the learning outcome, keep goals as the learner's own tool, so learners do not set easy goals to secure a mark
rows.if: High-stakes assessment or graded goals

rows.basis: untested; from the earlier page; [self-efficacy predicts persistence](claims/self-efficacy-predicts-academic-persistence.md) [~W] is associational and does not test this move
rows.change: Start with a goal the learner judges reachable, show early success, then raise difficulty; give feedback on progress, not on the person
rows.if: Low self-efficacy or a history of failure on the task

rows.basis: [Graphic Organizers Support Novice Comprehension](claims/graphic-organizers-support-novice-comprehension.md) [~M] (in five studies each, low-ability learners gained from maps and high-ability learners did not; underpowered subsets); [Instructional guidance that helps novices can become redundant or counterproductive as expertise grows.](claims/expertise-reversal-effect.md) [~M] (a review, not tested on organizers)
rows.change: Drop the provided organizer; ask learners to sketch their own quickly, or use none; spend the time on application
rows.if: Learners are `advanced` on this material, or already explain its structure

rows.basis: [Story Mapping Improves Comprehension](claims/story-mapping-improves-comprehension.md) [+M] (third and fourth graders; 22 and 6 students; no standardized effect size)
rows.change: Use a story map (setting, characters, problem, goal, events, resolution), taught by modelling, leading and then testing; withdraw the map once accuracy holds
rows.if: Learners are `child` (primary age) reading stories, including learners with learning disabilities

rows.basis: untested; from the earlier page and its sources on adult literacy writing, which no claim records
rows.change: Use a planning organizer matched to the genre (claim–reasons–evidence for argument, a sequence for narrative), modelled, then used before each draft, then dropped once the plan can be made in note form
rows.if: Learners are `adult` literacy learners, and the goal is writing

rows.basis: [The same quizzing or concept-mapping activity produces more learning when done without viewing the material](claims/closed-book-versions-of-quizzes-and-concept-maps-outperform-open-book-versions.md) [+M] (second-hand); [Concept mapping improves learning over most comparison conditions by a moderate average amount, but not over time-matched retrieval practice](claims/concept-mapping-improves-learning.md) [~S] (with time matched, mapping beside the text lost to retrieval practice at one week, undergraduates)
rows.change: After comprehension, have learners build or complete the organizer with the text closed, then check against the text; or replace some mapping time with free recall
rows.if: Goal is `delayed-retention` of the content

rows.basis: [Learner-constructed graphic organizers are not shown to outperform provided ones: the one direct test, with college readers, favoured provided organizers on transfer](claims/learner-constructed-graphic-organizers-outperform-provided.md) [~M] (college readers, three experiments; transfer favoured provided organizers)
rows.change: Give a complete, author-built organizer with the text rather than asking for construction; add explanation prompts on its links
rows.if: Goal is `conceptual-understanding` or transfer from a demanding text, with novice readers

rows.basis: [Adding relevant pictures or graphics to text improves learning from it, with a small pooled effect on reading comprehension, though whether dual coding explains the benefit is disputed](claims/dual-coding-improves-learning.md) [+M] (graphics added to text helped reading comprehension, elementary to adult; carried to organizers, which it did not isolate); the reveal-and-compare step is untested
rows.change: Place the organizer next to the text it summarises (not on a separate page); give partial organizers with a reference version revealed after the learner submits; add one explanation question per organizer
rows.if: Setting is `online-self-paced`, no teacher present

rows.basis: [Teacher-student interactive semantic mapping produced higher EFL reading comprehension posttest scores than teacher-initiated and student-mediated semantic mapping](claims/interactive-semantic-mapping-outperforms-teacher-initiated-and-student-mediated.md) [+M] (EFL university students); [Collaborative concept mapping enhances learning more than individual concept mapping](claims/interactive-beats-constructive-concept-mapping.md) [+W] (second-hand)
rows.change: Have pairs build the organizer together; collect a few, project two that differ, and discuss which fits the content better and why
rows.if: `classroom` with a large group

rows.basis: [Teacher-student interactive semantic mapping produced higher EFL reading comprehension posttest scores than teacher-initiated and student-mediated semantic mapping](claims/interactive-semantic-mapping-outperforms-teacher-initiated-and-student-mediated.md) [+M] (187 Egyptian EFL freshmen, 20 one-hour sessions)
rows.change: Build a semantic map of the text with the class before and during reading, the teacher drawing out students' contributions, over many sessions
rows.if: Learners read in a second language

rows.basis: untested proposal; construction costs time and load ([Placing heavier cognitive demands on learners can be counterproductive in mapping tasks](claims/heavy-cognitive-demands-of-mapping-can-be-counterproductive.md) [~W])
rows.change: Provide one organizer with the material, one completion task and one explanation prompt; do not ask for construction from scratch; record what an unaided check shows and do not claim retention
rows.if: Time is one session only

rows.basis: [A hierarchical organization facilitates tasks only when matched to the task domain](claims/organization-task-match-determines-benefit.md) [~M] (20 high-school physics students); [Recall from bar graphs is more accurate when the recall format matches the studied graph format](claims/mismatched-graphic-organizers-increase-extraneous-load.md) [~M] (bar graphs, university students; carried to organizers)
rows.change: Do not force a template: use a sparse outline, or two organizers for two relations; align the organizer with the relation the assessment asks about
rows.if: The content has no single clear structure, or the assessment asks about a different relation than the organizer shows

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Judge readiness only on tasks done without the organizer; keep the organizer as a study and planning tool, not something that must be reproduced
rows.if: Stakes are high, or the assessment is unaided

rows.basis: untested; mechanism from [Chunking reduces working memory load by grouping information into fewer, more meaningful units.](claims/chunking-reduces-working-memory-load.md) [+M] (memory research, not organizer design)
rows.change: Split it into an overview of about five nodes and one linked view per branch; reveal branches as they are taught
rows.if: A dense organizer already exists (a course map, a 30-node concept map)

rows.basis: [Instructional guidance that helps novices can become redundant or counterproductive as expertise grows.](claims/expertise-reversal-effect.md) [~M] (review of cognitive-load studies; gives no crossover point)
rows.change: Drop most guided rounds; give one check item, then independent or whole-task practice with selective feedback
rows.if: Learners are `advanced` on this task, or succeed on the first item unaided

rows.basis: Child: [Contingent scaffolding improves learning more than fixed or absent support.](claims/contingent-scaffolding-improves-learning.md) [+M] (fourth and fifth graders, long division, 8 per condition). Adult: untested proposal
rows.change: Child: keep the cue–hint–demonstration ladder with one-to-one or small-group checking, and short rounds. Adult or professional: ask what they already do, and move guided items onto tasks from their own work as soon as the step is stable
rows.if: Learners are `child` (primary age), or `adult` / professionals

rows.basis: [In one experiment with 256 undergraduates, computer-based lesson versions that included practice produced significantly higher posttest scores than versions without practice](claims/practice-presence-raises-cbi-posttest-achievement.md) [+M] (undergraduates, one computer-based lesson; horizon not reported)
rows.change: Build practice items with automatic checking and feedback after each item into the lesson; do not cut them to save time; add an unaided check item before the next topic
rows.if: Setting is `online-self-paced`, no teacher present

rows.basis: [Taking initial multiple-choice tests without feedback can lead students to later produce the incorrect lure answers they selected](claims/multiple-choice-lures-can-be-learned-as-false-knowledge.md) [+W] (college students, retrieval testing, reported second-hand; untested for skill practice)
rows.change: Give the correct answer and a short reason after every item, so a chosen wrong option is not kept
rows.if: Practice items are multiple choice

rows.basis: untested proposal; contingent-support evidence is one-to-one and its classroom-scale effect is not shown ([Contingent scaffolding improves learning more than fixed or absent support.](claims/contingent-scaffolding-improves-learning.md) [~M])
rows.change: Have every learner show each attempt at once (mini-whiteboards, cards, a quick poll) so the teacher can scan them all; give whole-class feedback on the commonest error, then go to those who still fail. With older learners, pairs can also check each other against a worked answer; with young children, or when one misconception is widespread, the teacher's scan is safer than peer checking. Collect one unaided item from everyone before independent work
rows.if: `classroom` with one teacher and a large group

rows.basis: [Human tutoring has a medium effect over no tutoring, and in one small study students learned as well when tutors only prompted them as when tutors also explained and gave feedback](claims/tutoring-effectiveness-comes-from-scaffolding-and-feedback.md) [~M] (eighth graders, 11 tutor–student pairs: prompting without feedback learned as well)
rows.change: Replace some feedback-giving with prompts that ask the learner to explain or predict the next step; include one changed item in each round
rows.if: Goal is a `concept`, `principle` or transfer, not only a `procedure`

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Plan the session as model, three or four guided items, one unaided check; record what the check shows and do not claim retention
rows.if: Time is one session only

rows.basis: untested proposal; no claim sets a success rate for skill practice (a retrieval-practice moderator, [Retrieval practice effects become more robust as initial retrieval success increases, especially above 75%](claims/retrieval-practice-effects-more-robust-when-initial-retrieval-success-exceeds-75-percent.md) [~M], is about recall)
rows.change: Failing: return to the model or simpler items. Succeeding unaided: shorten or end guided practice. Set the threshold locally and record it
rows.if: Many attempts fail with help, or nearly all succeed without it

rows.basis: untested proposal; from the earlier page ("multiple steps, hidden decision points, or a high likelihood of early error")
rows.change: Plan more guided rounds per step; raise the release criterion (more consecutive unaided successes, on representative tasks); add a stage of unassisted work under supervision before full independence; define what "working alone" means (no supervision, or supervision with a way to escalate)
rows.if: The task has many steps or hidden decision points, or an error on the job is costly (safety, compliance, harm to a client)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Judge readiness only on unaided items, never on assisted success during practice; keep a record of every hint given
rows.if: Stakes are high, or the assessment is unaided

rows.basis: untested; from the earlier page (adult literacy and numeracy settings)
rows.change: Keep the language of practice items simpler than the target task; let learners show a step by doing it before explaining it; gloss terms the objective does not include
rows.if: Instruction is in the learners' second language, or learners have low literacy

rows.basis: [Part-task practice for novices](claims/part-task-practice-reduces-load-for-novices.md) [~M] (one experiment; sample and horizon not reported); [pretraining](claims/pretraining-improves-transfer.md) [+M] (one VR lesson, carried to other content)
rows.change: Keep the first whole to two or three ideas; pre-teach the one or two elements it depends on in a short isolated segment, then present the whole in the same session; make each later part small
rows.if: Learners are `novice` and the content is `high` in element interactivity

rows.basis: [Expertise reversal](claims/expertise-reversal-effect.md) [~M] (review of cognitive-load studies, carried to overviews; no crossover point)
rows.change: Replace the overview with the opening sketch; start at the first part they cannot explain; spend the time on integrative tasks
rows.if: Learners are `intermediate` or `advanced` for this content

rows.basis: [Ability moderates the benefit](claims/ability-moderates-hierarchical-organization-benefit.md) [~M] (college physics volunteers); [advance organizers](claims/advance-organizers-improve-learning.md) [~M] (older meta-analyses); the confidence part is untested
rows.change: Add a closing placement every session, a check on the top-level ideas before moving down, extra practice per part; praise correct placements privately
rows.if: Learners have weaker prior attainment, or low confidence

rows.basis: untested proposal; the hierarchy studies used college and advanced high-school students
rows.change: Make the whole concrete (a picture, story or physical model of the whole), keep each part to one lesson, and have the teacher lead the placement aloud before learners do it
rows.if: Learners are `child` or `adolescent`

rows.basis: untested proposal; [whole-task practice and transfer](claims/whole-task-performance-improves-transfer.md) [+W] is an argument, not a study
rows.change: Take the whole from their own work: the complete workflow or a real case they handle; elicit what they already do and start at the part where their account breaks down
rows.if: Learners are adults in a work setting (`adult-workplace`)

rows.basis: [No effect on local tasks](claims/no-organization-effect-on-local-tasks.md) [~M] (non-significant, not equivalence)
rows.change: Do not build a whole-first sequence; group the items plainly and use retrieval practice
rows.if: The goal is `verbal-association` (facts, names, vocabulary)

rows.basis: untested proposal; [whole-task practice and transfer](claims/whole-task-performance-improves-transfer.md) [+W]
rows.change: Make the whole a complete simple task, sequence tasks from simple to complex with the [4C/ID pattern](patterns/4cid-four-component-instructional-design.md), and keep the conceptual map as supporting information around the tasks
rows.if: The goal is a `complex-skill` (whole-task performance)

rows.basis: [Organisation–task match](claims/organization-task-match-determines-benefit.md) [~M] (20 high-school physics students, two-week test)
rows.change: Put the ideas that task draws on at the top of the map and of every closing placement; assess a matched task, not a recall of the map
rows.if: The assessment is high-stakes and uses one kind of task

rows.basis: [Learner-built organisation](claims/strong-acquisition-tasks-improve-internalization.md) [+M] (classroom study, untested online); [concept mapping](claims/concept-mapping-improves-learning.md) [~S] for the redraw; the persistent map is untested
rows.change: Keep the map on every screen with today's part highlighted; make the closing placement an arrange-or-label activity the system checks; add a redraw-from-memory item from the middle of the course
rows.if: `online-self-paced`, no teacher present

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Share the map as one image everyone can see on a small screen (few labels, large type); do the closing placement as a numbered poll or chat answer ("which of the five ideas does this detail belong to?") so remote and in-room answers are seen together
rows.if: Mixed mode: some learners remote, some in the room, or phone-only

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Have every learner show their placement at once (cards, mini-whiteboards, a poll), address the commonest misplacement to the whole group, then go to those still misplacing
rows.if: One teacher with a large group

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Give the whole and one part only; end with one placement and one integrative task; do not compress later parts into the same session or claim retention
rows.if: Time is one session only

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: State the whole as a labelled diagram with short phrases; keep the same term for the same idea in every session; let learners place items by arranging cards rather than writing a summary
rows.if: Learners study in a second language, or have low literacy

rows.basis: untested proposal; [whole-task practice and transfer](claims/whole-task-performance-improves-transfer.md) [+W]
rows.change: Make that product the whole: show a complete simple example of it first, then teach parts as the pieces of the product, and end with learners making a short complete version
rows.if: Learners will produce something for a real audience (a report, performance, product, or a talk to neighbours)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Keep the order but overlay a one-page map shown at the start and end of each topic, with the closing placement; add one integrative task per two or three topics
rows.if: The syllabus or textbook is fixed in topic-by-topic order

rows.basis: untested here; from the brief's statement that reward and emotion systems mature before control systems at these ages ([adolescent brain imbalance](claims/adolescent-brain-imbalance-reward-versus-control.md) [+W], the brief's summary of research, `q2`)
rows.change: Put more of the component into the adults (teachers and carers cue in the moment, structure the setting); keep the youth's practice short and frequent; give emotion regulation a large share
rows.if: Learners are `adolescent`, 11–15

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: The young person names the adult (mentor, supervisor, tutor, peer mentor); the adult's role is coaching on request and a regular short review, not monitoring; skip parents unless the learner asks
