rows.if: Learners are young `adult` (18–25), at college or work

rows.basis: [Parent-mediated intervention](claims/parent-implemented-intervention-improves-outcomes.md) [+M] (children with autism, ages 1–6 and school age); [parent coaching](claims/parent-coaching-outperforms-information-only.md) [+M] (ages 0–7). Both outside this page's 14–25 range
rows.change: Train the parent to deliver the practice at home, with coaching and rehearsal; expect larger effects where the parent delivers practice than from information
rows.if: Learners are `child` (under 12), or have autism or another developmental condition

rows.basis: [Empathic discipline](claims/brief-intervention-empathic-discipline-cuts-suspensions.md) [+M] (middle-school mathematics teachers; overall effect small and marginal in the preregistered replication, larger for students at high risk)
rows.change: Add a short exercise on the teachers' stance towards discipline (relationships first, the student's perspective) before or alongside the student programme; track exclusions by group of students
rows.if: Setting is a school `classroom` and the problem is conduct, exclusions or suspensions

rows.basis: [SEL and achievement](claims/sel-programs-improve-behavior-and-achievement.md) [~S] (K–12; academic gains significant only with school-staff delivery; negligible in recent randomised trials); [SRL training](claims/self-regulated-learning-improves-achievement.md) [~M] (larger effects with researchers than with regular teachers delivering)
rows.change: Have the regular teacher deliver or cue the skills inside academic lessons; promise only a small achievement effect; measure achievement on an independent test
rows.if: The goal is academic achievement

rows.basis: untested; from the brief's constraint that carers in chronic adversity have fewer resources for their own regulation and for co-regulation. The brief's stress claim ([toxic stress](claims/toxic-stress-disrupts-self-regulation-development.md) [~W], its summary of research) concerns the young person, not the carer
rows.change: Reduce the carers' stressors and support their own regulation before coaching co-regulation; add a mentor or programme facilitator as a second adult; keep adult sessions practical, short and at times they can attend
rows.if: Carers live with chronic adversity, poverty or overwhelming stress

rows.basis: [Co-regulation implementation](claims/co-regulation-implementation-factors-context-experience-strategy-ease.md) [~W] (facilitators' reports, adolescent programmes: welcoming easiest, breathing exercises hardest; class size and session length shaped use)
rows.change: Spend the adult time on the three or four adults who see the most young people (teachers, house staff); teach one move per session; replace weekly coaching with a 10-minute check on one logged incident; start with the welcoming routine, which facilitators found easiest
rows.if: One facilitator for many young people, or scarce facilitator time (volunteers, a busy shift, a brief check-in)

rows.basis: untested; the claim page on parent coaching says its evidence does not test remote coaching
rows.change: Hold the first adult session live (in person or video) so moves can be rehearsed and watched; run weekly coaching by phone or messaging around one logged incident; send the youth's cue cards as images
rows.if: Mixed modes: some adults remote, some in the room, or phone-only

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Spend it on the adults, not only the youth: one own-regulation routine and one co-regulation move, rehearsed; leave a cue card both sides share; do not promise lasting change
rows.if: A single session only

rows.basis: untested; coached practice beat written self-directed materials for parents at post-test ([parent coaching](claims/parent-coaching-outperforms-information-only.md) [+M], ages 0–7)
rows.change: Teach by demonstration and role-play, not handouts; one move per session; let adults log by voice note or a tick; praise what they already do well
rows.if: Adults have low literacy or low confidence

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Make the supervisor the co-regulating adult; fit coaching into existing supervision meetings (10–15 minutes); use the workplace's own incident types as role-play scenarios
rows.if: Adults in a work setting (supervisors of apprentices or trainees, `workplace-clinical`)

rows.basis: untested; [parent coaching](claims/parent-coaching-outperforms-information-only.md) [+M] for rehearsal over information
rows.change: Keep it; train the adults to run that routine and add only what the evidence says matters: rehearsal with feedback and one specific prompt to the young person
rows.if: The brief names its own routine (its check-in, its breathing step, its behaviour card)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Use them as the skill names the adults cue and the incident log's categories; do not substitute the programme's
rows.if: The brief has its own categories, criteria or behaviour rubric

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: The young person decides what adults see; adults are coached on their own responses, not given the youth's journal or check-in entries; agree in advance what a teacher or parent will be told
rows.if: Private or sensitive material (feelings, family conflict, a young person's disclosures)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Give minutes: 75 minutes for the first session (own regulation and one move, rehearsed), then six 15-minute coaching contacts; drop content, not rehearsal
rows.if: A fixed short time budget (for example 3 hours of adult time in a term)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Keep the performance whole; the adult rehearses with the young person a pre-performance routine and a debrief afterwards, rather than splitting the skill into exercises
rows.if: The young person is to use the skill in a whole real performance (a match, a placement, a presentation to a real audience, a job interview)

rows.basis: [Training facilitators](claims/srae-co-regulation-training-increases-self-regulation-knowledge.md) [~W] (gains were in self-reported knowledge only); [coaching components](claims/coaching-components-inconsistently-reported.md) [~W]
rows.change: Add an observed or recorded outcome (incidents, attendance, a rated observation) and a record of whether coaching happened
rows.if: Evaluation relies on the adults' or youth's self-report

rows.basis: [Creating community and interacting with students online required deliberate, planned effort unlike spontaneous face-to-face co-presence](claims/online-community-requires-conscious-effort.md) [+W] (interviews with web-based high-school teachers; carried to adult courses); the channel choices are untested
rows.change: Make the forum and private message the main routes with a published reply window of one working day; put live slots outside working hours and record them; accept questions as text or a short voice note
rows.if: `online-instructor-led`, asynchronous, `adult` learners working or caring

rows.basis: untested proposal; the queue-ordering finding ([NSF](claims/nsf-strategy-increases-helped-students-busy-normal-queues.md) [~M]) is from a simulated online office-hours queue, not a mixed room
rows.change: Run one help queue for both groups (a shared ticket list or chat), alternate between room and remote in it, repeat each in-room question aloud and post it with the answer, and give remote learners a turn first after each in-room one
rows.if: Mixed mode: some learners in the room, some joining remotely

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Use a text channel that works on a phone (messaging, forum app); never require video for help; send replies as short text with one image at most
rows.if: Learners work on phones only, or have poor bandwidth

rows.basis: [NSF](claims/nsf-strategy-increases-helped-students-busy-normal-queues.md) [+M] and [no strategy changes wait or resolved requests](claims/scheduling-strategy-no-effect-resolved-requests-wait-time.md) [~M] (simulation from one CS2 course's office hours; outcome is who gets help, not learning)
rows.change: Route task questions to a public forum with peer answers first and staff confirming; turn repeated questions into a frequently-asked page weekly; in live help, serve learners not yet helped first and cap each conversation; add staff or sessions when waits grow, since ordering does not shorten them
rows.if: One instructor for many learners (a large lecture course or an open online course)

rows.basis: [The NSF advantage over FCFS appears only above an arrival-rate threshold](claims/arrival-rate-threshold-nsf-advantage.md) [~M] (simulation: under a relaxed queue no ordering made a difference); the scheduling of extra slots is untested
rows.change: Add live slots in the two or three days before a deadline, publish a cut-off time for questions, and post a common-errors note the day before; outside peaks, one slot may be enough
rows.if: Deadline or exam surges

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: State before the end how learners can reach you afterwards, for how long and for what (a two-week reply window by email, say), and collect one question from each learner before they leave
rows.if: A single session only (a workshop, a one-off training)

rows.basis: [Positive teacher–student relationships are associated with greater student engagement and, more weakly, with achievement](claims/teacher-student-relationships-improve-engagement.md) [~M] (correlational meta-analyses, preschool to high school; negative relationships mattered more in primary school); the routines are untested
rows.change: Accessibility means routines in the room: the teacher circulates on a set route, learners have a help signal (a card or cup) so they need not call out, and the teacher holds brief informal talks with each pupil over a fortnight
rows.if: Learners are `child` (primary age)

rows.basis: [Belonging Interventions Improve Outcomes](claims/belonging-interventions-improve-outcomes.md) [~M] (college entrants; worked only where the setting afforded opportunities to belong); [Minority students visited the tutoring center more often, yet tutored minority and first-generation students had lower average GPAs](claims/minority-students-more-tutoring-visits-lower-gpas.md) [~W] (one college, associational)
rows.change: Invite each one personally to a first short contact; offer a private route and say that asking is expected, not remedial; follow up by name after the first quiet week; do not read high use of help as proof that the help works
rows.if: Learners with low confidence or literacy, first in family, or with bad past experiences of school

rows.basis: [Resolving a participation double-bind requires redesigning activity structures, not just adding outreach](claims/resolving-participation-double-bind-requires-redesigned-activity-structures.md) [~W] (one case of Spanish-speaking volunteers in civic budgeting committees; carried from civic participation to courses)
rows.change: Offer a route in the learners' stronger language (a bilingual assistant, written questions that can be translated, a separate session) rather than only interpreting into the main channel
rows.if: Learners study in a second language, or the instructor and learners do not share a language

rows.basis: [Tutors and trainee researchers most value supportive attitude, mastery of the research field, and accessibility in a research project supervisor](claims/supervisor-desirable-characteristics-survey.md) [+W] (online doctoral supervision; what people value, not an effect); the arrangement is untested
rows.change: Name the person to ask on each shift or project and a back-up; agree an escalation route for urgent questions and a slower one for learning questions; schedule short regular meetings rather than relying on ad hoc asking
rows.if: Adults in work settings (workplace training, clinical placement, supervision)

rows.basis: [Contingent scaffolding improves learning more than fixed or absent support.](claims/contingent-scaffolding-improves-learning.md) [+M] (one-to-one tutoring; not a test of access)
rows.change: Schedule contact (a booked slot or a required check of the first attempt) rather than waiting to be asked, and answer with prompts before explanations
rows.if: Learners are `novice` on the course's tasks

rows.basis: untested proposal (the expertise reasoning is on [Ask Experts](principles/ask-experts.md))
rows.change: Make contact on request and use it for critique of their work and for decisions they are unsure of, not explanation; keep the reply window but drop the required first contact
rows.if: Learners are `advanced` (experienced professionals, final-year students)

rows.basis: [Human embodiment in video: perceived social presence benefits learning ratings, but instructor-face inclusion shows no significant learning-performance difference](claims/human-embodiment-video-presence-effects.md) [~W] (second-hand review; learners rated learning higher, performance did not differ)
rows.change: Spend effort on replies and live contact rather than on putting the instructor's face in every video
rows.if: The course is pre-recorded video and the budget goes on production

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Publish what kinds of help are allowed before assessed work (clarifying the task, not checking answers), give every learner the same access to that help, and log it
rows.if: High stakes for the learner (a licensing exam, a grade that decides progression)

rows.basis: [Self Assessment Accuracy Is Low Without Training](claims/self-assessment-accuracy-is-low-without-training.md) [~M] (secondary and university students); [structured reflection](claims/reflective-practice-improves-outcomes-when-structured.md) [+M] (first-year engineering students, school writing-to-learn)
rows.change: Two or three specific prompts per entry with sentence starters; every "I understand" line followed by one check item scored against a key; teacher reply on a rotating sample in the first weeks.
rows.if: `novice` to the content or the practice (first-year students, first placement)

rows.basis: untested proposal; peer interaction is a reported moderator in [reflection interventions](claims/reflective-practice-evidence-mixed-in-professional-education.md) [~M], direction not stated on the claim page
rows.change: One open prompt about a decision or case, a fortnightly review entry, and peer reading in small groups; drop sentence starters.
rows.if: `advanced` learners or practitioners

rows.basis: untested proposal; the writing-to-learn synthesis covered elementary to college but reports no age-specific result except smaller effects in grades 6–8 ([Writing To Learn Improves Understanding](claims/writing-to-learn-improves-understanding.md) [~M])
rows.change: Entries of a sentence or two, or a drawing with a label, at the end of a lesson; one specific question at a time; the teacher reads and replies orally to a few each day.
rows.if: `child` (primary school)

rows.basis: [Dialogue journals meet SLA conditions](claims/dialogue-journals-meet-sla-conditions.md) [+W] (a theoretical argument, no data); from the earlier page's adult ESL source
rows.change: Use a dialogue journal: the learner writes, the teacher answers in a few sentences that model correct forms without marking errors, weekly; let the learner choose topics.
rows.if: Learners are learning a second language (adult ESL, multilingual classroom)

rows.basis: untested proposal; the writing-to-learn claim page's Discussion warns that transcription demands can crowd out the thinking writing is meant to prompt
rows.change: Allow spoken entries (a voice note), drawing, or sentence frames; shorten to one prompt; never correct form in a reflection entry.
rows.if: Low confidence in writing, or low literacy

rows.basis: [training with diary](claims/web-based-srl-training-with-diary-raises-srl-knowledge-and-self-efficacy-not-math.md) [~M] and [diary alone](claims/learning-diary-alone-no-significant-srl-gains-online-math-prep-course.md) [-M] (prospective university students, online mathematics preparation; no mathematics gain either way)
rows.change: Put the prompts in the platform at the end of each module, tied to that module; require a "next step" line; show the learner their last "next step" at the start of the next module; pair the diary with short self-regulation training.
rows.if: `online-self-paced`, no teacher present

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: One shared prompt posted where everyone sees it; entries submitted the same way for all (a short form or message works on a phone, typed or voice); the next-session summary drawn from all entries, remote and in-room alike.
rows.if: Mixed mode: some learners in the room, some remote, or phone-only

rows.basis: untested proposal; the reason for keeping some use of entries is [diary alone](claims/learning-diary-alone-no-significant-srl-gains-online-math-prep-course.md) [-M]
rows.change: Do not promise individual replies. Read a rotating sample (for example five entries a week), give one whole-group reply on the commonest confusion, and use peer reading in pairs with one question each; keep the learner's own reread of their last next step every time.
rows.if: One teacher for many learners, or scarce facilitator time (volunteers, a busy shift, a mentor who checks in briefly)

rows.basis: untested proposal; the gains above come from term-long programmes ([Writing To Learn Improves Understanding](claims/writing-to-learn-improves-understanding.md) [+M], larger with longer treatment)
rows.change: Do not set up a journal. Use one end-of-session reflection of three prompts (see [Reflection](principles/reflection.md)), ending in one change to try.
rows.if: One session only

rows.basis: [reflection interventions](claims/reflective-practice-evidence-mixed-in-professional-education.md) [+M] (higher education, pooled across reflective activities; not specific to logs or workplaces)
rows.change: A fieldwork log: after each shift or visit, one observed event, what was done and why, what to try next; the mentor reads the "try next" line before the next shift; a monthly review entry discussed with the mentor.
rows.if: Adults in work settings (placements, clinical rotations, apprenticeships, coaching)

rows.basis: [public vs private reflection](claims/public-vs-private-reflection-mixed.md) [~W]; [guided vs free reflection](claims/guided-reflection-yields-more-higher-order-paragraphs-than-free.md) [+W] (one graduate service-learning course)
rows.change: Grade completion, the use of the prompt and whether the planned next step was tried, not candour or prose; offer private entries alongside public ones.
rows.if: Entries are graded, or shared publicly (class blog, portfolio for assessors)

rows.basis: untested proposal; public blog paragraphs were more often descriptive but nearly a third were integrative in one course ([public vs private reflection](claims/public-vs-private-reflection-mixed.md) [~W])
rows.change: Keep a private working journal for analysis, and draw the public piece from it as a separate, revised product; judge the public piece as writing for its reader (see [Process-Based Writing](principles/process-based-writing.md)).
rows.if: The journal is written for a real audience (a published blog, a reflective piece shared with a community partner)

rows.basis: [Expressive Writing Improves Health Outcomes](claims/expressive-writing-improves-health-outcomes.md) [~M] (146 randomized studies, very small average effect on health); [Expressive Writing Improves Exam Performance](claims/expressive-writing-improves-exam-performance.md) [~M] (medium effect for test-anxious ninth graders; negligible across a later meta-analysis)
rows.change: Keep emotional writing private and optional, in a few short sessions, and do not expect learning gains from it; keep content prompts separate. Before a high-stakes exam, a short worry-writing exercise may be offered but should not be relied on.
rows.if: The aim is wellbeing, or processing emotionally charged material

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Shorten the entry to one line ("which items did I miss, and what will I do about them?") and spend the time on retrieval practice with feedback.
rows.if: Goal is `verbal-association` (vocabulary, facts)

rows.basis: [structured reflection](claims/reflective-practice-improves-outcomes-when-structured.md) [+M]; [diary alone](claims/learning-diary-alone-no-significant-srl-gains-online-math-prep-course.md) [-M]
rows.change: Keep it. Change only what the evidence says matters: make at least one prompt specific to the day's content and metacognitive (what is unclear, how do I know), add a "next step" line, and make sure someone or something uses the entries before the next session.
rows.if: The brief names its own journal routine, template or prompt set

rows.basis: untested proposal; specific prompts rest on the [structured reflection claim](claims/reflective-practice-improves-outcomes-when-structured.md) [+M]
rows.change: Make the prompt scaffold map line for line onto those criteria, five short lines at most so it fits a phone screen, with feelings optional and named as such; agree in writing who reads entries and what must never appear (names, identifying details), and let the learner choose which entries anyone reads (for example two or three anonymised entries a fortnight), the rest staying private, instead of rotating teacher replies; use the in-person session to rehearse one learner's chosen next step as a role-play
rows.if: The brief gives its own criteria for a good entry (a rubric or checklist), and entries are written privately on phones

rows.basis: [A hierarchical internal knowledge organization facilitates performance on complex recall and problem-solving tasks more than a single-level organization of the same knowledge](claims/hierarchical-organization-improves-complex-task-performance.md) [+M] (college physics, one report)
rows.change: Give the organization complete at first, with sorting tasks; move to partial frames only after they rebuild the top level from memory
rows.if: Learners are `novice` on this topic, holding unconnected facts

rows.basis: [Instructional guidance that helps novices can become redundant or counterproductive as expertise grows.](claims/expertise-reversal-effect.md) [~M] (review of cognitive-load studies; carried to organizations, which it did not test)
rows.change: Skip the given organization; ask them to rebuild it from memory, then reorganize it for a new task or critique where it fails
rows.if: Learners are `advanced`, or already state the organization unaided

rows.basis: [Ability moderates the hierarchical-organization advantage: low-ability subjects showed no significant benefit, while medium-ability subjects did](claims/ability-moderates-hierarchical-organization-benefit.md) [~M] (college physics; the adjustments are untested)
rows.change: Fewer items per sort, top level first and checked alone, more sort-and-rebuild cycles before adding levels; check whether they use the organization at all
rows.if: Learners are low-attaining, or struggled with the topic before

rows.basis: untested for organization design; narrative recall is better when stories follow a familiar story structure ([Narrative memory is superior when content follows stereotypical story grammar structure, and goal information is critical to comprehension](claims/story-grammar-structure-aids-narrative-memory.md) [+W], second-hand review, narratives only)
rows.change: Use story-like or picture-card organizations of two levels, sorted physically; for narrative content, organize around goal, events and outcome
rows.if: Learners are `child` (primary age)

rows.basis: [A hierarchical organization facilitates tasks only when matched to the task domain](claims/organization-task-match-determines-benefit.md) [+M] (advanced high-school physics, two weeks)
rows.change: Put the principles at the top and examples and procedures beneath them; test with problems that need two branches at once
rows.if: Goal is solving problems that use several principles (`principle`, `near-transfer`)

rows.basis: [Hierarchical versus single-level organization does not significantly affect performance on local tasks relying only on individual detailed steps](claims/no-organization-effect-on-local-tasks.md) [~M] (null result; equivalence not tested)
rows.change: Do not build a hierarchy for its own sake; practise the items with retrieval and feedback; use organization only where items need connecting
rows.if: Goal is recall of individual facts or carrying out single steps

rows.basis: [Comparing cases side by side improves learning and transfer by a moderate average amount, though in one algebra study it raised procedural knowledge and flexibility but not conceptual knowledge](claims/comparing-contrasting-cases-improves-learning.md) [+S] (tests comparison, not organization as such)
rows.change: Organize as a comparison: place two or three cases side by side and have learners list similarities and differences before the principle is named
rows.if: Goal is telling similar categories or cases apart (`concept`)

rows.basis: untested; the closed-book rebuild rests on [The same quizzing or concept-mapping activity produces more learning when done without viewing the material, as retrieval, than while viewing it](claims/closed-book-versions-of-quizzes-and-concept-maps-outperform-open-book-versions.md) [+M] (second-hand, settings not stated)
rows.change: Use drag-and-drop sorting into the organization with automatic checking, then a closed-book rebuild the learner compares with a reference map; do not drop the rebuild to save time
rows.if: `online-self-paced`, no teacher present

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Keep the organization as an indented outline that fits a phone screen, not a wide diagram; remote and in-room learners sort into the same shared document; read the top level aloud for those who cannot see the board
rows.if: Mixed modes: some learners remote, some in the room, or phone-only

rows.basis: untested at class scale; pairs building maps together is reported to beat individuals ([An ICAP theory article reports, second-hand and without describing the design, a study in which concept mapping with a peer enhanced learning more than concept mapping alone](claims/interactive-beats-constructive-concept-mapping.md) [+W], one study reported second-hand)
rows.change: One shared organization on the board; pairs sort printed cards into it; the teacher checks only top-level placement across the room, then everyone rebuilds individually from memory
rows.if: `classroom`, one teacher and a large group

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Show the organization, one sort task, one explained link, one closed-book rebuild at the end; record what the rebuild shows and claim nothing about retention
rows.if: Time is one session only

rows.basis: untested; mapping is slow and its advantage over time-matched retrieval is not shown ([Concept mapping improves learning over most comparison conditions by a moderate average amount, but not over time-matched retrieval practice](claims/concept-mapping-improves-learning.md) [~S])
rows.change: Give a finished organization rather than having learners build maps from scratch, which is slow; use the tutor's minutes only to look at a 3-minute closed-book sketch and ask about one link
rows.if: Facilitator time is scarce (volunteers, a busy shift, a tutor checking in briefly)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Use pictures or objects on cards for items, let learners explain links aloud or by pointing, and keep labels to a few words; sort before writing
rows.if: Learners have low confidence or low literacy

rows.basis: untested; the task-match finding is carried from physics students to workplace tasks ([A hierarchical organization facilitates tasks only when matched to the task domain](claims/organization-task-match-determines-benefit.md) [~M])
rows.change: Build the top level from the decisions or tasks of the job (for example, "what to check first, what to escalate"), using the learners' own cases as the items to sort
rows.if: Adults in a work setting

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Have them build their own organization of the topic first, then select from it what this audience needs; the audience sees the explanation, not the working map
rows.if: Learners must produce an explanation, talk or product for a real audience

rows.basis: [Hierarchical versus single-level organization does not significantly affect performance on local tasks relying only on individual detailed steps](claims/no-organization-effect-on-local-tasks.md) [~M]
rows.change: Keep separate retrieval practice on the details; judge readiness on both kinds of item, never on the organization exercise alone
rows.if: Stakes are high, and the exam mixes detail items with integrative ones

rows.basis: untested; the rebuild rests on [The same quizzing or concept-mapping activity produces more learning when done without viewing the material, as retrieval, than while viewing it](claims/closed-book-versions-of-quizzes-and-concept-maps-outperform-open-book-versions.md) [+M]
rows.change: Keep it; change only two things: tie its top level to the tasks learners will face, and add one closed-book rebuild of it per session
rows.if: The brief names its own routine (a note-taking template, a KWL chart, a unit map the school uses)

rows.basis: [concerns shifted from nonuser towards user profiles after a two-week workshop](claims/workshop-shifts-concerns-toward-user-profile.md) [+M] (one science curriculum, elementary teachers, no comparison group)
rows.change: Lead with clear information, visits and examples of the innovation in use, and individual reassurance; hold back detailed logistics and student-outcome data until use begins
rows.if: Most people have not used the innovation yet (`novice` for this innovation)

rows.basis: [concerns moved from lower to higher stages over a year of use](claims/stages-of-concern-developmental-trend.md) [+M] (associational, one curriculum); the matching move is untested
rows.change: Drop introductory sessions; give time to look at student work and effects, to collaborate and to try modifications; keep a short check for leftover management problems
rows.if: People are experienced users (`advanced` in this innovation), or already show impact concerns

rows.basis: [individual profiles diverge from group trends](claims/individual-concern-profiles-vary-widely.md) [+W] (two case profiles)
rows.change: Plan whole-group sessions for the peak, then read individual profiles and arrange separate contact for those who differ
rows.if: A whole staff or department is adopting at once, and the group profile has one clear peak

rows.basis: [follow-up contact related most strongly to adoption success](claims/follow-up-contact-strongest-adoption-success-factor.md) [+M] (NDN evaluation, reported second-hand) for keeping contact at all; the triage is an untested proposal
rows.change: Use the written open-ended question instead of interviews; group people by peak stage and give each group one short contact every two to three weeks; let colleagues at later stages handle early-stage questions; keep the facilitator's own time for those with high personal concerns
rows.if: One facilitator for many staff, or scarce facilitator time (a busy term, a part-time coach)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Use the first 10 minutes to collect written concern statements, then spend the session on the commonest peak; give one practical next step for use, and name who will follow up and when; do not claim the session changed use
rows.if: Only a single session is possible

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Collect concern statements by a short online form before the session; hold one-to-one follow-ups by call or video, cameras optional for those with personal concerns; share examples of the innovation in use as short videos
rows.if: Some staff join remotely while others are in the room, or contact is by phone or video only

rows.basis: untested proposal; from the sources' description of personal concerns
rows.change: Keep early contact private and one-to-one; start with what will be expected and what help exists; pair them with a colleague who has been through it; avoid observed demonstrations until they ask
rows.if: People are anxious, have low confidence with the innovation, or have high personal concerns

rows.basis: [unmentored teachers reached impact concerns more often than mentored ones](claims/mentors-may-inhibit-concern-development.md) [~M] (four volunteer groups, 39 teachers, association only); untested as a design rule
rows.change: Have the mentor read the newcomer's concerns rather than assume them; check whether the mentoring is holding the person at task concerns, and widen their contacts if so
rows.if: New teachers with an assigned mentor, or a mentoring scheme is the main support

rows.basis: untested; every claim here is from teachers, carried by analogy
rows.change: Use the same diagnosis and stage-matched support, with the questions worded for their work; record whether the stages read the same way
rows.if: Adults in a non-school workplace adopting a new procedure or system (`adult-workplace`, e.g. clinical or office staff)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Keep concerns data confidential and separate from evaluation (report group profiles only); say so when collecting it; expect higher personal concerns and plan more individual contact
rows.if: The change is mandated, or reports of use feed into performance evaluation

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Keep it; add one concerns question ("When you think about it, what are you concerned about?") and one use question ("What are you doing with it now?"), and change only the content of the follow-up by what they show
rows.if: The brief names its own routine for checking in (its own survey, staff meeting slot or coaching log)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Use its categories for describing use (in place of the LoU chart) and map them to the stages; do not substitute this page's labels
rows.if: The brief supplies its own categories, rubric or implementation checklist

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: The person decides who sees them; the facilitator works from what the person chooses to share or from anonymous group profiles
rows.if: Concerns or reflections are private (a personal journal, confidential statements to a counsellor)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Split it: about 10 minutes of check-in on concerns, about 80 minutes of stage-grouped work, and short individual follow-ups by message between sessions; give minutes, not topics, to each group
rows.if: A fixed short time budget (for example two hours of PD per month)

rows.basis: [the LoU interview can be rated reliably](claims/lou-interview-interrater-reliability-high.md) [+M] (as a way to read use); untested as an outcome rule
rows.change: Judge progress by observed or reported use at the next level, not by session attendance or concern scores alone; keep support attached to real use with real students
rows.if: The goal is full use of the innovation in real classrooms or work (a whole-task performance), not knowledge of it

rows.basis: [follow-up contact related most strongly to adoption success](claims/follow-up-contact-strongest-adoption-success-factor.md) [+M]
rows.change: Add follow-up contacts across the first term of use and a second concerns reading at about week 8
rows.if: A launch workshop is planned and then nothing

rows.basis: [an innovation foreign to its system tends to be rejected](claims/isolated-innovations-are-rejected-by-the-system-they-enter.md) [~M] (two narrative reviews, one author)
rows.change: Pair person-level matching with changes at the game-plan and policy levels (time, materials, assessment) that make the innovation fit
rows.if: The innovation is a single change foreign to the rest of the school's system

rows.basis: [Chunking reduces working memory load by grouping information into fewer, more meaningful units.](claims/chunking-reduces-working-memory-load.md) [~S] (reviews and lab experiments on immediate memory; carried to recall planning, untested); gap choice in [Spaced Learning](principles/spaced-learning.md)
rows.change: Keep the opening recall close to how it was taught, with answers shown at once; group the material into a few units before recall; plan returns at short gaps first
rows.if: Learners are `novice` on this material

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Drop it from the opening rotation; keep one item in cumulative checks; spend the time on newer material
rows.if: Learners are `advanced` or already recall it on a delayed check

rows.basis: untested; the spacing evidence comes mostly from young adults and is thin for children's long-term retention ([Spaced Practice Improves Retention](claims/spaced-practice-improves-retention.md) [~S])
rows.change: Keep recall items short and low-stakes, read aloud where reading is weak, and space returns across days in class time rather than homework
rows.if: Learners are children (`child`, `adolescent`)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Make the later encounters job tasks that need the material (a case at a team meeting, a checklist step on shift), and check unaided in the form the job uses; agree the horizon with the learner
rows.if: Adults in work settings, learning for use on the job

rows.basis: [Spaced Practice Improves Retention](claims/spaced-practice-improves-retention.md) [~S] (one meta-analysis summarised there: longer lags helped verbal tasks up to a point but reduced effects for skill tasks such as typing and music)
rows.change: Reactivate by doing the procedure, not by recalling a description of it; for motor skills use shorter gaps than for verbal material and check on the whole performance
rows.if: Goal is a `procedure` or motor skill, not facts or vocabulary

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Teach, then put a different 10–15 minute task in between, then an unaided recall; hand over a dated self-test sheet for days 2, 7 and 21; state that retention was not measured
rows.if: Only one session, no follow-up

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Spend 2–3 of the 10 minutes on recall of earlier items before new material; never let the review queue take the whole slot; cap new items so returns fit
rows.if: A fixed short time budget (for example 10 minutes a day)

rows.basis: [Learners Misjudge Spacing Benefits](claims/learners-misjudge-spacing-benefits.md) [+M] (adults, lab and flashcard software: learners prefer massing, so do not leave scheduling to them)
rows.change: Put the returns in the app's queue or a dated reminder, with automatic checking; show a delayed check, not a streak, as the progress signal
rows.if: Online, self-paced, or phone-only

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Run the opening recall on a shared form or poll both groups answer at once; send remote learners the same dated self-test sheet as those in the room
rows.if: Some learners remote, some in the room

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Use self-marked recall (learners check against an answer card) and look only at the items many missed; spend facilitator time on re-explaining those, not on marking
rows.if: One teacher or tutor for many learners, or scarce facilitator time (volunteers, a busy shift)

rows.basis: [Gains from an intensive period of second-language study persist for weeks without rehearsal.](claims/l2-fluency-gains-persist-weeks-without-practice.md) [~M] (18 undergraduates, one pilot, no control group; carried to other material untested)
rows.change: Give a short unaided check first; resume from it; do not reset progress or repeat the whole unit by default
rows.if: A learner returns after a gap with no practice

rows.basis: untested; learners read ease as learning ([Fluent Illusions Mislead Self Assessment](claims/fluent-illusions-mislead-self-assessment.md) [~M], adult lab studies)
rows.change: Keep recall private and ungraded; use oral or picture-cued items; say that forgetting between sessions is expected and that recall that feels hard is still useful
rows.if: Learners have low confidence or low literacy

rows.basis: [Spaced Practice Improves Retention](claims/spaced-practice-improves-retention.md) [+S] (spacing against massing at equal time); release rule untested
rows.change: Plan backwards from the date: at least three spaced cumulative checks before it, the last a few days out, not the night before; judge readiness only on unaided delayed checks
rows.if: Stakes are high, or the assessment date is fixed

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Keep it; change only what matters here: that the items are answered unaided before the answer is shown, that they include material from two or more sessions back, and that a delayed check decides when an item retires
rows.if: The brief names its own review routine (its own warm-up, flashcard deck, check-in or weekly quiz)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Use them as the units for grouping and as the criteria on the delayed check; do not substitute this page's
rows.if: The brief gives its own categories, criteria or rubric

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Learners keep their own recall answers and mark them themselves; report only whether they want help, never the content
rows.if: The material or the learner's answers are private or sensitive

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Reactivate by doing a smaller whole version of the task at later sessions (a short presentation, a full but brief case), not by splitting it into recall items; keep the final performance whole
rows.if: The goal is a whole-task performance, or a product for a real audience

rows.basis: [The timing of acute exercise relative to learning modulates memory consolidation](claims/acute-exercise-timing-memory.md) [~S] (healthy adults, lab episodic-memory tasks; carried to classrooms untested)
rows.change: Schedule the activity after the learning episode, not during it; an activity some hours after has shown more effect than one straight after in adult lab studies
rows.if: The brief plans physical activity or breaks around learning

rows.basis: [Instructional guidance that helps novices can become redundant or counterproductive as expertise grows.](claims/expertise-reversal-effect.md) [~M] (review of cognitive-load studies; no crossover point)
rows.change: Skip the full model: let them attempt first, then compare their work with an expert model and name the differences; model only the one new decision
rows.if: Learners are `advanced` on this task, or succeed on the first item unaided

rows.basis: [Lower-prior-knowledge learners scored higher on an algebra posttest after full-worked than completion-worked examples, while higher-prior-knowledge learners' non-significant advantage ran the other way](claims/lower-prior-knowledge-learners-score-higher-with-full-than-completion-worked-examples.md) [~M] (college algebra, one experiment; carried to live modelling)
rows.change: Keep complete models (every step shown and narrated) for longer before any partial or completion model; slow down and segment further (one decision per pause)
rows.if: Learners have very low prior knowledge of the task

rows.basis: [Modeling training improved imaginative play in disadvantaged kindergartners, with gains in imaginativeness, verbal communication, spontaneity, and attention span persisting two months](claims/modeling-training-improves-imaginative-play.md) [+W] (80 kindergartners, a 1973 report read second-hand; modelling combined with direct teaching)
rows.change: Model by acting out with materials in small groups, over several short sessions (the study used eight), and let children re-enact straight after
rows.if: Learners are young `child`ren, and the target is play, social or motor behaviour

rows.basis: [Prompting learners to self-explain improves understanding and problem solving on immediate tests by a moderate average amount, with little evidence yet on delayed or classroom gains.](claims/self-explanation-improves-conceptual-understanding.md) [+S]; [Erroneous examples improve conceptual understanding by forcing comparison with correct models.](claims/erroneous-examples-build-conceptual-knowledge.md) [+M] (grades 4–5, decimals, tutoring; carried to live modelling)
rows.change: Model on two items that differ on the surface; at each pause ask why, not what; include one error and its repair, and ask learners what gave it away
rows.if: Goal is a `concept` or `principle`, or transfer, not only a `procedure`

rows.basis: [Learners' task-specific self-efficacy beliefs predict whether they initiate, persist through, and recover from difficulty on academic tasks.](claims/self-efficacy-predicts-academic-persistence.md) [+M] (two reviews; names watching similar others as one source of self-efficacy, does not compare model types). [Proximal goals and ability attributional feedback for early learning raise self-efficacy more than distant goals and effort feedback, by a review's report of earlier studies](claims/proximal-goals-feedback-peer-models-build-learning-efficacy.md) [~W]: its title names peer models, but neither of its entries reports them
rows.change: Use a model the learners see as like themselves (a peer, a former student, the teacher showing an early struggle), who makes and recovers from mistakes and says what they did next; pair it with an early task they can succeed at
rows.if: Goal is confidence, persistence or willingness to try (`attitude-motivation`), not only skill

rows.basis: [Mentor modelling and a school-wide behaviour program's strategies transferred to the mentee's classroom management practices](claims/mentor-modelling-strategies-transfer-mentee-behaviour-management.md) [+W] (one preservice teacher, qualitative case); [Vicarious experiences are positively related to agriculture teachers' general teaching efficacy, with observing a first year teacher explaining 11% of variance](claims/vicarious-experiences-positive-teaching-efficacy.md) [+W] (correlational, reported in a review)
rows.change: Model the performance in the real setting (the mentor's own lesson, a supervised shift), then debrief the decisions it involved, then have the novice try the same move with the mentor watching
rows.if: `adult` learners in a work setting (`workplace-clinical`), or teachers in training

rows.basis: [Comparing original texts to model paragraphs prompted noticing that was again focused on lexical features](claims/model-comparison-noticing-lexical.md) [~W] (one EFL learner, case study); [Teacher modeling with worked examples helped EFL students internalize reading comprehension strategies](claims/teacher-modeling-internalizes-reading-strategies.md) [+W] (students' questionnaire comments, one study); otherwise untested
rows.change: Draft live in front of learners, thinking aloud about audience and choices, and revise visibly; show two different good products and name the features they share, so learners do not copy one product's wording
rows.if: Writing, composing or other open tasks with no single right answer

rows.basis: [Students are more attentive to the teacher's model track when they hear their own recording first](claims/student-recording-first-increases-attention-to-model.md) [+W] (language lab, design report; attention, not learning, was observed). For true novices on a new performance, model first (step 2 of the default)
rows.change: Have learners record their own attempt, listen to it, then hear the model, then try again
rows.if: Pronunciation, music or other performances learners can record

rows.basis: untested proposal; the explanation prompt is carried from [Prompting learners to self-explain…](claims/self-explanation-improves-conceptual-understanding.md) [+S]
rows.change: Record short clips, one decision each (about 2–5 minutes), each ending in a predict-or-explain question the learner must answer before the next clip; follow with automatically checked practice items
rows.if: Setting is `online-self-paced`, or video only

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Model on a shared screen or document camera rather than a whiteboard; narrate into the microphone; at each pause collect predictions in the chat or a poll from everyone, remote first; record the model and share it after for replay. For phone-only learners, send the recording cut into short clips with the pause questions in text
rows.if: Some learners are remote while others are in the room, or some join by phone only

rows.basis: untested proposal; the explanation step is carried from [Prompting learners to self-explain…](claims/self-explanation-improves-conceptual-understanding.md) [+S], and the large field study under [Constructive learning beats active and passive learning](claims/constructive-learning-beats-active-passive.md) [~M] found only the most interactive activities ahead of passive ones in real classes
rows.change: Give one live model to all; at each pause have every learner show a prediction at once (cards, mini-whiteboards, a poll); then in pairs, one learner narrates the next item while the other checks against the modelled decision list; re-model only for the error most pairs show
rows.if: One teacher with a large group

rows.basis: [Example-based sequences outperform problem-only practice for novices, and fading support is argued to aid transfer](claims/worked-examples-with-practice-improve-transfer.md) [+M] (example-first beat problem-first in one short troubleshooting task, immediate test)
rows.change: Model one item fully with narration, then a partial model the learners finish, then one unaided item; record what the unaided item shows and do not claim retention
rows.if: Time is one session only

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Model by doing more than by telling: fewer words, gestures, labelled pictures; name and display only the key terms; let learners show the next move rather than explain it in words
rows.if: Learners have low literacy, or work in a second language

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Model the finished performance once at full speed as the audience would see it; then model it again slowed down with the reasoning narrated, in a rehearsal space the audience never sees; keep the reasoning in a debrief or a separate annotated version
rows.if: The performance is for a real audience, or a product whose audience should not see the reasoning (a client-facing call, a published piece)

rows.basis: untested proposal; the error step is carried from [Erroneous examples improve conceptual understanding by forcing comparison with correct models.](claims/erroneous-examples-build-conceptual-knowledge.md) [+M]
rows.change: Model the whole procedure once at normal speed, then step by step with what to check and why; include the commonest error and how it is caught; require an unaided demonstration under supervision before the learner works alone
rows.if: High stakes or safety (clinical, lab, machinery)

rows.basis: [Process goals lead to better skill acquisition for novices than outcome goals.](claims/process-goals-outperform-outcome-goals-for-novices.md) [+M] (high-school writing revision); [self-efficacy predicts persistence](claims/self-efficacy-predicts-academic-persistence.md) [+M] (predictive reviews, not a test of the move)
rows.change: Treat expectancy as the low component: an item they can do first, process goals, feedback naming the strategy that worked; hold back rewards and hooks
rows.if: Learners are `novice` on the task and withdraw after early failure

rows.basis: [Expected tangible rewards reduce later free-choice engagement with a rewarded task, while verbal praise does not](claims/rewards-undermine-intrinsic-motivation.md) [~S] (undermining is for tasks already found interesting); choice and challenge untested here
rows.change: Do not add tangible rewards or points for taking part; offer harder goals and choices of topic or product
rows.if: Learners are `advanced` or already interested in the topic

rows.basis: [Rewards](claims/rewards-undermine-intrinsic-motivation.md) [~S] (one meta-analysis found rewards more detrimental for children than college students); [praise for intelligence](claims/feedback-praise-reduces-learning.md) [~M] (fifth graders, nonverbal problems)
rows.change: No tangible rewards for merely taking part; praise the strategy or effort, not the child's cleverness, especially before harder work; the teacher keeps the progress chart
rows.if: Learners are `child` (primary age)

rows.basis: [Task value](claims/task-value-increases-motivation-and-engagement.md) [+M] (reviews; the writing exercise reported second-hand)
rows.change: Value first: the relevance-writing exercise at each unit start, two or three options of topic within the unit
rows.if: Learners are `adolescent` and say the subject is pointless

rows.basis: untested proposal; [task value](claims/task-value-increases-motivation-and-engagement.md) [+M] carried from school and college reviews to the workplace
rows.change: Ask what each learner wants from it; tie each module to a task from their own job; cut time cost (short modules in work time); give a reason for each required item
rows.if: Adults in work settings, training they did not choose (compliance, onboarding)

rows.basis: [Belonging Interventions Improve Outcomes](claims/belonging-interventions-improve-outcomes.md) [+M] (college entry only; no effect where belonging was not afforded)
rows.change: A short belonging exercise at entry (adversity is common and passes, written in their own words); check that the setting gives them real ways to take part
rows.if: First year of college, a new school, or learners from groups who are often told they do not belong

rows.basis: [Math anxiety has a small-to-moderate negative correlation with math achievement (r = −.28) in a meta-analysis of correlations from 223 studies](claims/math-anxiety-degrades-performance.md) [~M] (correlation r = −.28 across 223 studies; direction not established); the moves are untested
rows.change: Private, untimed first attempts; no public answering until the learner has succeeded privately; simpler language in instructions than in the target task
rows.if: Learners with low confidence, low literacy, or anxiety about the subject (for example mathematics)

rows.basis: [Pre-tests reduced adult learners' persistence in a MOOC, though they improved post-test scores among those who completed it](claims/pretesting-can-harm-motivation.md) [~M] (one randomized MOOC experiment, abstract); the rest untested
rows.change: Do not open with a test on material not yet taught, or make it optional and say errors are expected; track return days and completion, not clicks; build the four questions into the first activity
rows.if: `online-self-paced` and voluntary (an open online course)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Contact remote learners by name in the first minutes of each session; give them the same private first attempt (a message or form) the room gets; keep choices workable on a phone
rows.if: Mixed modes: some learners remote, some in the room, or phone-only

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Spend the scarce minutes on one question about the likely low component, and on the learners whose behaviour dropped; let relevance sentences and progress records be written by learners without the facilitator
rows.if: One teacher with many learners, or scarce facilitator time (volunteers, a busy shift, a tutor checking in briefly)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Give the reason, one first success, and one choice; record the behaviour; do not claim lasting motivation
rows.if: Time is one session only

rows.basis: untested proposal; how audiences work is on [Authentic Audiences and Purposes](principles/authentic-audiences-purposes.md)
rows.change: Let the audience supply the reason; lower the cost of public failure with a private rehearsal and feedback before the audience sees it
rows.if: A product or performance for a real audience

rows.basis: [Rewards](claims/rewards-undermine-intrinsic-motivation.md) [~S]; [math anxiety](claims/math-anxiety-degrades-performance.md) [~M] (correlational); untested as a package
rows.change: Present grades as information about what to do next; do not add prizes; reduce timed public performance for anxious learners
rows.if: Stakes are high (grades, certification)

rows.basis: [Growth-mindset interventions have weak average effects on achievement, including a negligible GPA gain (d = 0.11) for lower-achieving US ninth-graders in one preregistered national trial](claims/growth-mindset-improves-achievement.md) [~S] (ninth-graders; about a tenth of a grade point for lower achievers, weak overall)
rows.change: Keep it short, pair it with strategy instruction on the actual work, and make sure effort visibly changes results in the course; aim it at lower-achieving learners; expect a small effect
rows.if: The plan relies on a mindset message, a motivational talk or an assembly

rows.basis: untested proposal; [rewards](claims/rewards-undermine-intrinsic-motivation.md) [~S] for the points change
rows.change: Keep it; change only what the evidence says matters: points tied to progress or performance rather than mere participation, the check-in asking about the low component, the survey followed by a probe of learning
rows.if: The brief names its own routine (its own points system, motivation survey, check-in or reward chart)

rows.basis: [Positive motivational assessments of introductory activities correlate weakly with learning outcomes on near-in-time tests but not with distant exam results](claims/motivational-assessments-correlate-weakly-near-tests.md) [~M] (elementary pupils, one study)
rows.change: Measure voluntary return or later course choice, not enjoyment at the end of a session
rows.if: The goal is `attitude-motivation` itself (continued study, voluntary practice)

rows.basis: Novice: [multiple representations](claims/multiple-representations-improve-learning.md) [~M] (the review ties the benefit to representational competence). Advanced: untested proposal (the claim pages discuss expertise reversal; no entry here tests it for modes)
rows.change: Novice: use words plus one visual type. Teach how to read it first (what the axes, arrows or symbols mean), add one explicit translation prompt per idea, and hold back a second visual type until learners can read the first. Advanced: cut to the most efficient representation, drop duplicating modes, and use translation tasks for checking rather than teaching.
rows.if: Learners are `novice` on this content and unfamiliar with its representations; or `advanced`

rows.basis: [Dual coding](claims/dual-coding-improves-learning.md) [+M]: the meta-analysis effect held across grade levels (elementary to adult); [learning-styles matching](claims/learning-styles-matching-does-not-improve-learning.md) [-M]: no style × modality interaction with 5th graders
rows.change: Pair text with a relevant graphic, picture or flow diagram. Do not sort children by a style inventory.
rows.if: Learners are `child` (primary school) readers

rows.basis: [Multiple representations](claims/multiple-representations-improve-learning.md) [+M]: one undergraduate electrodynamics course; untested with children or outside physics
rows.change: Add a dynamic or manipulable representation (simulation) and a learner-made sketch beside the symbolic form. Budget for higher effort while learners work.
rows.if: The goal is a `principle` or `concept` in a mathematical or physical domain (how a quantity behaves)

rows.basis: untested; from the earlier page (demonstration and gesture are untested here)
rows.change: Show it (a demonstration or video) with spoken steps, and have learners perform it. Keep a short written step list to consult.
rows.if: The goal is a `procedure` or physical action (`skill-performance`)

rows.basis: [Modality](claims/modality-effect-narration-over-text.md) [~M]: its advantage shrinks when learners control pacing
rows.change: On-screen text beside a static visual is acceptable. Give pause, replay and a text version. Do not convert all text to audio.
rows.if: `online-self-paced`, learner-paced media

rows.basis: [Modality](claims/modality-effect-narration-over-text.md) [~M]; [redundancy](claims/redundancy-principle.md) [~M]
rows.change: Narrate the explanation over the animation. Keep only labels and key terms on screen. Avoid full-sentence duplicate text.
rows.if: Live lecture, broadcast or other system-paced video with animation

rows.basis: [Video with narration and text](claims/video-narration-text-improves-immediate-macs-comprehension.md) [+M]: one randomized study of Chinese-speaking university EFL learners, immediate test only; [redundancy](claims/redundancy-principle.md) [~M] reports reversals for abridged text
rows.change: Keep the text available alongside narration and video rather than removing it as redundant. Monitor comprehension of the words alone.
rows.if: Learners work in a second language (`adult` L2 readers)

rows.basis: [Dual coding](claims/dual-coding-improves-learning.md) [+M]: graphics helped more on open-ended and mixed-format tests than on true/false ones
rows.change: Assess in a format that asks learners to use the representation (explain, predict, sketch), not only true/false recall. Decide in advance whether diagrams may be consulted at the test.
rows.if: Assessment is open-ended or high-stakes

rows.basis: untested; from the earlier page ("attention to access"); captions count as accommodation, not redundancy
rows.change: Give every essential meaning a second accessible route: captions and transcripts, text descriptions of visuals, signed or spoken versions. Test the materials on the device learners will use.
rows.if: Deaf, hard-of-hearing or blind learners, or no sound or small screens available

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Use one representation pair, not a full set. Build the translation prompts and their model answers into the material, so a learner without a teacher can check a sketch or explanation.
rows.if: One session only, or no teacher present

rows.basis: [Self Assessment Accuracy Is Low Without Training](claims/self-assessment-accuracy-is-low-without-training.md) [~M] (secondary students, one randomised experiment; a higher-education meta-analysis read as an abstract)
rows.change: Teacher-chosen methods; criteria with an example of each level; postpone learner choice of format and self-assessment that counts until learners have practised judging two or three examples
rows.if: Learners are `novice` on the goal and new to judging quality

rows.basis: untested; from the earlier page (adults with rich applied experience)
rows.change: Let them propose a method and the evidence it will produce, checked against the criteria before they start; accept work products from their practice
rows.if: Learners are `advanced`, or adults with applied experience

rows.basis: [Preschool children demonstrate behavioral knowledge of classification, one-to-one correspondence, and seriation during everyday free play with everyday materials](claims/free-play-reveals-behavioral-math-knowledge.md) [+W] (one observed play episode, two children); [Assessment tasks built on family-identified funds of knowledge elicited computational thinking from K-2 children in a small design-based study that made no comparison with standard assessment](claims/funds-of-knowledge-tasks-reveal-computational-thinking.md) [+W] (13 K–2 children, design study, no comparison with a standard test)
rows.change: Observe the goal in play or with objects and pictures, with a short interview ("show me", "why there?"), alongside any written task; record what each child did
rows.if: Learners are young children (`child`, pre-school or early primary)

rows.basis: [Typical verbal achievement tests may underestimate students' subject-matter knowledge because of a mismatch between the test's symbolic form and students' symbolic encoding](claims/verbal-achievement-tests-may-underestimate-via-symbolic-mismatch.md) [+W] (an argument in a review, not tested)
rows.change: Pair every written method with a spoken, demonstrated or drawn one that does not need the same reading and writing; read instructions aloud; do not read a low written score as low knowledge until the second method agrees
rows.if: Learners have low literacy, are learning in a second language, or have low confidence

rows.basis: [Math anxiety has a small-to-moderate negative correlation with math achievement (r = −.28) in a meta-analysis of correlations from 223 studies](claims/math-anxiety-degrades-performance.md) [~M] (meta-analysis of correlations, r = −.28; does not test a change of format)
rows.change: Add an untimed or low-pressure second method (a conversation, a take-home task, an observed task) before judging; drop time limits unless speed is the goal
rows.if: Learners are anxious about tests, or a timed written test is the only method

rows.basis: untested; from the earlier page ("performance plus reflection"); the [Authentic Assessment](patterns/authentic-assessment.md) pattern holds the task design
rows.change: Combine an observed performance or product with the learner's short written or spoken account of the decisions behind it; use one rubric for both
rows.if: The goal is a `complex-skill` or performance (a lab, a clinical task, a design)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: One well-sampled method (many short items) is usually enough; add a second method only to check that a correct answer is not recognition alone
rows.if: The goal is `verbal-association` or a `procedure`

rows.basis: [Static individual assessment misses developing functions; ZPD-based assessment reveals potential competencies](claims/static-assessment-misses-emerging-functions.md) [+W] (a theoretical argument)
rows.change: Give a short third check that removes the demand that differs; for a capability that shows only with help, record what the learner did with one hint, and judge the unaided result
rows.if: A learner's methods disagree (strong in conversation, weak in writing; or the reverse)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Keep it; add only a second method for the goals the routine samples in one mode, and write the routine's criteria so they apply to both
rows.if: The brief names its own assessment routine (its own rubric, portfolio, check-in or exam)

rows.basis: [Raters differed significantly in severity/leniency in the MFRM analysis](claims/raters-differed-severity-mfrm.md) [~M] (three raters, open-ended items); [In one community-college lab class, six scorers rating six teams with an engineering rubric differed by a mean of 1.2 of 9 points, which the authors read as a sign the rubric may not be reliable](claims/engineering-rubric-low-scoring-reliability.md) [~W] (one class)
rows.change: Rest the decision on at least two methods per goal; calibrate markers on examples in each format and double-mark a sample; give a learner near the cut a third method before deciding; keep untrained peer judgements out of the mark
rows.if: Stakes are high: a grade boundary, pass mark or certification

rows.basis: [Autonomy support increases intrinsic motivation, engagement, and persistence in learning.](claims/autonomy-supports-intrinsic-motivation.md) [+M] (motivation, not achievement); [Learning Styles Matching Does Not Improve Learning](claims/learning-styles-matching-does-not-improve-learning.md) [-M] (tested for instruction, carried to assessment)
rows.change: Two or three options, one rubric, each option checked for equal demand before release; do not match formats to "learning styles"
rows.if: Learners are offered a choice of format

rows.basis: [Peer assessment improves academic performance by a small average amount relative to no assessment or to teacher assessment](claims/peer-assessment-improves-performance.md) [+M] (meta-analysis of 54 studies; about performance, not the accuracy of peer judgements); the targeting rule is untested
rows.change: Keep one quick common method for everyone; use the second method only for learners near a decision or out of line with their other work; use trained peer review for the second reading of products; a 2-minute oral check per learner at most
rows.if: One teacher for a large group, or scarce marker time (volunteers, a busy shift, a tutor who checks in briefly)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Use two methods inside the session (a written item and a 1-minute spoken or drawn one) for the one goal that matters; use the result to steer the next step, not to grade
rows.if: Time is one session only

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Choose methods every mode can do (a short spoken or recorded answer, a photo of a drawing or worked page, a poll); give remote and phone learners the same criteria and time; note the mode beside each result and compare across modes before combining
rows.if: Mixed modes: some learners in the room, some remote, some on phones only

rows.basis: untested proposal; from the earlier page (adults with applied experience)
rows.change: Combine observation of the task at work (a checklist) with a short conversation about why each step was done, and a work product; use the workplace's own records where they show the goal
rows.if: Adults in work settings, or the goal is a job task

rows.basis: untested proposal; the audience relationship is owned by [Authentic Audiences and Purposes](principles/authentic-audiences-purposes.md)
rows.change: Judge it against the criteria separately from the audience's response; record the audience's response as its own observation, and add the learner's account of decisions as a second method
rows.if: The work is a product or performance for a real audience

rows.basis: untested proposal; self-assessment limit from [Self Assessment Accuracy Is Low Without Training](claims/self-assessment-accuracy-is-low-without-training.md) [~M]
rows.change: Pair auto-scored items with one short constructed or recorded response per goal, reviewed by a peer with the criteria or sampled by a tutor; have the learner self-assess against the criteria with an example first
rows.if: `online-self-paced`, no teacher present

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Use two methods per decision, not three: the one that shows the performance (an observed task that changes the case, such as a changed order) decides, and the quick one (a quiz) screens; run them as a rotation so the assessor observes while the others work; write an evidence matrix in advance saying what each disagreement leads to (passes quiz, fails task → targeted practice and reassess; the reverse → a short oral check)
rows.if: Little time (one or two sessions) and one assessor

rows.basis: [Instructional guidance that helps novices can become redundant or counterproductive as expertise grows.](claims/expertise-reversal-effect.md) [~M] (review of cognitive-load studies; not tested on note-taking aids)
rows.change: Skip guided notes and modelling; state the purpose, keep one recall review; let them choose the format
rows.if: Learners are `advanced` on the content, or already take selective notes

rows.basis: [Guided Notes Improve Note Accuracy](claims/guided-notes-improve-note-accuracy.md) [+M] (meta-analysis reports the benefit "particularly for school-age students", abstract only); timings untested
rows.change: Guided notes with few, well-cued blanks; pauses every 5–8 minutes; teacher models notes on the board for several sessions, not one; review in class
rows.if: Learners are `child` (primary) or `adolescent` with little note-taking experience

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Notes are for doing something: a one-page template with "what to do", "when", "who to ask", "one question"; review is applying the note on the next real task, followed by a check with a colleague or supervisor
rows.if: Learners are `adult` in a work setting (training, briefings, meetings)

rows.basis: Pauses and outline: untested here. Quiz: [Retrieval Practice Improves Long Term Retention](claims/retrieval-practice-improves-retention.md) [+S] (carried to reviewing notes)
rows.change: Put the pause points into the video (a prompt screen at each break); give a downloadable outline for the first modules; end each module with a short recall quiz learners answer before reopening their notes
rows.if: Setting is `online-self-paced` video

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Share the outline in a form that works on a phone (a short list of headings with blanks, not a wide table or PDF); say the pause aloud and post it in the chat; ask remote learners to post their one-line restatement in the chat so everyone sees some; send the slides afterwards but not before the session
rows.if: Mixed mode: some learners in the room, some remote, or some on a phone only

rows.basis: [Guided Notes Improve Note Accuracy](claims/guided-notes-improve-note-accuracy.md) [+M] (one quasi-experiment with two intact undergraduate classes); pauses and sampling untested
rows.change: Guided-notes outline for everyone; two or three pauses per hour with a restatement written to a neighbour or a poll; collect a random sample of notes after the first week to check for errors and address the commonest one in the next lecture
rows.if: One teacher with a large lecture group

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Spend the facilitator's minute on one thing: a look at a learner's notes against the key points, naming one missing or wrong point; put the rest in the materials (outline, pause prompts, self-test questions at the end)
rows.if: Scarce facilitator time (volunteer tutors, a busy shift, one brief check-in)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Guided-notes outline, two pauses with a restatement prompt, and a 5-minute recall at the end from covered notes; do not plan the fade; do not claim retention
rows.if: A single session only

rows.basis: untested proposal; the earlier page's "working-memory constraints" learners, and Hughes & Suritsky (1994, Key Sources, no claim page) on university students with and without learning disabilities
rows.change: Fewer and shorter blanks, with word banks or first letters; allow symbols, sketches and first-language words in notes; give the full slides or a transcript after the session so missed content is recoverable; allow audio recording where it is permitted
rows.if: Learners have low literacy, a learning disability, or are working in a second language

rows.basis: [Retrieval Practice Improves Long Term Retention](claims/retrieval-practice-improves-retention.md) [+S] and [self-explanation](claims/self-explanation-improves-conceptual-understanding.md) [+S], both carried to notes; no claim compares note formats
rows.change: Keep it; change only what the evidence points at: add a review in which the learner covers the notes and recalls before checking, and one restatement prompt per section
rows.if: The brief names its own routine or template (Cornell notes, a school-wide organizer, a company note template)

rows.basis: [Laptop note-takers transcribed more verbatim and did worse on conceptual questions than longhand note-takers in one set of experiments, but a direct replication found no consistent difference in test performance](claims/laptop-notes-verbatim-shallower.md) [~M] (replication found no consistent difference)
rows.change: Do not ban on this evidence; instruct paraphrase, keep pauses, and check a sample of notes for verbatim copying; allow devices for learners who write slowly or with difficulty
rows.if: Learners take notes on laptops or tablets, or the brief asks whether to ban them

rows.basis: [Summarization Effective With Training](claims/summarization-improves-learning.md) [~M] (295 adults: summarizing each of five texts gave weaker integrated essays than rereading; carried from summaries to notes)
rows.change: Do not ask for a separate summary of each source; ask for notes organized by the question (a column per claim, with which source says what), then write from those
rows.if: The goal is writing or argument from several sources

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Do not rely on learners' notes as the record: supply a checked reference version after the session, keep the learner's notes for recall practice against it, and correct errors before the assessment
rows.if: Stakes are high (a licensing exam, a safety procedure)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Separate the two: a shared record written to a checklist and checked by a second person, and each learner's own notes kept for their own recall; do not treat reading someone else's notes as a substitute for taking and reviewing one's own
rows.if: Notes will be shared with others (class notes posted for absent peers, meeting minutes for a team)

rows.basis: untested; the [guided-notes claim](claims/guided-notes-improve-note-accuracy.md) [+W] tests teacher-made gapped notes with students, carried here only as "give the structure", not the worksheet form
rows.change: Replace fill-in-the-blank guided notes with a reusable domain grid the learner keeps, built from the categories the brief or the workplace already uses (if none are given, for a handover: facts, actions due, what is uncertain, what to report), with a pre-printed prompt for any item whose omission is dangerous, modelled once with a think-aloud, then used on a real or recorded case; check it by having the learner brief a partner from the grid, not by reading back. In one session of about 75 minutes: 10 minutes modelling the grid on a short clip, 20 minutes filling it on the full case, 10 minutes comparing grids in pairs, 20 minutes briefing a partner from it (with sentence frames such as "The priority is… because…" for learners working in a second language), 10 minutes fixing the grid for reuse
rows.if: Adults whose notes become a job aid (a handover, a shift, a procedure they will use again at work)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Judge the notes by use, not recall: the learner follows their own notes, on their own device, to do the task again while a partner watches (no swapping unfamiliar devices); fix any step the partner cannot follow. Keep any retrieval as optional self-checking, not a quiz
rows.if: The notes are a take-home aid, and the brief asks for an evaluation that does not feel like a test (older adults, community workshops, practical skills)

rows.basis: [Instructional guidance that helps novices can become redundant or counterproductive as expertise grows.](claims/expertise-reversal-effect.md) [~M] (cognitive-load studies on instructional formats; carried to observation guidance)
rows.change: Let them set their own focus, observe whole live performances, and compare directly with their own practice; replace the designer's focus sheet with the observed person's question; shorten or drop the corrective part of the debrief
rows.if: Learners are `advanced` or experienced practitioners (in-service teachers, senior staff observing each other)

rows.basis: [Expert teachers interpret complex classroom phenomena more accurately and fluidly than novices and postulants](claims/expert-teachers-interpret-classroom-phenomena-better.md) [~M] (novices struggled to monitor a complex scene); the sequence is untested
rows.change: Start with recorded clips, two focus items at most, a three-column record and a debrief after every clip; do not send them on a long live shadow before session 3
rows.if: Learners are complete newcomers to the practice (first placement, first week in a job)
