rows.basis: [In the initial skill acquisition phase, authentic video yielded higher overall observation assignment scores than virtual simulation](claims/av-outperforms-vs-total-observation-score.md) [+M]; [Analytical competence showed a leap-plateau trajectory across sequential authentic-video workshops, improving mainly between Workshops 2 and 3](claims/analysis-leap-plateau-trajectory.md) [+M] (one design-based study, 8 groups, fixed order)
rows.change: Run three or four workshops on authentic classroom video (a simplified simulation first if they are new to observing), each with a group observation assignment covering description, analysis and suggested support, and score it
rows.if: Learners are teacher candidates learning to observe children or classrooms

rows.basis: untested proposal; the debrief is carried from [Contingent scaffolding improves learning more than fixed or absent support.](claims/contingent-scaffolding-improves-learning.md) [+M] (one-to-one tutoring of children)
rows.change: Shadow on a real shift in blocks of 1–3 hours, with a pocket focus card of two to four items; a 5-minute check-in before and a 10–15-minute conversation after; follow within the week with the learner doing the same task under supervision
rows.if: `adult` learners in a work setting (`workplace-clinical`, `adult-workplace`): new staff shadowing a colleague

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Set the purpose as finding out what the work involves; give three questions to ask the host (what a typical day holds, what they decide, how they learned it); a short write-up or talk to peers afterwards; do not assess performance
rows.if: School pupils (`adolescent`) job shadowing for career exploration

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Move the explaining into materials: a written focus card and a one-page key of the decisions at stake; the observer brings two questions to a 5-minute conversation; a peer observer compares records with them instead of the mentor where possible
rows.if: Scarce facilitator or performer time (a busy shift, a volunteer host, a mentor who can give five minutes)

rows.basis: untested proposal; the group workshop format follows the teacher-candidate study ([Authentic video outperformed virtual simulation on the higher-order analysis and support dimensions of observation assignments](claims/av-advantage-analysis-support-dimensions.md) [+M])
rows.change: Do not rotate everyone through a live shadow; record one authentic performance, or have the group watch one live performance from the side (a fishbowl), each observer with a different focus item; debrief as a group, observers reporting by focus
rows.if: One expert or teacher for many observers

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Stream the performance with a fixed camera and a microphone near the performer, with consent; an in-room observer types short time-stamped notes into a shared document remote observers can see; in the debrief, take remote observers' records first. Phone-only observers get the recording afterwards, cut into clips with the focus questions in text, and send their record by message
rows.if: Some observers remote while others are in the room, or some join by phone only

rows.basis: untested proposal; the explanation prompt is carried from [Prompting learners to self-explain improves understanding and problem solving on immediate tests by a moderate average amount, with little evidence yet on delayed or classroom gains.](claims/self-explanation-improves-conceptual-understanding.md) [+S]
rows.change: Short authentic clips (5–15 minutes) each with two focus questions the learner must answer before going on, then a written expert account of the clip's decisions to compare with; one replay of the clip after the comparison
rows.if: `online-self-paced`, recordings only, no one to debrief

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: 10 minutes brief and focus card; 25–30 minutes observing one whole short performance (or one clip); 15–20 minutes debrief ending in one thing to try; no more than two focus items
rows.if: A fixed short time budget (for example, 60 minutes in total)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: One focused observation of a whole performance and one debrief; state the outcome as what the observer can now name and explain, not as a change in their own performance
rows.if: One session only

rows.basis: untested proposal; the choice of a similar performer rests on a correlational finding in a review ([Vicarious experiences are positively related to agriculture teachers' general teaching efficacy, with observing a first year teacher explaining 11% of variance](claims/vicarious-experiences-positive-teaching-efficacy.md) [+W])
rows.change: Use a picture or tick-box record instead of written columns; debrief orally; let the observer point to moments on the recording rather than describe them; choose a performer the learner can see as like themselves when confidence is the problem
rows.if: Learners with low confidence, low literacy, or working in a second language

rows.basis: [Vicarious experiences are positively related to agriculture teachers' general teaching efficacy, with observing a first year teacher explaining 11% of variance](claims/vicarious-experiences-positive-teaching-efficacy.md) [+W] (associational, reported in a review; observing did not cause the efficacy)
rows.change: Arrange observation of someone a little ahead of the learner (a first-year colleague, a peer) as well as of an expert; ask the learner afterwards what the performer did when something went wrong
rows.if: Goal is confidence or willingness to take up the work (`attitude-motivation`), not skill

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: The observer is introduced and stays silent; all questions and reasoning are kept for the conversation away from the audience; the record holds no names; the audience can decline an observer
rows.if: The observed work is for a real audience (patients, clients, pupils, customers)

rows.basis: untested proposal; that clinical supervision tied to evaluation has inconclusive research results is a monograph's report ([Research on clinical supervision's effectiveness is inconclusive, partly because practice is diluted and tied to evaluation](claims/clinical-supervision-effectiveness-inconclusive.md) [~W])
rows.change: The observed person controls who sees the recording and the notes, and may end the arrangement; observers' notes are shared with the observed person first and with a supervisor only by agreement; keep observation for development apart from evaluation
rows.if: The material is private or sensitive (a colleague's own lesson video, clinical cases, a learner's reflective record)

rows.basis: the explanation prompt is carried from [Prompting learners to self-explain…](claims/self-explanation-improves-conceptual-understanding.md) [+S]; otherwise untested
rows.change: Keep it; do not substitute the three-column record. Change only what the evidence speaks to: add one prompt asking the observer to explain why, and one debrief that starts from their record
rows.if: The brief names its own observation protocol, form, rubric or categories

rows.basis: [A training-design argument, not tested by any study recorded here, holds that practising whole complex tasks improves transfer of complex skills](claims/whole-task-performance-improves-transfer.md) [+W] (an argument about practice, carried to observation)
rows.change: Observe it whole and debrief it whole; put the focus items on decision points across the whole, not on one segment; do not split it into separate fragments
rows.if: The brief wants a whole performance kept whole (a full lesson, a full client visit, a full shift)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Fix where the observer stands and when they must not speak or touch; brief the stop rules first; observe the procedure once before any hands-on part; require a supervised attempt before working alone
rows.if: High stakes or safety (operating theatre, laboratory, machinery, child protection)

rows.basis: [Systematic Phonics Improves Word Reading](claims/systematic-phonics-improves-word-reading.md) [+S] (kindergarten to grade 6; largest effects in kindergarten and grades 1–2)
rows.change: Run the full default: daily 20–30 minute lessons through the first school year, with phonemic-awareness work in the first term and decodable text from the first week
rows.if: Learners are `child`, kindergarten or first grade, beginning to read

rows.basis: [Phonemic Awareness Training Improves Reading](claims/phonemic-awareness-training-improves-reading.md) [+M] (preschool to grade 1); [Dialogic Reading Improves Expressive Language](claims/dialogic-reading-improves-expressive-language.md) [+M]
rows.change: Phonemic-awareness games with letters in view, one or two skills (blending, segmenting) at a time, in small groups, 5–18 hours in all; plus daily interactive read-alouds. Do not start a full decoding programme
rows.if: Learners are pre-readers (preschool)

rows.basis: [Instructional guidance that helps novices can become redundant or counterproductive as expertise grows.](claims/expertise-reversal-effect.md) [~M] (a cognitive-load review, carried to reading)
rows.change: Drop phonics lessons; give the screening only, teach the specific gaps it shows, and spend the time on fluency, vocabulary and comprehension
rows.if: Learners already decode accurately (`advanced` for decoding)

rows.basis: [Systematic Phonics Improves Word Reading](claims/systematic-phonics-improves-word-reading.md) [~S] (older readers with difficulties: decoding effects remained, comprehension and spelling effects not reliably above zero); [Morphological Instruction Improves Literacy](claims/morphological-instruction-improves-literacy.md) [+M] (largest gains on decoding, particular benefit for less-able readers, preschool to grade 8)
rows.change: Diagnose the gaps rather than restart the sequence; teach multisyllable decoding and word parts (prefixes, roots, suffixes); pair every phonics lesson with fluency and comprehension work; expect decoding gains before comprehension gains
rows.if: Older struggling readers (grade 2 and above, or `adolescent`)

rows.basis: [Phonics instruction has a small but statistically confirmed effect for children with reading disabilities, while Orton-Gillingham structured-literacy programs show positive but non-significant effects](claims/structured-literacy-interventions-help-struggling-readers.md) [~S] (22 RCTs: phonics the only approach with a confirmed effect, g′ = 0.198; Orton-Gillingham effects positive but not significant). Group size is an untested proposal
rows.change: Keep systematic phonics as the core, delivered one-to-one or in groups of two to four, with more cumulative review and a longer intervention; expect small gains; do not expect a branded multisensory programme to add to them, and do not use coloured overlays
rows.if: Learners have an identified reading disability or dyslexia

rows.basis: untested proposal for adult literacy. An artificial-script experiment with 24 adults found print-to-sound training made new words faster to read than print-to-meaning training, not more accurate ([Systematic phonics outperforms unsystematic or no-phonics instruction on children's reading overall, but its advantage over whole-word teaching on novel words is untested in children and contested](claims/phonics-instruction-outperforms-whole-word-for-generalization.md) [~S]). No claim page here tests phonics teaching with adults learning to read their own language
rows.change: Use adult texts and words from the learner's own life or job for blending and decodable reading; say why the sound work is there; keep checks private; move to the learner's real texts as soon as a correspondence is secure
rows.if: Learners are `adult`, in a literacy programme or at work

rows.basis: untested proposal. In adult ESL readers, phonological and orthographic processing efficiency is associated with reading measures ([Lower-level phonological processing efficiency contributes significantly to individual differences in adult ESL reading measures](claims/phonological-orthographic-efficiency-predicts-esl-reading.md) [+W]; correlational, reported second-hand)
rows.change: Teach the sounds orally before print, with minimal pairs for sounds absent from the first language; use only words whose meaning the learner knows for blending practice; teach meaning alongside
rows.if: Learners are learning English as a second language, or the language of instruction is not their first

rows.basis: [Systematic phonics outperforms unsystematic or no-phonics instruction on children's reading overall, but its advantage over whole-word teaching on novel words is untested in children and contested](claims/phonics-instruction-outperforms-whole-word-for-generalization.md) [~S] (whole-language comparison: d = 0.55 decoding, d = 0.19 comprehension); [Automatic word recognition frees resources for comprehension.](claims/automatic-word-recognition-frees-resources-for-comprehension.md) [+W] (a mechanism; no training study)
rows.change: Keep phonics, but do not expect it to carry comprehension: add vocabulary, oral-language and read-aloud discussion time, and measure comprehension separately
rows.if: The goal is reading comprehension, not only word reading

rows.basis: [Phonemic Awareness Training Improves Reading](claims/phonemic-awareness-training-improves-reading.md) [~M] (for phonemic-awareness training, small groups beat whole-class and individual delivery; carried to phonics); the rotation is untested
rows.change: Introduce the new correspondence to the whole class in 10 minutes with choral responses and every child showing a written answer at once (whiteboards); then small groups by placement for decodable reading while others practise independently; weekly one-to-one checks rotated across the class
rows.if: One teacher with a whole class of 25–30

rows.basis: untested proposal. Coaching parents in an interactive reading style changed home practice for families of 2- to 3-year-olds but not for families of children at greatest risk ([Dialogic Reading Improves Expressive Language](claims/dialogic-reading-improves-expressive-language.md) [~M])
rows.change: Record each model on video with the mouth visible; have the learner read the word list aloud into the phone for the teacher to hear; send decodable books home with a one-page guide for the adult on saying sounds without an added "uh" and on correcting by pointing to the letters
rows.if: Mixed modes: some learners at home, some in the room, or practice on a phone

rows.basis: untested proposal; no claim here tests phonics delivered without a teacher
rows.change: Choose or build software that models every sound in audio, has the learner blend before revealing the word, checks reading aloud (speech recognition or a recorded sample a person reviews), and gates new correspondences on the weekly check
rows.if: No teacher present: an app or self-paced programme

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Screen, then teach one correspondence and blend five to ten words with it; give the learner or family the next three correspondences to practise; do not report decoding gains
rows.if: A single session only

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Begin with a correspondence they will master in the first session; show progress on their own weekly chart; avoid reading aloud in front of peers until the text is fully decodable for them
rows.if: Learners with low confidence after years of failure (older children, adults)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Choose or write a text within the learner's taught code, rehearse it with corrections until accurate, and keep the audience performance after accuracy, not as the practice
rows.if: A performance for a real audience (reading to younger children, a class reading, reading aloud at work)

rows.basis: untested; the claim pages state this on general grounds and record no evidence for it
rows.change: Expect a shorter phonics phase; move to connected text and comprehension sooner, but keep the screening and weekly checks
rows.if: The language has regular spelling (Spanish, Italian, Finnish)

rows.basis: untested proposal; pseudoword decoding is where the phonics effect was largest ([Systematic Phonics Improves Word Reading](claims/systematic-phonics-improves-word-reading.md) [+S])
rows.change: Measure decoding with pseudowords as well as taught words, so memorised words do not count as decoding; record which correspondences have been taught
rows.if: Results will be reported or used for placement

rows.basis: [Self Talk Improves Learning And Performance](claims/self-talk-improves-learning-and-performance.md) [+S] (sport; larger on novel tasks); [Process goals lead to better skill acquisition for novices than outcome goals.](claims/process-goals-outperform-outcome-goals-for-novices.md) [~M] (writing revision, about goals)
rows.change: Write instructional cues that name the steps, as process phrases; model and rehearse them; prompt at the step that fails
rows.if: Learners are `novice` on a new skill with steps (a procedure, a technique)

rows.basis: [Instructional guidance that helps novices can become redundant or counterproductive as expertise grows.](claims/expertise-reversal-effect.md) [~M] (cognitive-load studies of instructional formats; carried to self-talk untested)
rows.change: Drop step cues; keep at most one motivational or focusing cue for pressure moments
rows.if: Learners are `advanced`, or the skill is already automatic

rows.basis: [Self Talk Improves Learning And Performance](claims/self-talk-improves-learning-and-performance.md) [+S] (the setting the evidence comes from)
rows.change: Use instructional cue words for fine, precise movements and motivational cues for endurance; train them before use
rows.if: The goal is a motor or performance skill (sport, a lab or clinical technique, an instrument)

rows.basis: [Strategy Instruction Improves Writing Quality](claims/strategy-instruction-improves-writing-quality.md) [+M] (grades 4–10; self-instruction bundled with three other components)
rows.change: Teach self-instructions as part of the strategy (its steps become the cues) with goal setting and self-monitoring, over several sessions
rows.if: The goal is academic writing or problem solving, `child` or `adolescent`

rows.basis: [Thought and language become increasingly interdependent in the first few years, with private speech evolving into inner speech as self-regulation](claims/vygotsky-private-speech-inner-speech.md) [+W] (a theoretical overview; no study)
rows.change: Let them talk aloud while working; the adult models the cue first and the child repeats it, then whispers it; do not treat talking aloud as off-task
rows.if: Learners are young children (`child`, early primary)

rows.basis: [Emotion Labeling Improves Regulation](claims/emotion-labeling-improves-regulation.md) [~M] (adults, spider fear, physiological only); [Expressive Writing Improves Exam Performance](claims/expressive-writing-improves-exam-performance.md) [~S] (a meta-analysis finds a negligible effect of one-session writing)
rows.change: Teach one name-it-then-act routine ("I'm nervous; read question 1 slowly") and rehearse it in a practice test; do not rely on a single pre-exam writing or self-talk exercise on its own
rows.if: Learners are anxious before a test or evaluation

rows.basis: Untested proposal; brief one-off psychological exercises have weak average achievement effects ([Growth-mindset interventions have weak average effects on achievement, including a negligible GPA gain (d = 0.11) for lower-achieving US ninth-graders in one preregistered national trial](claims/growth-mindset-improves-achievement.md) [~M], a different intervention)
rows.change: Give 10–15 minutes: find the moment, model one cue, each learner writes one or two cues and rehearses on two items; report use, not a lasting change
rows.if: Time is one session only

rows.basis: Untested proposal
rows.change: Spend it as 1 minute recalling the cue, 3 minutes using it on one hard item, 1 minute noting whether it helped; move modeling to the first session only
rows.if: A fixed short time budget per session (for example 5 minutes)

rows.basis: Untested proposal
rows.change: Show the learner's own cue at the point where errors or long pauses occur (after a wrong answer, after a set idle time), with the next action as a button; let the learner edit their cues
rows.if: `online-self-paced`, no teacher present

rows.basis: Untested proposal
rows.change: Model once for the whole class; learners write their own cue cards and rehearse in pairs; the teacher prompts "What's your cue?" only for learners who stall
rows.if: `classroom` with one teacher and many learners

rows.basis: Untested proposal
rows.change: One 10-minute teaching session and a pocket card; at each brief check-in the facilitator asks one question: "Where did you get stuck, and what did your cue tell you to do?"
rows.if: Facilitator time is scarce (volunteers, busy shifts, a tutor who drops in)

rows.basis: Untested proposal
rows.change: Keep the cues in a place every learner sees on their own device (a phone note or lock-screen line); model on a shared screen so remote and in-room learners see the same think-aloud
rows.if: Mixed mode (some remote, some in the room) or phone-only learners

rows.basis: Untested proposal, from the earlier page's credibility constraint
rows.change: Spoken cues in the learner's own words, a picture or symbol beside each; choose plainly true statements over upbeat ones; point out when a cue was followed by success
rows.if: Learners with low confidence or low literacy

rows.basis: Untested proposal
rows.change: Take cue words from the job's own procedure or checklist (the step names already used on the floor or ward); keep the cards private to the learner
rows.if: Adults in a work setting

rows.basis: Untested proposal, from the earlier page's pre-performance cue cards
rows.change: Prepare a pre-performance cue card with one calming and one first-action cue; rehearse with the card in front of a small audience; the audience sees the performance, not the cards
rows.if: A presentation or performance for a real audience

rows.basis: Untested proposal; training effect from [Self Talk Improves Learning And Performance](claims/self-talk-improves-learning-and-performance.md) [+S] (sport)
rows.change: Keep it word for word as the learner's cue; change only what the evidence says matters: make sure one line names an action, and rehearse it before it is needed
rows.if: The brief names its own routine or script (for example "stop, breathe, plan")

rows.basis: Untested proposal
rows.change: Write the instructional cues from those terms, not new ones
rows.if: The brief gives its own steps, categories or criteria (a rubric, a procedure, a checklist)

rows.basis: Untested proposal
rows.change: The learner keeps their notes on their own talk; no one collects or reads them unless the learner chooses to share; work on cues, not on the content of private thoughts
rows.if: What the learner says to themselves is private or sensitive

rows.basis: Untested proposal
rows.change: Place cues at the decision points inside full runs of the task rather than splitting it into drills
rows.if: The brief wants a whole task or performance kept whole

rows.basis: [Self Talk Improves Learning And Performance](claims/self-talk-improves-learning-and-performance.md) [~S] (the systematic review found negative self-talk did not impede performance; sport)
rows.change: Do not intervene on tone alone; add an action cue only where performance or persistence falters
rows.if: Learners already talk negatively to themselves but perform well

rows.basis: Untested proposal, from the earlier page's context-blindness constraint
rows.change: Never treat self-talk as a substitute for preparation or support; judge readiness on performance, not on the learner's stated confidence
rows.if: Stakes are high

rows.basis: [Pretesting enhances learning](claims/pretesting-enhances-learning.md) [+M] (undergraduates, items answered at floor, laboratory)
rows.change: Keep the attempt-before-reading step; tell them most guesses will be wrong; keep to two or three questions
rows.if: Readers are `novice` on the topic and will know almost none of the answers

rows.basis: untested; the earlier page's caution against over-directing applies
rows.change: Replace teacher questions with one higher-order question, or with the reader's own questions about what they still want to know
rows.if: Readers are `advanced` on the topic, or answer most questions before reading

rows.basis: [Advance organizers aided learning …, but activating prior topic knowledge did not improve primary pupils' text comprehension in one experiment](claims/activation-improves-learning.md) [~M] (88 primary pupils: metacognitive activation helped, topic activation did not)
rows.change: Ask two questions aloud and record answers for them; add one question about how they will check they understood ("What will you do if a part doesn't make sense?"), not only questions about the topic
rows.if: Readers are primary-age children (`child`)

rows.basis: [Reading Strategy Instruction Improves Comprehension](claims/reading-strategy-instruction-improves-comprehension.md) [+M] (English L2 meta-analysis g = 0.72; whole-classroom interventions d = .186 on standardized tests), carried from multi-strategy programmes to this routine; the wording moves are untested
rows.change: Write the questions in simpler language than the text; pre-teach the key words the questions use; accept guesses in the first language or as a drawing; move to learner-written questions only within a longer strategy programme
rows.if: Readers are second-language learners or have low literacy

rows.basis: [Question prompts improve learning](claims/question-prompts-improve-learning.md) [~M] (higher-order adjunct questions generalised further; abstract only); no claim tests pre-questions on inference
rows.change: Make most questions why/how/predict questions; in the check, ask for the reasoning in the text, not just the answer
rows.if: The goal is understanding or inference (`conceptual-understanding`, `near-transfer`), not memory of facts

rows.basis: [Question prompts improve learning](claims/question-prompts-improve-learning.md) [~M] (factual pre-questions depressed learning of unquestioned content)
rows.change: Use fewer factual pre-questions, add a whole-text summary after reading, or move some questions to after each section instead of before
rows.if: The later check covers the whole text

rows.basis: [Pre-tests reduced adult learners' persistence in a MOOC, though they improved post-test scores among those who completed it](claims/pretesting-can-harm-motivation.md) [-M] (399 adults in a MOOC: pre-tests reduced persistence; post-test gains only among those who finished)
rows.change: Keep pre-questions to two, framed as a puzzle with no score; show the answer straight after the relevant section; track drop-off at the pre-question screen and remove it if completion falls
rows.if: `online-self-paced` course or module, no teacher present

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Put the questions in one place everyone answers privately (a poll or a shared form) before the text opens; on phones, one question per screen with a short typed or multiple-choice answer; run the check in the same tool so remote learners' guesses are seen too
rows.if: Mixed modes: some learners in the room, some remote, or some on phones only

rows.basis: untested proposal; the confront-the-misconception move is from [Instruction that confronts science misconceptions … produces conceptual change more often than standard exposition](claims/misconceptions-interfere-with-new-learning.md) [~M] (science and reading syntheses, abstracts only)
rows.change: Collect every learner's guesses at once (cards, mini-whiteboards, a poll), scan for the commonest confident wrong prediction, and spend the after-reading check on that one, with the text's refutation
rows.if: One teacher with a large class

rows.basis: untested beyond the laboratory sessions on [Pretesting enhances learning](claims/pretesting-enhances-learning.md) [~M]
rows.change: Two questions, attempt, read, check, one whole-text summary; do not claim a lasting effect
rows.if: One session only

rows.basis: untested; the low-confidence risk is the motivation claim's own speculation, not a finding ([Pre-tests reduced adult learners' persistence in a MOOC, though they improved post-test scores among those who completed it](claims/pretesting-can-harm-motivation.md) [~M])
rows.change: Keep answers private; offer forced-choice guesses instead of blank lines; open the check with what the class predicted well; never display individual guesses
rows.if: Learners have low confidence, or a history of failing at reading

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Write questions as decisions they will face ("A patient refuses X: what does the policy let you do?"); check against the exact clause; ask what they do now that the text changes
rows.if: Adults in work settings reading a procedure, policy or case

rows.basis: untested proposal; links to [Inquiry-based Learning](principles/inquiry-based-learning.md)
rows.change: Let the learner's project question be the pre-reading question; ask what the source must show to be usable, and after reading, what it does and does not support
rows.if: Learners are reading sources for their own inquiry or for a product an audience will see

rows.basis: [Pre-tests reduced adult learners' persistence in a MOOC, though they improved post-test scores among those who completed it](claims/pretesting-can-harm-motivation.md) [-M] (persistence fell even unscored); scoring itself untested
rows.change: Remove the score from pre-questions; score only the later check
rows.if: The pre-questions are scored, or the course is high stakes

rows.basis: [Prior-knowledge activation instructions before study had little effect on retention in Experiment 2](claims/prior-knowledge-activation-little-effect-on-retention.md) [-M] (1.5 minutes of talk produced about one relevant idea per topic)
rows.change: Replace it with two specific questions the text answers
rows.if: Open brainstorming ("What do you know about…?") is planned instead of questions

rows.basis: [Instructional guidance that helps novices can become redundant or counterproductive as expertise grows.](claims/expertise-reversal-effect.md) [~M] (cognitive-load studies; gives no crossover point)
rows.change: Skip modelling and guided attempts; give mixed, spaced practice on full tasks and selective feedback, and refine weak components
rows.if: Learners are `advanced` on this procedure, or complete the first item unaided

rows.basis: [Part-task practice reduces cognitive load for absolute novices during initial skill acquisition.](claims/part-task-practice-reduces-load-for-novices.md) [+M]; joining: [whole-task argument](claims/whole-task-performance-improves-transfer.md) [~W] (no experiment)
rows.change: Teach the hardest steps in isolation for one or two short rounds, then join them on a simple whole task in the same or next session; never leave the parts unjoined
rows.if: The procedure has many interacting steps and learners are `novice`

rows.basis: untested proposal; [whole-task argument](claims/whole-task-performance-improves-transfer.md) [~W]
rows.change: Keep every practice attempt a whole task; simplify the task (fewer variables, an easier case) rather than splitting it, and put the support around the whole; isolate a step only for a few minutes when one step keeps failing
rows.if: The brief wants a whole-task performance kept whole (a full clinical procedure, a complete repair, a full presentation)

rows.basis: [Contingent scaffolding improves learning more than fixed or absent support.](claims/contingent-scaffolding-improves-learning.md) [+M] (fourth and fifth graders, long division, one-to-one); round size untested
rows.change: Shorter rounds (3–5 items), concrete materials or a physical model of each step, one-to-one or small-group checking during supported attempts
rows.if: Learners are `child` (primary age)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Ask what they already do; use items from their own work as soon as the steps are stable; give a job aid laid out in the workplace's own categories and step names, used during practice and kept afterwards; check on a real or realistic task
rows.if: `adult` learners in a work setting, using the procedure on the job

rows.basis: untested proposal; feedback before the next attempt from [contingent scaffolding](claims/contingent-scaffolding-improves-learning.md) [+M] (one-to-one)
rows.change: Keep it and its categories as given; teach and practise with it, and change only what the evidence speaks to: one model of each decision point, feedback before the next attempt, a delayed unaided check
rows.if: The brief names its own checklist, job aid, rubric or routine for the procedure

rows.basis: [Comparing cases side by side…](claims/comparing-contrasting-cases-improves-learning.md) [+M] (raised procedural flexibility, not conceptual knowledge, in one algebra study); [Strategy Instruction Needs Conditional Knowledge](claims/strategy-instruction-needs-conditional-knowledge.md) [~M]
rows.change: After accurate steps, add side-by-side comparison of two methods, items where the procedure does not apply, and "why does this step work?" prompts; check with one changed item per round
rows.if: Goal includes transfer to changed problems, or understanding why, not only accuracy

rows.basis: [Students can apply procedural knowledge to solve integration problems but show limited understanding of basic integration concepts](claims/procedural-strong-conceptual-limited-integral.md) [~W] (calculus, reported second-hand)
rows.change: Do not add more of the same practice; pose items the memorised steps will not solve and ask learners to explain or draw what each step does
rows.if: Learners can already run the procedure but cannot say what it means (e.g. can integrate but cannot explain the integral)

rows.basis: [Interleaving Improves Discrimination](claims/interleaving-improves-discrimination.md) [+M] (mathematics problem types; benefit largest when types are confusable)
rows.change: Once each is accurate alone, practise them shuffled so the learner must choose; warn learners that mixed practice feels harder and is slower
rows.if: Several similar procedures are taught in one unit (e.g. problem types, grammar forms, drug calculations)

rows.basis: [practice included in computer-based lessons](claims/practice-presence-raises-cbi-posttest-achievement.md) [+M] (undergraduates, one lesson; horizon not reported); schedule untested
rows.change: Build the worked example and five to eight practice items with automatic checking and a worked answer after each into the lesson; one step per screen on a phone; an unaided check item before the next procedure; scheduled review prompts two days and one week later
rows.if: `online-self-paced`, no teacher present, or phone-only

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Show the model on a shared screen or camera pointed at the hands or the work, not the whole room; have every learner, remote or present, submit each attempt the same way (photo, poll, shared document) so all are seen before feedback
rows.if: Mixed modes: some learners in the room, some joining remotely

rows.basis: untested proposal; contingent-support evidence is one-to-one ([contingent scaffolding](claims/contingent-scaffolding-improves-learning.md) [~M])
rows.change: Every learner shows each attempt at once (mini-whiteboards, cards, a poll); whole-class feedback on the commonest error, then the teacher goes to those still failing; pairs check each other against a worked answer for routine steps
rows.if: `classroom`, one teacher and a large group

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Spend the facilitator's minutes on the first one or two supported attempts and the unaided check; give everything between to self-checking items with worked answers or a job aid; the facilitator looks only at the step the learner flags
rows.if: Scarce facilitator time (volunteers, a busy shift, a tutor checking in briefly)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Model, three or four supported attempts, one unaided item at the end; record what the unaided item shows and do not claim retention or fluency; give learners a job aid and items to practise later
rows.if: Time is one session only

rows.basis: untested proposal; spacing across sessions from [Distributed Practice Improves Retention](claims/distributed-practice-improves-retention.md) [+M] (verbal recall, carried)
rows.change: Per session: 1–2 minutes of unaided items on earlier procedures, 3–5 minutes of model or worked example on the new step only if it is new, the rest supported or mixed practice; one new step per session at most
rows.if: A fixed short time budget per session (e.g. 10 or 15 minutes a day)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Let learners show a step by doing it before explaining it; keep written instructions short with pictures of each step; let early attempts be private (checked by software or one-to-one) before anything is shown to the group
rows.if: Learners have low confidence or low literacy, or work in a second language

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: More supported rounds per step; release only after several consecutive unaided successes on representative tasks; a stage of supervised unaided work before full independence; judge readiness only on unaided performance
rows.if: Errors are costly on the job (safety, compliance, harm to a client) or stakes are high

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Practise the procedure to accuracy first in private, then rehearse the whole performance under the audience's conditions (time, setting, interruptions) at least twice before the real one
rows.if: The procedure is a performance for a real audience (a demonstration, a recital, a service to a client)

rows.basis: [Practice of grammar rules improves only the practiced skill…](claims/skill-specificity-l2-grammar-practice.md) [+W] and [Automatization of L2 skills requires extensive practice in a consistent environment…](claims/automatization-requires-practice-consistent-environment.md) [+W] (both from one review, reported second-hand)
rows.change: Practise the form in the same kind of task the learner will use it in (meaningful communication, comprehension or production), since gains may stay in the skill practised
rows.if: Learners are second-language learners automatizing grammar or speech

rows.basis: [Process Writing Improves Writing Quality](claims/process-writing-improves-writing-quality.md) [~M] (no significant gain for struggling writers); [Strategy Instruction Improves Writing Quality](claims/strategy-instruction-improves-writing-quality.md) [+M] (struggling writers 1.02); transcription supports untested
rows.change: Teach planning and revising strategies explicitly with self-regulation steps (goal setting, self-recording, self-instruction) over several weeks; do not rely on drafting and feedback cycles alone; reduce transcription load (dictation, scribe, keyboard) while strategies are learned
rows.if: Writers are struggling, have a learning disability, or cannot yet write fluently by hand or keyboard

rows.basis: [Instructional guidance that helps novices can become redundant or counterproductive as expertise grows.](claims/expertise-reversal-effect.md) [~M] (cognitive-load review, not writing); untested for writing
rows.change: Drop the scripted strategy and prompt cards; let the writer set the revision focus; keep one outside reader's response per piece
rows.if: Writers are `advanced` in the genre (they already plan and revise globally)

rows.basis: [Collaborative Writing Improves Text Quality](claims/collaborative-writing-improves-text-quality.md) [+M] (grades 4–12, and one randomised study of 10–11-year-olds that found larger gains in later individual writing); younger children untested
rows.change: Shorter texts; plan orally or with drawings; co-write with a partner in structured pairs (the more able writer helping the less able); revise one thing per piece
rows.if: Learners are `child` in the early primary grades

rows.basis: untested; neither meta-analysis covers adults (strategy studies stop at grade 10)
rows.change: Use the writer's own work documents as the texts; take the reader from the real setting (the manager, the client, the colleague); keep the strategy modelling but shorten it; respond as that reader first
rows.if: Learners are `adult`, including in work settings (reports, case notes, proposals)

rows.basis: [Review: language proficiency and feedback literacy moderate uptake of written corrective feedback](claims/student-factors-moderate-wcf-engagement.md) [~W] (second-hand); [noticing errors](claims/noticing-errors-decreases-errors-preserves-quality.md) [+W] (second-hand, EFL college writing)
rows.change: Respond to meaning and structure first, in plain language; correct language separately, on two or three error types the writer can recognise, and ask the writer to find further instances; allow planning in the first language
rows.if: Writers are writing in a second language, or have low literacy

rows.basis: [Process Writing Improves Writing Quality](claims/process-writing-improves-writing-quality.md) [~M] (no gain in motivation); [Explicit statement of tasks and standards](claims/explicit-tasks-standards-boost-writing-motivation.md) [+W] (argument only)
rows.change: Do not expect process instruction alone to raise it: add a real reader and purpose, explicit task and standards, and reader-response comments; measure motivation separately
rows.if: The goal includes motivation to write or confidence as a writer

rows.basis: [Feedback Most Effective At Task And Process Levels](claims/feedback-most-effective-at-task-and-process-levels.md) [+M]; [Praise for intelligence, rather than for effort, after success undermines children's motivation and performance after a later failure](claims/feedback-praise-reduces-learning.md) [~M] (person praise; children, not writing)
rows.change: Open every response as a reader (what you understood and found interesting); direct criticism at the text and the next move, never at the writer; give a specific positive comment tied to a criterion, not generic praise
rows.if: Writers have low confidence, or have had harsh feedback before

rows.basis: [Peer Feedback Improves Writing](claims/peer-feedback-improves-writing.md) [+M] (peer vs teacher feedback not reliably different); [Students report teacher feedback on writing is insufficient](claims/insufficient-writing-feedback-scores-over-feedback.md) [~W] (interviews; teachers' load)
rows.change: Peers give the first response with criteria; the teacher reads a sample of peer comments and responds to each writer on two or three priorities only; rotate 5-minute conferences so each writer gets one per composition; do not grade drafts
rows.if: One teacher with a large class or many sections

rows.basis: [peer reviewer accuracy and helpfulness](claims/peer-feedback-accuracy-depends-on-expertise.md) [~M] (secondary writers, correlational); [rubrics and peer reviewers](claims/rubrics-improve-peer-feedback-quality.md) [~M] (online, two quasi-experiments; one found less reflective comments)
rows.change: Train them on example texts with the criteria first; ask them to point to the place in the text and say what a reader would experience; teacher checks a sample
rows.if: Peers are novices as reviewers

rows.basis: [rubrics and peer reviewers](claims/rubrics-improve-peer-feedback-quality.md) [~M] (one MOOC writing course, one online graduate course); [Peer assessment improves academic performance by a small average amount](claims/peer-assessment-improves-performance.md) [+M] (online and offline did not differ)
rows.change: Build in a rubric-guided peer review with practice on rated examples, a reviewer memo with each revision, and a self-check against the criteria before submission
rows.if: `online-self-paced` or asynchronous course, no teacher reading every draft

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Put drafts in one shared document with comment threads so remote and in-room writers review the same way; pair a remote writer with an in-room one for peer review; for phone-only writers keep pieces short, accept voice comments and spoken memos
rows.if: Mixed modes: some writers remote, some in the room, or some on phones only

rows.basis: untested; the strategy studies taught over at least three days ([strategy instruction](claims/strategy-instruction-improves-writing-quality.md) [+M])
rows.change: Plan for 10 minutes against a model text, draft, then one revision against a single criterion with a partner's response; collect the draft and the revision; do not claim a gain in writing ability
rows.if: Only one session is available

rows.basis: untested proposal, from the earlier pages on appropriation and responding as a reader (Shvidko 2020, an essay from practice)
rows.change: Keep the writer as the owner of the decisions: teacher and peers comment as readers and pose options; the writer's memo records what they accepted; add a final edit for conventions before release; keep drafts and comments out of the published version
rows.if: The text goes to a real audience (publication, a client, a public performance), or the audience should see only the final text

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Practise planning and revising under time limits (for example 5 minutes planning, 5 minutes rereading in a 40-minute task); keep the multi-draft cycle for learning the strategies, and the timed form for applying them
rows.if: Assessment is a timed, unaided essay

rows.basis: [Students report teacher feedback on writing is insufficient, and they value scores over feedback](claims/insufficient-writing-feedback-scores-over-feedback.md) [~W] (one interview study); grade withholding untested
rows.change: Withhold the grade until the final version; require the reviewer memo before revision; give credit for the revision itself
rows.if: Drafts are graded, or writers care only about the score

rows.basis: [Self-assessment accuracy](claims/self-assessment-accuracy-is-low-without-training.md) [~M]; tested with secondary and university students
rows.change: Give a rubric row or an exemplar pair before asking for evaluation; prompts name process steps ("which step?") rather than "how did it go?"; check a sample of self-ratings against a scored result before relying on them.
rows.if: `novice` to the task (first placements, first problem sets)

rows.basis: untested proposal; peer interaction is a moderator in [reflection interventions](claims/reflective-practice-evidence-mixed-in-professional-education.md) [~M], direction not stated on the claim page
rows.change: Use fewer, more open prompts; add peer discussion of cases; ask for alternatives considered, not a recount.
rows.if: `advanced` learners or practitioners

rows.basis: untested proposal; the school-based meta-analysis in [structured reflection](claims/reflective-practice-improves-outcomes-when-structured.md) [+M] used written tasks and the claim page does not report ages
rows.change: Reflection is oral or drawn, led by the teacher, one specific question at a time, immediately after the task; no written journal.
rows.if: `child` (primary school)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Drop or shorten reflection; spend the time on retrieval practice and feedback, with at most a one-line "which items did I miss?"
rows.if: Goal is `verbal-association` (facts, vocabulary)

rows.basis: [Reflection interventions in higher education](claims/reflective-practice-evidence-mixed-in-professional-education.md) [+M]; tested with `adult` learners in higher education, outcomes pooled
rows.change: Reflect on a recorded or observed performance against named criteria, then reattempt a comparable task; repeat over the course.
rows.if: Goal is a `complex-skill` or professional practice (teaching, clinical, design)

rows.basis: [Formative assessment with reflection](claims/formative-assessment-embedded-explicit-reflective-higher-posttest-nos-sks.md) [~W]; tested with prospective pre-school teachers
rows.change: Pair each reflection with a formative check and feedback on the learner's stated view; do not rely on reflection alone.
rows.if: Goal is `attitude-motivation` or a disposition (beliefs about a discipline)

rows.basis: [Structured reflection](claims/reflective-practice-improves-outcomes-when-structured.md) [+M]; tested in a classroom engineering course, untested self-paced
rows.change: Use task-specific prompts tied to that week's content, require a written next step, and open the next module by showing it back; flag entries that repeat word for word.
rows.if: `online-self-paced`, no teacher present

rows.basis: single session untested, from the earlier page; intervention duration is a moderator in [reflection interventions](claims/reflective-practice-evidence-mixed-in-professional-education.md) [~M], direction not stated on the claim page
rows.change: One session: one reflection of three prompts, about five minutes, at the end, ending in one change to try; no portfolio. A term: reflect after each comparable performance, keep the same criterion, and compare across attempts at least once.
rows.if: Time available: one session (`single-session`) or a `term-plus` course

rows.basis: [Guided vs free reflection](claims/guided-reflection-yields-more-higher-order-paragraphs-than-free.md) [~W], same study as [public vs private reflection](claims/public-vs-private-reflection-mixed.md) [~W]: private journals more analytic; one graduate service-learning course
rows.change: Grade the use of the criterion and whether the planned change was tried, not candour; offer a private channel for analysis of failures.
rows.if: Reflections are graded, or shared publicly

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Allow spoken or recorded reflection, or sentence frames; judge the analysis, not the prose.
rows.if: Learners write in a second language, or writing is a barrier

rows.basis: [Prior Knowledge Needed For Accurate Self Assessment](claims/prior-knowledge-needed-for-accurate-self-assessment.md) [~M] (synthesis of 22 meta-analyses; undergraduates' exam predictions); [Process goals lead to better skill acquisition for novices than outcome goals.](claims/process-goals-outperform-outcome-goals-for-novices.md) [~M] (writing revision, high school)
rows.change: Use a printed process checklist, checks that are tests (answer a question, rework a step) not ratings, every record co-checked in the first two sessions, and more sessions at the shared stage before hand-over
rows.if: Learners are `novice` on the task, or low achievers

rows.basis: Untested; the age and expertise moderators on the self-assessment claims ([Self Assessment Accuracy Is Low Without Training](claims/self-assessment-accuracy-is-low-without-training.md) [~M]: closer agreement in advanced courses) suggest it
rows.change: Start at the low-support stage: learner-chosen checkpoints, no printed checklist, a weekly outside check
rows.if: Learners are `advanced`, or their first checks already match an outside score

rows.basis: [Self Monitoring Improves On Task Behavior](claims/self-monitoring-improves-on-task-behavior.md) [+M] (single-case studies, grades 4–12, on-task behaviour only)
rows.change: Self-recording of on-task behaviour at short cued intervals (an app, a vibrating timer or a tone), after a training session; record the behaviour, not the learning, and check separately whether work completed changes
rows.if: Learners are `child` or `adolescent` with, or at risk for, attention difficulties or disabilities, and the problem is staying on task

rows.basis: [Self Monitoring Comprehension Improves Learning](claims/self-monitoring-comprehension-improves-learning.md) [+M] (one non-randomised study, 127 Nigerian senior-secondary students, raw gains 18.92 against 0.93; plus a meta-analysis of metacognitive strategy instruction, g = 0.50 at posttest and 0.63 at follow-up, of which monitoring is one part)
rows.change: Teach a comprehension-monitoring routine (stop, summarise, mark what is unclear, repair) over several weeks, with a stop at every section
rows.if: Goal is reading comprehension, learners are low-achieving secondary students

rows.basis: [Metacognitive prompts improve learning](claims/metacognitive-prompts-improve-learning.md) [+M] (meta-analysis in computer-based environments, g = 0.40 on learning outcomes, larger with feedback, task-specific and adaptive prompts); [diary alone](claims/learning-diary-alone-no-significant-srl-gains-online-math-prep-course.md) [-M]
rows.change: Build the checks into the software as task-specific prompts at natural pauses, each followed by an item with automatic feedback that shows the learner whether their judgement was right; do not rely on a free-text diary
rows.if: Setting is `online-self-paced`, no teacher present

rows.basis: Untested; the behaviour evidence is from individual students in single-case designs
rows.change: Run whole-class checkpoints on a common signal; every learner records on a one-line card; the teacher compares the cards of four or five learners per checkpoint with their work, rotating so each learner is checked at least weekly; whole-class feedback on the commonest mismatch
rows.if: `classroom` with one teacher and many learners

rows.basis: Untested proposal; the partner check stands in for the outside score in step 6, which [self-assessment accuracy is low without training](claims/self-assessment-accuracy-is-low-without-training.md) [~M] says is needed
rows.change: Keep the routine to two fixed pauses per session (one early, one midway) with a three-line card: what I am confident about and the check that shows it, what I am unsure about, my next move. Partners check each other's cards against the posted criteria (the task's own standard, or pictures of it); the group keeps one shared progress board; the facilitator looks at one pair's cards per pause instead of every record, and cards are kept, not graded
rows.if: Facilitator time is scarce: volunteers, busy shifts, a facilitator who drops in

rows.basis: Untested proposal; the check on the "know" line is what [judgments of learning are often inaccurate](claims/fluent-illusions-mislead-self-assessment.md) [-M] calls for
rows.change: Use that routine as the learner's script, word for word, at the checkpoints the brief sets; attach one quick check to the "what I know" line (redo the step, answer one item, compare with the standard) so a confident wrong answer is caught, and let the "unsure" line trigger the next move from the menu in step 4. Do not replace the requested routine with a different one
rows.if: The objective itself names a self-check routine (pause, say what I know, what I am unsure of, my next move)

rows.basis: Untested proposal
rows.change: Use one shared digital record for everyone (a form or poll with one tick per checkpoint and the check item beside it), so remote and in-room records are checked the same way; on a phone, keep the checklist to three items and the check to one tap or one short answer
rows.if: Mixed mode: some learners remote, some in the room, or learners on phones only

rows.basis: Untested proposal
rows.change: Teach and run the routine once on two or three items with every record checked; report the match between judgement and score; do not claim a habit or later effect
rows.if: Time is one session only

rows.basis: Untested proposal; underconfidence is described in the [self-assessment accuracy](claims/self-assessment-accuracy-is-low-without-training.md) [~M] claim's Discussion, not its entries
rows.change: Use pictures or a three-point face scale instead of written criteria, let learners show the check by doing (point to the error, redo the step), and point out where their judgement was right as well as where it was wrong; underconfident learners may stop using a strategy that is working
rows.if: Learners have low confidence, or low literacy

rows.basis: Untested proposal
rows.change: Write the checklist from the job's own standard (a procedure, a safety step, a quality criterion); keep records private to the learner and a supervisor, so the check is not read as surveillance; check against outcomes the work already produces (errors caught, rework)
rows.if: Adults in a work setting

rows.basis: Untested proposal
rows.change: Monitor drafts privately against the audience's criteria (what the reader or client needs) before anything is shown; the audience sees the product, not the checklist or the learner's ratings
rows.if: A product or performance for a real audience

rows.basis: [Judgments of learning are often inaccurate](claims/fluent-illusions-mislead-self-assessment.md) [-M] (laboratory and video-lecture experiments; carried here to adaptive and graded use)
rows.change: Never route a learner on a self-rating alone; use the check items' scores, and keep the self-ratings as data about calibration
rows.if: Stakes are high, or the self-record will feed a grade or an adaptive system

rows.basis: Untested; the self-assessment claim's Discussion says calibration is weaker on open-ended work, but its entries do not test it
rows.change: Give an annotated exemplar for each criterion and ask the learner to point to the evidence in their own draft for each, rather than score it
rows.if: Task is open-ended (an essay, a design) with no single right answer

rows.basis: [Instructional guidance that helps novices can become redundant or counterproductive as expertise grows.](claims/expertise-reversal-effect.md) [~M] (a review of cognitive-load studies; gives no point at which to switch)
rows.change: Skip the early stages; start at the first stage they cannot do unaided; drop the primer and the part-task runs; use problem-first and mixed practice from the start
rows.if: Learners are `advanced` on this target, or pass the prerequisite check

rows.basis: [Part-task practice reduces cognitive load for absolute novices during initial skill acquisition.](claims/part-task-practice-reduces-load-for-novices.md) [~M] (one experiment; the joining step is untested)
rows.change: Practise the two or three hardest parts in isolation first, then join them in a whole task within the same week
rows.if: Learners are absolute novices and the task's parts interact heavily (several decisions at once)

rows.basis: [Productive Failure Improves Conceptual Learning](claims/productive-failure-improves-conceptual-learning.md) [~S] (the meta-analysis's advantage reversed for second to fifth graders)
rows.change: Teach first, then practise; do not put problem solving before instruction
rows.if: Learners are children in the early primary grades

rows.basis: [Productive Failure Improves Conceptual Learning](claims/productive-failure-improves-conceptual-learning.md) [~S] (no difference on procedural knowledge; mostly mathematics and physics)
rows.change: Put a short problem-solving attempt before instruction, then teach from learners' attempts; judge it on conceptual and transfer items, not on procedural ones
rows.if: Goal is conceptual understanding or transfer (a `concept` or `principle`), learners older than the early primary grades

rows.basis: [Example–problem sequences reduce cognitive load and improve learning outcomes](claims/example-problem-sequences-reduce-cognitive-load.md) [+M] (secondary-school novices, circuit troubleshooting, immediate test); the advantage was not detected at the final test with identical pairs ([identical pairs](claims/identical-example-problem-order-advantage-not-detected-at-final-test.md) [~M])
rows.change: Show a worked example before the first problem, then alternate example and problem
rows.if: Goal is a `procedure`, `novice` learners, an immediate test

rows.basis: [Interleaving category examples improves inductive category learning for visual and mathematical materials](claims/interleaving-improves-inductive-learning.md) [~M] (classification tests; reversed for word categories, no benefit for expository texts)
rows.change: Block each new category for a few items, then mix them; test with mixed items at a delay
rows.if: Goal is telling confusable categories or problem types apart

rows.basis: [Pretraining learners on a system's key parts and terms before the main lesson improved knowledge and real-world transfer in one VR experiment](claims/pretraining-improves-transfer.md) [+M] (one VR experiment against no pretraining; carried to other media untested)
rows.change: Give a primer of a few minutes naming the parts and what each does, before the lesson
rows.if: The main lesson is a simulation, demonstration or new tool, and learners do not know its parts

rows.basis: [Refutational text enhanced free recall relative to traditional text](claims/refutational-text-order-enhances-retention.md) [+M] (one experiment with written science text; carried to spoken teaching untested)
rows.change: State the misbelief, then the fact that refutes it, in that order
rows.if: Learners arrive with a known misconception

rows.basis: [Ability moderates the hierarchical-organization advantage](claims/ability-moderates-hierarchical-organization-benefit.md) [~M] (one physics report: low-ability students showed no benefit)
rows.change: Keep the general-ideas-first opening, but add prerequisite checks and corrective rounds at each stage; do not rely on the organisation alone
rows.if: Learners have low prior attainment in the subject

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Put a step they can succeed at first in each session; teach terms in the primer, before they are needed; show a step by doing it before reading about it
rows.if: Learners have low confidence or low literacy

rows.basis: untested proposal; [skill develops through engaging in the target activity](claims/skill-develops-through-engagement-not-drill.md) [~W] (an argument from second-language acquisition, no study)
rows.change: Order by the job's own sequence where it has one, start from a task they already do, and bring forward the steps they need soonest at work
rows.if: Adults in a work setting

rows.basis: untested proposal; [whole-task argument](claims/whole-task-performance-improves-transfer.md) [~W] (a design argument, no study); [4C/ID](patterns/4cid-four-component-instructional-design.md) is the full sequence
rows.change: Keep the whole task as the unit at every stage and simplify the version of the whole, not split it into paper items; isolate a part only where learners stall on it, then put it straight back
rows.if: The target is a whole-task performance the brief wants kept whole (a full procedure, a performance for a real audience, a product)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Build the prerequisite check and the move-on rule into the software or the materials: each stage ends with two unaided items that unlock the next or route back
rows.if: `online-self-paced`, no teacher present

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Keep one shared order and one shared check per stage; send the primer and the map as a short item readable on a phone before the session; give remote learners the same stage-end items in a form they can answer by message
rows.if: Mixed modes (some learners remote, some in the room; phone-only learners)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Give the prerequisite check and the stage-end items to everyone at once (cards, a quick poll), keep one main order for the class, and give a short branch (back to a prerequisite, or ahead to mixed practice) to the learners the check sorts out
rows.if: One teacher for many learners

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Put the order in the materials so learners can follow it alone; spend the facilitator's time only at the stage gates, on the learners who did not pass
rows.if: Scarce facilitator time (volunteers, a busy shift, one brief check-in)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Order the session as primer or map (5 minutes), one example, guided items, one unaided check; teach only as many stages as the check can confirm, and do not claim retention
rows.if: A single session only

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Fit the order to the minutes: cut stages rather than compress them, keep the move-on check, and put the rest of the map on a list for later sessions
rows.if: A fixed short time budget (for example 20 minutes a day, or two sessions where three were planned)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Keep its order and categories; change only what the evidence says matters (a prerequisite check before a stage, an example before the first problem, a mixed review once categories are met, an explicit transition)
rows.if: The brief names its own sequence, scope and sequence, syllabus or categories

rows.basis: untested proposal; one emotional-literacy curriculum is described as ordered cognitive to behavioural to affective and external to internal ([PATHS within-lesson order](claims/paths-within-lesson-cognitive-to-affective-sequencing.md) [+W], a document analysis, no outcome); see [affective sequencing](principles/affective-sequencing-requires-own-principles.md)
rows.change: Move from others' or fictional cases to the learner's own experience, from recognising to reflecting; let the learner decide whether and with whom to share their own
rows.if: Content is personal or sensitive (emotions, identity, experience of harm)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Do not move on by the calendar; require unaided success at each stage on representative tasks, and keep a cumulative check of earlier stages in every later one
rows.if: Stakes are high or errors are costly (safety, compliance, a licensing exam)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Use the brief's stages as the skeleton and change only what the evidence speaks to inside them: what each stage checks before moving on, where a worked example or partial task goes, and how the trainer samples work when alone with a group; keep time reserved for the brief's own final assessment
rows.if: The brief already names its stages or order ("first the screens, then one field, then a full note")

rows.basis: [Group rewards combined with individual accountability](claims/cooperative-learning-group-rewards-and-individual-accountability.md) [+M] (64 at-risk 4th and 5th graders, maths computation; reward plus structure best; effect figures second-hand)
rows.change: Use pairs with scripted tutor and tutee roles, switching each session; team score = sum of both members' daily individual quiz scores
rows.if: Learners are `child` (upper primary), or at risk of failure

rows.basis: [Cooperative learning improves achievement](claims/cooperative-learning-improves-achievement.md) [+S] (meta-analysis of 148 studies of early adolescents, direction only; Learning Together method d = 0.70–0.91 from an unpublished report)
rows.change: Use cooperative goal structures as the default arrangement for multi-week units, with individual checks feeding a team score
rows.if: Learners are `adolescent` (early secondary)

rows.basis: [Small group learning improves STEM achievement](claims/small-group-learning-improves-stem-achievement.md) [+M] (39 undergraduate STEM studies, d = 0.51; compared groups with non-group instruction and does not isolate interdependence)
rows.change: Use small structured groups for problem sets, labs and design tasks, with individual assessment kept separate from the group product
rows.if: Learners are `adult` / `postsecondary`, in a live course

rows.basis: [Interdependence type did not affect posttest achievement](claims/interdependence-type-no-achievement-effect-asynchronous.md) [~M] (280 undergraduate business majors, triads; non-significant, no effect size); [more interactions went with higher posttest scores](claims/interaction-quantity-correlates-posttest-online-groups.md) [+W] (same study, correlational)
rows.change: Do not rely on assigned roles or a group reward to raise achievement; require each member to post a stated number of contributions that respond to others', and assess individually
rows.if: Setting is `online-self-paced` or asynchronous online groups

rows.basis: [Structured interdependence and obligation to contribute](claims/structured-interdependence-contribution-obligation-attitude.md) [+M]; [reward interdependence and benefit attitudes](claims/reward-interdependence-benefit-attitudes.md) [+M] (self-report, same online study; not achievement)
rows.change: Assign roles or a group reward: members in any structured condition agreed more that teammates' duty to contribute helped them learn; reward groups agreed more that they gained from others
rows.if: The aim includes participation, sense of obligation or attitudes to group work

rows.basis: untested proposal; improvement-based scoring from the Discussion of [group rewards combined with individual accountability](claims/cooperative-learning-group-rewards-and-individual-accountability.md) [~M], not from its entries
rows.change: Teach and model the content first; use interdependence for practice and explanation, not first acquisition; set improvement-based team scores so low starters can contribute
rows.if: Learners are `novice` on the content, or members differ widely in what they know

rows.basis: untested; the reward evidence comes from programmes of four weeks or more ([free-riding without accountability](claims/cooperative-learning-group-rewards-and-individual-accountability.md) [~M])
rows.change: Use pairs, one short shared task, and an individual check at the end; do not claim an achievement effect
rows.if: Time is one session only

rows.basis: [Pairs worked better than triads in one inquiry](claims/pairs-better-than-triads-in-stellar-inquiry.md) [~W] (authors' teaching experience, one astronomy activity, no measured outcome)
rows.change: Prefer pairs for tightly coupled tasks and three or four for tasks needing several skills; watch for a member drifting out in larger groups
rows.if: Group size is open

rows.basis: [Secondary-school review: STAD most and Jigsaw least successful](claims/secondary-cooperative-learning-newmann-thompson.md) [~M] (review of 27 secondary studies; the link to missing reward and accountability is the authors' speculation)
rows.change: Add an individual quiz on all segments and a team score from it, so experts are rewarded for teaching, not only for presenting
rows.if: The structure is Jigsaw or another resource-only design

rows.basis: [Free-riding without individual accountability](claims/cooperative-learning-group-rewards-and-individual-accountability.md) [~M] (school studies; carried to high-stakes settings untested)
rows.change: Never give every member the same grade for one product; grade the group from individual results, or grade individually and report the group product separately
rows.if: Stakes are high (the group grade counts toward a qualification)

rows.basis: [Social interdependence, not role interdependence, correlated with performance](claims/social-interdependence-predicts-performance.md) [~W] (40 brokerage offices, correlational; "social interdependence" there means team belonging, not goal structure)
rows.change: Build belonging and shared goals (harmony, a sense of one team) rather than formal role dependence alone; measure what each member can do
rows.if: Learners are `adult-workplace` teams

rows.basis: [High affiliation motive and attitudes to group work](claims/high-affiliation-motive-favorable-group-attitudes.md) [~M] (attitudes differed, achievement did not; online undergraduates); culture untested, from the earlier page
rows.change: Explain how the team score works and why, before the first cycle; let them see that their own score is counted in it; expect less favourable attitudes at first, not lower achievement
rows.if: Some learners expect individual, competitive evaluation, or are low in affiliation motive

rows.basis: [Online community required deliberate, planned effort](claims/online-community-requires-conscious-effort.md) [+W] (interviews with web-based high-school teachers; carried to adult courses); the steps are untested
rows.change: Run the full default: course-tied introductions with two named replies, weekly named announcements, small stable groups, a reply frame, one optional live meeting a fortnight at a time outside working hours, recorded
rows.if: `online-instructor-led`, asynchronous, text-only, `adult` learners who work or care for others

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Put remote and in-room learners in the same small groups, with a shared text chat for each group; in plenary, take a remote contribution after each in-room one; ask in-room learners to introduce themselves in the same shared space as remote ones, so the remote learners see who is in the room
rows.if: Mixed mode: some learners in the room, some joining remotely

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Make every presence activity possible by text or a short voice note; never require video or a photo; keep live meetings to audio with chat
rows.if: Learners work on phones only, or have poor bandwidth

rows.basis: untested proposal; the earlier page says benefits shrink at large enrolment. Structuring roles or rewards in online triads did not change achievement in one experiment ([Structuring positive interdependence did not affect posttest achievement](claims/interdependence-type-no-achievement-effect-asynchronous.md) [~M]; undergraduates, a non-significant difference, not equivalence)
rows.change: Do not promise personal replies to all; make presence a property of small groups (4–6, kept for several weeks, with rotating roles) and of a weekly whole-course message that quotes or names a few contributions; let peers answer peers first
rows.if: One instructor for many learners (a large online course, a MOOC)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Spend it on three things only: a templated but personal welcome, one weekly message naming a few contributions, and one private message to anyone silent after week 2 (about 30–45 minutes a week for 20 learners); hand reply-giving to peer roles; skip live meetings rather than run them badly
rows.if: Scarce facilitator time (a volunteer tutor, a teacher on a busy shift, one brief check-in a week)

rows.basis: untested proposal; the earlier page says benefits shrink in short settings
rows.change: Replace profiles with a 3–5-minute paired introduction that asks each person what they want from the session and one related experience, then use those answers in the session's first task
rows.if: A single session only (a workshop, a one-off training)

rows.basis: [Positive teacher–student relationships are associated with greater student engagement and, more weakly, with achievement](claims/teacher-student-relationships-improve-engagement.md) [+M] (correlational meta-analyses, preschool to high school, plus a learner-centred synthesis; not a test of any routine)
rows.change: Presence cues are already there; spend effort on names, on the teacher's warmth and expectations, and on routines that let quiet pupils be heard (pairs before plenary), not on profiles
rows.if: Face-to-face `classroom`

rows.basis: [Teacher–student relationships](claims/teacher-student-relationships-improve-engagement.md) [+M] (associations; negative relationships mattered more in primary school); the routines are untested
rows.change: No public photos or personal profiles; introductions through a class activity the teacher runs (what I like, what I am good at); presence comes mainly from the teacher's relationship with each pupil, built in short regular contacts
rows.if: Learners are `child` or `adolescent`

rows.basis: [Belonging Interventions Improve Outcomes](claims/belonging-interventions-improve-outcomes.md) [~M] (college entrants, randomised; worked only where the setting afforded opportunities to belong); [peer contact judged needed against isolation in online supervision](claims/virtual-communities-counter-supervision-isolation.md) [+W] (one design case)
rows.change: Offer a private, low-risk first contact (small group only, audio, a short call); say early that difficulty and doubt are common and pass; follow up by name after a quiet week; make sure there are real chances to be part of the group, not only a message
rows.if: Learners with low confidence or literacy, first in family, or at risk of isolation or dropping out

rows.basis: [Peer monitoring among MBA learners goes beyond CoI social presence by involving professionally relevant evaluation of peers' contributions](claims/peer-monitoring-exceeds-social-presence.md) [~W] (interviews with six MBA students)
rows.change: Make introductions professional: role, expertise, a problem from their work they want help with; group learners so their expertise complements; let them judge peers by what they offer, and build peer review of work on that
rows.if: Adults in work settings or professional programmes (an MBA, clinical or workplace training)

rows.basis: untested; from the earlier page's constraint that forced self-disclosure can reduce trust across cultural contexts
rows.change: The learner controls what is shared and who sees it: disclosure optional at every step, a professional-only introduction always acceptable, small-group rather than whole-course spaces for anything personal, and no grade for personal disclosure
rows.if: Private or sensitive material, or norms that discourage self-disclosure (cultural, professional, a history of harm)

rows.basis: [Discussion boards produced no corrective feedback](claims/discussion-board-no-negative-feedback-synchrony-required.md) [-W] (one study of second-language learners); [Audio discussions produced no significant change in willingness to communicate](claims/audio-discussions-no-significant-wtc-change.md) [~W] (36 language students, self-report; non-significant, not equivalence)
rows.change: Use a synchronous channel (text chat or video) where correction and negotiation are wanted, and the forum for prepared posts; offer voice notes as an introduction mode
rows.if: Learners study in a second language, or the goal includes spoken interaction

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Have them post first in their small group or as a draft that peers comment on before the whole class sees it; the instructor replies to the attempt, not only to the correct posts
rows.if: `novice` learners on the content, afraid of being wrong in public

rows.basis: [Peer monitoring](claims/peer-monitoring-exceeds-social-presence.md) [~W] (MBA interviews); otherwise untested
rows.change: Shorten the social opening; move quickly to peer critique of each other's work and decisions; presence comes from the value of what peers offer
rows.if: `advanced` learners or experienced professionals

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Keep it; change only what the evidence points to: make disclosure optional, add one step that asks for a named reply to a peer, and tie its output to the next task
rows.if: The brief names its own routine for presence (its introduction activity, a weekly check-in, a discussion template or rubric)

rows.basis: untested; interaction counts are associated with posttest scores ([interaction quantity](claims/interaction-quantity-correlates-posttest-online-groups.md) [+W]), which is not a reason to reward volume
rows.change: Use those criteria to judge and give feedback on posts; do not add a separate score for social presence, and do not grade posts by count
